course.title: Genetics: From Genes to Genomes
course.description: How a gene's sequence becomes a protein, how variants and inheritance patterns behave in families and populations, and what genetic tests, genome scans, gene editing and epigenetics can and cannot show. Each lesson practises one judgement a geneticist or genetic counsellor makes.
course.audience: Adults who have finished Biology: Cells to Ecosystems (DNA copying, meiosis, single-gene Punnett squares, mutation and selection in outline) and are comfortable multiplying and adding chances and reading ratios. No chemistry beyond that is needed.

paragraphs: How a gene's sequence becomes a protein, how variants and inheritance patterns behave in families and populations, and what genetic tests, genome scans, gene editing and epigenetics can and cannot show. Each lesson practises one judgement a geneticist or genetic counsellor makes.
outcomes: You'll be able to read a coding sequence with the codon table and say what a change to it does to a protein.
You'll be able to predict gene expression from conditions and mutations in a simple regulatory circuit.
You'll be able to infer genotypes from offspring counts, recombination frequencies and pedigrees, and work out a carrier chance.
You'll be able to use Hardy-Weinberg proportions to estimate carriers and to read a departure from them.
You'll be able to choose between chance and selection for a change in allele frequency and say what evidence would decide.
You'll be able to say what a genetic test result, a genome-wide association or a polygenic score does and does not tell a person.
introduction.prerequisites: It builds on Biology: Cells to Ecosystems, Probability and Statistics.

modules.title: From DNA to protein
modules.description: What a genome holds, how a gene's sequence is read into a protein, and how cells decide which genes to read.

modules.title: Mutation and single-gene inheritance
modules.description: What different changes do to a protein, and how to read offspring counts to infer genotypes and gene interactions.

modules.title: Inheritance in families
modules.description: Linked genes, pedigrees and carrier chances, and traits that have many causes.

modules.title: Genes in populations
modules.description: Allele frequencies, Hardy-Weinberg as a null model, and the roles of chance and selection.

modules.title: Genomes in practice
modules.description: Reading genetic tests, genome scans and risk scores, weighing gene editing, and judging epigenetic claims.

concepts.title: Gene
concepts.summary: A stretch of DNA that is a unit of heredity; about 19,900 human genes code for proteins and many others make RNA or help control other genes.

concepts.title: Allele and variant
concepts.summary: Alleles are forms of the same gene that differ in sequence; a variant is any permanent change in the DNA sequence, and most variants have no effect on health.

concepts.title: Noncoding DNA
concepts.summary: About 99 percent of human DNA does not code for protein, and some of it holds regulatory elements, RNA genes and chromosome structures.

concepts.title: SNP
concepts.summary: A single-letter difference found in at least 1 percent of people; most lie between genes and have no effect, but they can act as markers.

concepts.title: Gene expression
concepts.summary: Transcription copies a gene's information into messenger RNA; translation reads that mRNA to build a protein.

concepts.title: Codon and reading frame
concepts.summary: A codon is three nucleotides; reading proceeds in non-overlapping triplets from the start, so the frame fixes every amino acid.

concepts.title: Start and stop codons
concepts.summary: AUG starts translation and reads as methionine; three codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) code for no amino acid and end the chain.

concepts.title: Degeneracy
concepts.summary: Several codons can name the same amino acid, but no codon names two; changes at the third position are often silent.

concepts.title: Gene regulation
concepts.summary: Each cell expresses only some of its genes at a time; control is mostly at transcription, where regulatory proteins raise or lower it.

concepts.title: Repressor and operator
concepts.summary: In the lac operon a repressor protein bound to the operator blocks RNA polymerase; lactose binding releases it.

concepts.title: Cis and trans
concepts.summary: A regulatory DNA sequence acts only on genes on the same DNA (cis); a diffusible protein can act on both copies in a cell (trans).

concepts.title: Enhancers and transcription factors
concepts.summary: In eukaryotes, enhancers bind tissue-specific factors, so different cell types switch on different genes from the same DNA.

concepts.title: Silent, missense and nonsense
concepts.summary: A substitution may keep the amino acid (silent), swap it (missense) or create a stop (nonsense).

concepts.title: Insertions, deletions and the frame
concepts.summary: An insertion or deletion that is not a multiple of three shifts every codon downstream (frameshift); a multiple of three adds or removes whole amino acids.

concepts.title: Loss and gain of function
concepts.summary: Alleles lose function completely (amorph) or partly (hypomorph), gain more of it (hypermorph), gain a new one (neomorph) or poison the normal product (antimorph).

concepts.title: Haplosufficient and haploinsufficient
concepts.summary: If one good copy makes enough product the null allele is recessive; if not, it is dominant.

concepts.title: Test cross
concepts.summary: Crossing an individual of unknown genotype to a homozygous recessive reveals its genotype from the offspring ratio.

concepts.title: Incomplete dominance and codominance
concepts.summary: In incomplete dominance the heterozygote is intermediate; in codominance it shows both alleles at once.

concepts.title: Dihybrid ratios and epistasis
concepts.summary: Independent loci give 9:3:3:1; when one locus masks another the classes merge (9:3:4, 12:3:1).

concepts.title: Sex linkage and reciprocal crosses
concepts.summary: Reciprocal crosses that differ, with sons and daughters unlike, point to an X-linked gene in a hemizygous male.

concepts.title: Linkage
concepts.summary: Loci close together on one chromosome tend to be inherited together, an exception to independent assortment.

concepts.title: Recombination frequency
concepts.summary: The share of gametes (or test-cross offspring) that carry a combination not found in the parents' chromosomes; about 50 percent for unlinked loci and the most that can be observed.

concepts.title: Coupling and repulsion
concepts.summary: A dihybrid AaBb may carry AB and ab together (coupling) or Ab and aB (repulsion); the parents' genotypes decide which offspring are recombinant.

concepts.title: Map units
concepts.summary: A recombination frequency of 1 percent is about 1 centiMorgan, accurate for short distances; double crossovers hide recombination at long ones.

concepts.title: Pedigree
concepts.summary: A family tree of one trait, with circles for females, squares for males, filled symbols for affected people and a proband who brought the family to attention.

concepts.title: Features of each mode
concepts.summary: Autosomal dominant: every affected person has an affected parent. Autosomal recessive: unaffected parents can have affected children. X-linked recessive: mostly males, never an affected daughter of an unaffected father.

concepts.title: Carrier probability
concepts.summary: An unaffected child of two carriers is a carrier with probability 2/3; chances along a chain multiply (and alternatives add).

concepts.title: Each pregnancy independent
concepts.summary: Chances for a recessive condition are 1/4 per pregnancy whatever happened before.

concepts.title: Penetrance
concepts.summary: The share of people with a particular variant who show the associated trait or disorder.

concepts.title: Expressivity
concepts.summary: The range of severity among people with the same variant.

concepts.title: Heritability
concepts.summary: A statistic for how much of the variation in a trait, in one population and environment, goes with genetic differences; it is not the share of a trait caused by genes.

concepts.title: Polygenic and multifactorial
concepts.summary: Many variants of small effect plus environment, with no clear-cut inheritance pattern.

concepts.title: Allele frequency
concepts.summary: The share of copies of a gene that are one allele; for two alleles p + q = 1, found by counting alleles (homozygotes count twice).

concepts.title: Hardy-Weinberg proportions
concepts.summary: With random mating and no other forces, genotypes occur as p squared, 2pq and q squared after one generation.

concepts.title: Carrier estimate
concepts.summary: For a rare recessive condition the carrier frequency is close to 2q, where q is the square root of the incidence.

concepts.title: Departures
concepts.summary: Fewer heterozygotes than 2pq suggest inbreeding or population mixing; allele frequency changes over time suggest selection, drift, migration or mutation.

concepts.title: Genetic drift
concepts.summary: Chance change in allele frequency from random sampling; it has no direction and acts faster in small populations.

concepts.title: Bottleneck and founder effect
concepts.summary: A population that shrinks, or a small group that splits off, keeps a random sample of the alleles.

concepts.title: Selection versus drift
concepts.summary: Selection pushes frequencies in a direction that depends on effects on survival and reproduction; drift can overwhelm weak selection in small populations.

concepts.title: Heterozygote advantage
concepts.summary: If carriers survive better than either homozygote, the allele is kept even though one homozygote is disabled.

concepts.title: Kinds of test
concepts.summary: Targeted single-variant, single-gene, panel, exome or genome sequencing, chromosomal, expression and biochemical tests answer different questions.

concepts.title: What a result means
concepts.summary: A positive result shows a variant, not a diagnosis or a date; a negative result means only that the test found nothing it can detect; some results are uninformative.

concepts.title: Variant classes
concepts.summary: Variants are classed pathogenic, likely pathogenic, of uncertain significance, likely benign or benign, and the class can change as evidence grows.

concepts.title: Validity and utility
concepts.summary: Analytical validity is whether the test detects the variant; clinical validity whether the variant matters for disease; clinical utility whether the result helps care.

concepts.title: Genome-wide association study
concepts.summary: Compare allele frequencies at a million or more SNPs between cases and controls; report an odds ratio and a p-value for each.

concepts.title: Significance threshold
concepts.summary: Because so many SNPs are tested, a p-value below 5×10⁻⁸ is required.

concepts.title: Tag SNPs
concepts.summary: An associated SNP may only travel with the causal variant, so fine-mapping is needed.

concepts.title: Polygenic risk score
concepts.summary: A sum over many small-effect variants that ranks relative risk; it gives no baseline or timing and works best in the ancestry it was built on.

concepts.title: Cas9 and guide RNA
concepts.summary: A guide RNA matches a target sequence and Cas9 cuts the DNA there; Cas9 also needs a short adjacent site (PAM, NGG) that occurs every 8 to 12 base pairs.

concepts.title: Two repair routes
concepts.summary: End joining leaves random insertions or deletions (knockout); homology-directed repair with a supplied template inserts a chosen sequence (knock-in); base editors change single bases without a template.

concepts.title: What can go wrong
concepts.summary: Off-target cuts, immune response to bacterial parts, vector capacity and mosaicism limit use.

concepts.title: Somatic and germline edits
concepts.summary: Edits in body cells stay in one person, while edits in eggs, sperm or embryos can be inherited, which raises ethical concerns that body-cell edits do not.

concepts.title: Epigenetic marks
concepts.summary: DNA methylation and histone modification change how a gene is expressed without changing the DNA sequence, and can be copied when cells divide.

concepts.title: X inactivation and imprinting
concepts.summary: One X is silenced at random in each cell of a female; imprinted genes are expressed according to which parent supplied them.

concepts.title: Reprogramming
concepts.summary: Most marks are erased after fertilisation and in germ-cell precursors, so inheritance across generations needs marks to escape both.

concepts.title: First generation free of exposure
concepts.summary: Proposed criteria require an effect in generations with no direct exposure: F2 or later for fathers, F3 or later for pregnant mothers.

lessons.title: Genes, variants and the rest of the genome

lead.text: A **gene** is a unit of heredity made of DNA, and in humans it runs from a few hundred base pairs to more than 2 million. Some genes carry the instructions for a protein, and about 19,900 human genes do. Many other genes code for no protein at all and help to control other genes instead.

afterFigure.text: The coding parts of the genome are a small share of it, about 1 percent of the DNA, which leaves about 99 percent noncoding. Differences between people are smaller still. A person carries roughly 4 to 5 million single-base differences called SNPs, which the second view shows is only a position or two in every thousand.

diagram.alt: Two views of the human genome as a bar of about 3 billion bases. The first marks the 1 percent that is protein-coding and the 99 percent that is noncoding. The second zooms in on 1,000 positions to show that about 1 or 2 of them are SNPs in one person.
diagram.caption: The first view shows how small the coding share is. The second shows how few positions differ in one person. Use the buttons to switch.

reveal.text: The headline is true, and the share is small. Differences at under 0.2 percent of positions leave more than 99 percent of bases the same.

lead.text: A person usually carries two copies of each gene, one from each parent. Nearly all genes are identical across people, and fewer than 1 percent differ slightly from one person to another. The different versions of a gene, whose DNA sequences differ in small ways, are called **alleles**.

A **variant** is any permanent change in the DNA sequence. It can alter one base or several, and it can lie inside a gene or elsewhere in the genome. The older name was mutation, and variant is now preferred because a change need not lead to disease. Few variants cause a genetic disorder, and most do nothing to health or development.

The phrase 'the cystic fibrosis gene' shows why the words need care. The gene CFTR lies on chromosome 7, and variants in it can cause cystic fibrosis. Someone who is said to have the cystic fibrosis gene has a version of CFTR that carries a variant causing the disease, and everyone, including people without cystic fibrosis, has a version of CFTR. Genes do not cause disease. Disorders arise from variants that alter or remove a gene's function.

reveal.text: Naming the variant, and not the gene, says what is different about a person.

lead.text: Noncoding DNA gives no instructions for making proteins. Scientists once called it junk, but at least part of it is now known to be essential to how cells work, particularly in controlling genes.

Some noncoding sequences are **regulatory elements**. They give proteins called transcription factors a place to attach, and so decide when, and in which cells, a gene is active. A promoter, typically just ahead of a gene, is where the machinery that reads the gene attaches. An enhancer helps to activate a gene and can lie before or after it, sometimes far away. Other noncoding stretches are genes for RNA that is never made into a protein, such as the transfer and ribosomal RNAs that help assemble amino acids into a chain, the microRNAs that block protein production and the long noncoding RNAs that help regulate genes. Further sequences give chromosomes their structure, such as the telomeres at their ends.

Inside a protein-coding gene, the noncoding stretches called **introns** are removed before a protein is made, and a regulatory element such as an enhancer can sit in one. The regions between genes are called intergenic.

afterFigure.text: How much of the 99 percent has a function is not yet known, because the identity of many regulatory and other functional regions is still being worked out.

lead.text: A single-base change does different things depending on where it falls, so the first question to ask about a variant is where it lies on the map. A change inside the coding part of a protein-coding gene can alter an amino acid, or leave it as it was, because several codons can name the same amino acid. A change in a regulatory element leaves the protein's amino acids alone and can alter when or how much of the protein is made. A change in a gene for a non-protein RNA can alter that RNA. A change between genes, or in an intron where no regulatory element sits, most likely does nothing.

afterFigure.text: Location gives a first guess about a variant and does not settle it. Only a small percentage of variants cause disorders, so even a change inside a gene often has no effect, and a change in a regulatory element can matter.

diagram.alt: The same strip of DNA with each kind of place coloured by what a change there can affect: exons by the amino acids, the promoter and enhancer by when or how much protein is made, the RNA gene by that RNA, and the intervening DNA by most likely nothing.
diagram.caption: What a change can affect depends on where it falls.

reveal.text: A variant in an intron is not read as a codon, which leaves open that it can still change how the gene is controlled.

lead.text: A **SNP**, short for single nucleotide polymorphism, is a difference in one DNA building block that at least 1 percent of people carry. A SNP may, for example, put a T in place of a C at one position. More than 600 million SNPs are known from people across the world, and one person carries roughly 4 to 5 million of them.

Most SNPs lie in the DNA between genes, and most do nothing to health or development. A SNP between genes can still be useful, because it can act as a biological marker that helps scientists locate genes associated with disease. When a SNP sits inside a gene, or in a regulatory region close to one, it can affect the gene more directly.

reveal.text: A marker only points to a region, and working out which part of the region matters takes further evidence.

lessons.orientation: Place a DNA difference on the genome's map (protein-coding exon, regulatory sequence, RNA gene or the DNA between genes), judge how likely it is to matter, and use the words gene, allele and variant correctly.
lessons.reviewLabel: Genes, variants and the rest of the genome
lessons.nextAction: Translate a coding sequence into amino acids with the codon table.

blocks.text: The human genome is about 3 billion bases long. About 19,900 of its genes make proteins, yet only about 1 percent of the DNA is protein-coding, so the genes that draw the most attention cover a small part of the whole.

A person's genome also carries roughly 4 to 5 million single-base differences called SNPs, and where one of them falls decides whether it can matter at all. Knowing the map of the genome, and keeping the words gene, allele and variant apart, is what lets you judge a difference when you meet one.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to place a DNA change on the genome's map and say what it can do.
intro.whyItMatters: Most DNA differences do nothing, so knowing where one falls tells you whether it deserves attention.

recap.keyIdea: A gene is a stretch of DNA, an allele is one version of it and a variant is a change in the sequence, and where a variant falls on the genome's map tells you what it can do.

blocks.text: About 99 percent of the genome is noncoding, and that DNA holds regulatory elements, genes for RNA that is never made into protein, and structural sequences. A person carries 4 to 5 million SNPs, under 0.2 percent of 3 billion positions, and most lie between genes and have no effect.

To judge a difference, ask where it falls. In coding sequence it can change amino acids, in a regulatory element it can change when or how much protein is made, in an RNA gene it can change that RNA, and anywhere else it most likely does nothing.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson reads the genetic code itself, to see how a change inside a coding sequence becomes a change in a protein.

lessons.title: Reading the genetic code

lead.text: A gene makes a protein in two steps that together are called **gene expression**. In **transcription**, a gene's DNA is copied into a related molecule, RNA, in the nucleus. The RNA that carries the instructions for a protein is called messenger RNA, or **mRNA**, because it takes the message out of the nucleus into the cytoplasm.

In **translation**, which takes place in the cytoplasm, a ribosome reads the mRNA. Each sequence of three nucleotides is a **codon**, and a codon usually names one particular amino acid. Transfer RNA brings in the amino acids that build the protein, one at a time, until the ribosome meets a stop codon, a group of three nucleotides that names no amino acid. Information passes from DNA to RNA to protein in this way, a principle sometimes called the central dogma.

diagram.alt: A flow diagram. A gene in DNA inside the nucleus is transcribed into mRNA, which carries the message into the cytoplasm, where a ribosome translates it into a chain of amino acids called a protein.
diagram.caption: Transcription happens in the nucleus and translation in the cytoplasm.

lead.text: There are 64 possible codons, since each of the three positions can hold any of four bases. The table that matches codons to amino acids is the **genetic code**. In the figure the first base is on the left, the second base runs along the top and the third base is listed inside each box. The NCBI prints its table with T where an mRNA has U, following the convention of GenBank records, so the figure writes U to match the mRNA you will read.

afterFigure.text: Reading the table takes three lookups. For the codon CAU, the first base C picks the second row, the second base A picks the third column, and the third base U picks the first line of that box, which gives His. Of the 64 codons, 61 name an amino acid and 3 are stop codons: UAA, UAG and UGA. AUG names methionine, Met, and it is also the most common start codon.

diagram.alt: The standard genetic code as a table of 64 codons. Rows give the first base, columns the second base, and the lines inside each box the third base, each followed by the amino acid it names. The three stop codons and the start codon AUG are marked.
diagram.caption: The standard code, written with U as in an mRNA. Stop codons are marked in orange and AUG in green.

lead.text: Reading begins at a start codon, and the most common one is AUG, which is read as methionine. A protein-coding frame is usually set by the first AUG in the mRNA. From there the ribosome reads groups of three that do not overlap, so the first codon fixes the **reading frame**: each later codon is the next three bases after the one before it.

A sequence can be read in three frames, depending on which base starts the first group, and each frame can give a different chain of amino acids. Reading ends at a stop codon, which no transfer RNA matches, so the chain is released and any bases after the stop are not translated.

diagram.alt: One mRNA of 18 bases shown read in three frames. From the first base the codons give Met, Lys, Trp, His and then a stop. From the second base the first codon is a stop. From the third base the codons give Glu, Met, Ala, Leu and Arg.
diagram.caption: The same 18 bases read from the first, second and third base. Grey bases are outside the codons, and dashed boxes come after a stop.

steps.headline: Translate the mRNA `AUGCGUGCCAAUUGACAG` from its start codon, and say how many amino acids it makes.

workedSteps.text: The mRNA begins with the start codon AUG, so reading starts at the first base. Split it into codons: `AUG CGU GCC AAU UGA CAG`.
Look each codon up in the table: `AUG` is Met, `CGU` is Arg, `GCC` is Ala and `AAU` is Asn.
The fifth codon, `UGA`, is a stop codon, so translation ends there.
The chain is Met-Arg-Ala-Asn, which is 4 amino acids long, and `CAG` after the stop is never read.

steps.headline: Translate the mRNA `CGAUGCCUUGGAGUAAUCGAUAG` and say which stop codon ends the chain.

workedSteps.text: Reading begins at the first AUG, not at the first base. The AUG starts at the third base here, so the first two bases, `CG`, are left out.
Split the rest into codons from the AUG, `AUG CCU UGG AGU AAU CGA UAG`, and look up each codon up to the first stop.
Check where the chain ends. Some stop-like triplets in the sequence do not line up with the frame.
The chain is 6 amino acids long, and the bases after the stop are not read.

lead.text: The table has 61 codons that name amino acids but only 20 amino acids, so most amino acids have more than one codon. This is called **degeneracy**, the redundancy of the code. It is redundancy without ambiguity: the codons GAA and GAG both name glutamic acid, but neither names another amino acid, and no codon names two.

The codons for one amino acid often differ only at the third base. In eight of the sixteen boxes of the table, among them those for glycine, alanine and proline, all four codons name the same amino acid, so a change at the third base is always silent there. Counting every single-base change among the 61 codons that name amino acids shows how the position matters: about 7 in 10 changes at the third base leave the amino acid as it was, a few changes at the first base do, and none at the second base does. A change that leaves the amino acid unchanged is called **silent**.

reveal.text: Changes at the first or second base of GGU swap glycine for another amino acid, and only a change that gives another glycine codon is silent.

lessons.orientation: Translate a coding sequence into amino acids with the standard codon table, find where translation starts and stops, and say which changes to a codon alter the protein.
lessons.nextAction: Predict whether a gene is switched on from the conditions in a cell.

blocks.text: A protein is a chain of amino acids, and the order of the chain is written in a gene as an order of bases. A ribosome translates between the two by reading the message three bases at a time, and the table that pairs each of the 64 possible groups of three with an amino acid is the genetic code, which is highly similar in all organisms.

Reading the code takes the table and some care about where reading begins and where it ends, because a shift of one base changes every group that follows it. With that care you can predict what a change in a gene will do to the protein.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to translate an mRNA into amino acids and say which changes to a codon alter the protein.
intro.whyItMatters: Every later question about what a change in DNA does depends on reading the code correctly.

recap.keyIdea: A ribosome reads an mRNA in non-overlapping codons from a start codon to a stop codon, using a code in which several codons can name one amino acid and no codon names two.

blocks.text: Transcription copies a gene into mRNA, and translation adds one amino acid for each codon, from the first AUG until a stop codon, after which nothing is read. The first codon fixes the reading frame, so starting one base later gives different codons all the way along.

The code has 64 codons, 61 for amino acids and 3 for stop, so most amino acids have several codons, and these often differ only at the third base. A change at the third base is therefore often silent, though not always.

recap.nextHook: Reading the code says what a protein is made of, and the next lesson asks what decides whether a cell makes it at all.

lessons.title: Switching genes on and off

lead.text: The bacterium E. coli meets many sugars, and each needs its own enzymes. Three of the enzymes for digesting lactose are encoded by genes called lacZ, lacY and lacA, which sit side by side in one transcription unit called an **operon**. The three genes share the same regulation and are copied into one mRNA, which is then translated gene by gene. LacZ encodes the enzyme beta-galactosidase, which splits lactose into glucose and galactose, and lacY encodes a protein that helps to bring lactose into the cell.

The operon is normally transcribed only when lactose is there to digest, which presumably saves the energy of making enzymes that would have nothing to act on. The control rests on two short stretches of DNA beside the genes, the promoter, where RNA polymerase attaches, and the operator. A protein called the **repressor**, made from a gene called lacI, binds to the operator and keeps RNA polymerase off the promoter, so the operon is not transcribed while the operator is occupied.

afterFigure.text: Lactose releases the block because the repressor can also bind lactose. When lactose is bound the repressor changes shape and can no longer bind the operator, RNA polymerase attaches to the promoter, and the three genes are transcribed at a moderate level. A protein that changes its shape and behaviour when it binds a molecule in this way is said to be regulated allosterically.

diagram.alt: The lac operon as a strip of DNA with a promoter P, an operator O and the three genes lacZ, lacY and lacA. Without lactose a repressor sits on the operator and RNA polymerase is blocked. With lactose the repressor is bound to lactose and has let go, and RNA polymerase transcribes the three genes into one mRNA at a moderate level.

lead.text: A second protein adds a further layer. CAP can bind a short sequence near the promoter, but only when it has the small molecule cAMP bound to it, and when it is attached RNA polymerase binds the promoter more readily. The amount of cAMP is inversely related to the amount of glucose: cAMP is made when glucose is low and not when glucose is plentiful.

E. coli prefers glucose to lactose, so the operon reaches a high level of expression just when lactose is there and glucose has run out. With lactose and glucose both present the repressor lets go, but CAP is not bound, and transcription is moderate. With glucose and no lactose the repressor stays on the operator.

diagram.alt: Three states of the lac operon. With lactose and glucose both present the repressor is released, CAP is free, and transcription is moderate. With lactose present and glucose absent the repressor is released and CAP with cAMP is bound near the promoter, and transcription is high. With glucose and no lactose the repressor blocks the operator and transcription is off.

reveal.text: The repressor decides whether the operon can be transcribed at all, and CAP only raises transcription once the operator is free.

lead.text: Mutants showed how the circuit works. Some strains make the lac enzymes whether or not lactose is present, and are called **constitutive**. In the mutant $O^c$, a change in the operator means that the repressor can no longer recognise and bind it. In the mutant $I^-$, a change in lacI means either that no repressor is made or that the repressor cannot bind the operator. In both strains the operator stays free, so nothing blocks transcription.

A third kind of lacI mutant, $I^s$, makes a repressor that cannot bind lactose. This repressor stays on the operator, and the operon is never switched on, whether lactose is present or not. Normal forms of the genes carry a plus sign, as in $I^+$, $O^+$ and $Z^+$, and $Z^-$ stands for a lacZ gene that makes no working enzyme.

reveal.text: Working backwards from a strain's behaviour to its defect uses the same circuit as working forwards from a defect.

lead.text: The sites that proteins bind are short stretches of DNA that do not code for proteins. The promoter, the operator and the CAP-binding site are called **cis-elements**, because they have to sit on the same DNA molecule as the genes they control. The proteins that bind them, such as the repressor and CAP, are **trans-regulators**: they diffuse through the cell, so they need not be encoded on that DNA.

The distinction predicts what mutations do in a cell that has two copies of the operon. One copy can be carried on a separate piece of DNA called an F factor, alongside the copy on the main chromosome, which gives a partial diploid. A mutation in a cis-element changes only the copy it lies on, whereas a mutation in a protein-coding gene such as lacI changes a protein that can reach both copies.

afterFigure.text: The experiments with partial diploids show that the $O^c$ mutation acts only in cis, while lacI acts in trans. They also give the order of dominance of the three lacI alleles, $I^s$ over $I^+$ over $I^-$.

steps.headline: A cell has $I^+ O^c Z^-$ on its chromosome and $I^+ O^+ Z^+$ on an F factor. With no lactose present, does it make working beta-galactosidase?

workedSteps.text: Both copies carry $I^+$, so the cell makes working repressor, and the repressor is a trans-regulator that can reach both copies of the operon.
On the chromosome the operator is $O^c$, so the repressor cannot bind it and that copy is transcribed without lactose. Its $Z^-$ gene is defective, so the enzyme made from this copy does not work.
On the F factor the operator is normal, so the repressor binds it and that copy is not transcribed while lactose is absent.
So with no lactose the cell makes no working beta-galactosidase. The $O^c$ mutation has not switched on the normal copy, because an operator acts only in cis.

steps.headline: A cell has $I^- O^+ Z^+$ on its chromosome and $I^+ O^+ Z^-$ on an F factor. With no lactose present, does it make working beta-galactosidase?

workedSteps.text: The $I^+$ copy on the F factor makes working repressor, and the repressor is a trans-regulator, so it can reach the operators on both copies.
Decide whether that repressor binds the operator on the chromosome copy, which carries the normal $Z^+$ gene.
Decide what the cell makes, using the operator in front of $Z^+$ and the defective $Z^-$ on the other copy.
With lactose the repressor would release both operators, and the $Z^+$ copy would make working enzyme, so the cell is inducible and not constitutive. This shows that $I^-$ is recessive to $I^+$.

lead.text: Eukaryotic cells use the same two kinds of part, in larger numbers. A promoter lies near the start of a gene, and **enhancers** are cis-elements that can lie near the promoter or far from it, upstream or downstream. Transcription factors are proteins that recognise enhancer sequences and attach to them, and because DNA is flexible they can reach RNA polymerase and its partner proteins at the promoter and raise the rate of transcription. Each transcription factor recognises a specific DNA sequence.

The yellow gene of the fruit fly shows how this makes cells different. It encodes an enzyme in the pathway that makes a dark pigment in the insect's exoskeleton, and it has three enhancers, one for the wing, one for the body and one for the mouth. Each enhancer binds a different tissue-specific transcription factor, which is present only in cells of that tissue.

afterFigure.text: Which genes are active in which tissues therefore depends on particular combinations of cis-elements and trans-factors. The same logic accounts for the cells of one person: they carry the same DNA, and a liver cell differs from a muscle cell in which transcription factors it makes, and so in which genes it turns on.

diagram.alt: A strip of DNA with three enhancers, for the wing, the body and the mouth, then a promoter P and the yellow gene. In a wing cell a transcription factor binds the wing enhancer and the gene is on. In a body cell a different factor binds the body enhancer and the gene is on.
diagram.caption: Each enhancer is used only in the tissue whose cells make the factor that binds it.

reveal.text: Separate enhancers make a gene's control modular, so a loss in one module leaves the others working.
Gal4 is a trans-regulator, so it can act on the responder from another piece of DNA, and the enhancer decides which cells make it.

lessons.orientation: Predict whether a gene is expressed from the cell's conditions and the state of its regulatory sequences and proteins, using the lac operon as a worked system, and explain how one genome gives different cell types.
lessons.nextAction: Classify a change in a coding sequence and predict what it does to the protein.

blocks.text: The cells of a person's body almost all carry the same DNA, yet a liver cell, a muscle cell and a brain cell make very different sets of proteins. At any moment a cell uses only some of its genes and holds the others off, so what distinguishes one cell from another is which of its genes are on.

Most of this control happens when a gene is copied into RNA, so transcription is where the switches are found. The best understood switch is in a bacterium, where three genes for digesting a sugar are turned on only when the sugar is present, and the same two kinds of part, sites on DNA and proteins that bind them, recur in human cells.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to predict whether a gene is on from the state of its regulatory sites and proteins.
intro.whyItMatters: One genome makes many kinds of cell only because genes are switched on in different combinations.

recap.keyIdea: A gene is switched on or off by regulatory proteins that bind sites on the DNA, and a site (cis) acts only on its own DNA while a diffusible protein (trans) can act on every copy.

blocks.text: In the lac operon a repressor bound to the operator blocks RNA polymerase, lactose makes the repressor let go, and CAP with cAMP raises transcription further when glucose is low. Mutations in the operator act only in cis, and mutations in lacI act in trans, which is why a cell with two copies of the operon can be read copy by copy.

In eukaryotes the same logic works through enhancers and transcription factors, which can act from a distance and are specific to a tissue. A liver cell and a muscle cell carry the same DNA and differ in which factors they make, and so in which genes they switch on.

recap.nextHook: A gene that is switched on still has to be read correctly, and the next lesson asks what different kinds of change in a coding sequence do to the protein.

lessons.title: What a mutation does to a protein

lead.text: A **substitution** replaces one base with another, and what it does to the protein depends on the codon it falls in. In the figure the sequence `AUG GCU AAG CUU` gives Met, Ala, Lys and Leu. A change in a codon from one to another that names the same amino acid is **silent**, a change to a codon for a different amino acid is a **missense** change, and a change to a stop codon is a **nonsense** change. This lesson follows each change through the mRNA codons, using the codon table from 'Reading the genetic code'.

afterFigure.text: A nonsense change gives a shortened protein that may function improperly, may be nonfunctional or may be broken down. A missense change can affect how the protein works, and sometimes does not.

diagram.alt: Four views of a short mRNA of four codons. The original reads Met, Ala, Lys, Leu. A silent change in the last codon still gives Leu. A missense change in the third codon gives Glu in place of Lys. A nonsense change in the third codon makes a stop codon and the chain ends after Met and Ala.
diagram.caption: One short mRNA and three single-base substitutions. The changed base is outlined in orange.

lead.text: An insertion adds bases and a deletion removes them. The reading frame groups the bases into threes from the start codon, so a change that adds or removes a number of bases that is not a multiple of three shifts the grouping of every codon after it. This is a **frameshift**. It usually gives a completely different translation, it often brings a stop codon into the reading and so shortens the protein, and the protein is usually nonfunctional.
A change of three bases, or of any multiple of three, keeps the frame. The codons after it are read as before, and the chain loses or gains whole amino acids.

lead.text: Most base changes have no effect on the phenotype. Many fall in noncoding DNA, and a change inside a codon may be silent. A missense change may also leave the protein working, because the new amino acid does not alter its function. Some changes matter a great deal. In sickle cell disease, the amino acid glutamic acid at position 6 of beta-globin is replaced by valine, written Glu6Val, and the abnormal haemoglobin S subunits then clump into long, stiff chains that distort red blood cells into a crescent. In the table Glu is named by GAA or GAG and Val by GUU, GUC, GUA or GUG, so a change of the middle base from A to U would turn either Glu codon into a Val codon.

A change that keeps the frame can matter as well. The commonest allele of the CFTR gene among people with cystic fibrosis deletes three nucleotides and so removes one phenylalanine from position 508 of a protein of 1,480 amino acids. The missing amino acid makes the protein fold wrongly in the endoplasmic reticulum, which prevents it from reaching the cell membrane.

reveal.text: The frame decides how many codons are changed, and the position and kind of the lost amino acid decide whether the protein still works.

lead.text: Alleles can also be sorted by what remains of a gene's activity. A complete loss of function is an **amorph**, which makes no active product and is often called a null allele. A partial loss is a **hypomorph**, which makes an incompletely working product. Two classes gain something: a **hypermorph** makes more of the same active product, and a **neomorph** makes an active product with a new function. An **antimorph** has an activity opposite to the normal one, and interferes with the normal allele's product.

diagram.alt: A table of five classes of mutant allele. An amorph makes no active product. A hypomorph makes a product that works only in part. A hypermorph makes more of the same active product. A neomorph makes an active product with a new function. An antimorph makes a product that interferes with the normal one.

lead.text: Whether a person with one mutant allele and one normal allele is affected depends on how much function the normal copy supplies. For most genes the normal allele is **haplosufficient**: even when the other allele is a complete loss of function, the normal one supplies enough activity for a normal phenotype, so loss-of-function alleles tend to be recessive. For some genes one normal copy does not make enough, and the gene is **haploinsufficient**, so that a null allele is dominant or semi-dominant to the normal allele.

Alleles that gain a function are nearly always dominant. An antimorph is dominant for a different reason. The simplest explanation is that its product works as a dimer, or another multimer, and a single mutant subunit poisons the whole complex. Such an allele is also called a dominant negative.

reveal.text: Only a quarter of the dimers work, whereas a null allele, which adds no poisoned subunits, would leave about half the normal number, so an antimorph can do more harm than a null allele.
Reading a codon change off the table works whichever amino acid pair is involved, and the first, second and third base of a codon have different effects.

lessons.orientation: Classify a DNA change as silent, missense, nonsense, in-frame deletion or frameshift from the codon table, and predict from the kind of change and the gene's dosage needs whether an allele will behave as recessive or dominant.
lessons.reviewLabel: What a mutation does to a protein
lessons.nextAction: Infer parent genotypes from the counts of offspring in a cross.

blocks.text: More than a thousand different mutant alleles of CFTR, the gene in which variants cause cystic fibrosis, have been described, and the commonest one worldwide deletes only three nucleotides. Those three nucleotides remove a single amino acid, a phenylalanine at position 508, from a protein of 1,480 amino acids. Yet the protein folds wrongly in the cell and never reaches the cell membrane, and the allele accounts for about 70 percent of cases of the disease in North America.

A change in DNA does not always change a protein, and a small change in a protein is not always small in its effect. Reading a change through the genetic code, and then asking how much of the protein's work is left, is how a variant is judged, and it also explains why some variants cause disease in one copy of a gene and others only in two.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what kind of change a variant is and whether its allele will act as recessive or dominant.
intro.whyItMatters: The same kind of change can be harmless in one gene and severe in another.

recap.keyIdea: A base change is silent, missense or nonsense depending on the codon it makes, an insertion or deletion that is not a multiple of three shifts the frame, and whether an allele is dominant depends on how much function one normal copy supplies.

blocks.text: Reading a change through the code sorts it into silent, missense, nonsense or frameshift, and a change of a multiple of three bases keeps the frame and alters whole amino acids only. Whether the protein still works depends on which amino acid is affected, which is why a three-base deletion in CFTR can cause severe disease.

Loss-of-function alleles are usually recessive, because one working copy is enough, unless the gene is haploinsufficient. Alleles that gain a function are nearly always dominant, and an antimorph is dominant because its subunits poison the complex, so that only one dimer in four stays normal in a heterozygote.

recap.nextHook: Single genes are only the start, and the next lesson reads the counts of offspring to work out what the parents carried and how their genes interact.

lessons.title: Reading offspring ratios

lead.text: A Punnett square predicts the offspring of a cross from the parents' genotypes, and geneticists also use one backwards. A genotype cannot be seen, only inferred from phenotypes, and because of dominance a heterozygote and a homozygote often look alike. A **test cross** gets around this by crossing the individual of uncertain genotype with one that is homozygous recessive for the loci being tested. If a purple-flowered pea plant is crossed with a white-flowered plant, aa, all the offspring are purple when the purple parent is AA, and purple and white offspring appear in a 1:1 ratio when it is Aa.

Real counts rarely match the expected ratio exactly. Sometimes the cause is sampling, the random choice of a group of offspring that does not represent the whole, and sometimes certain genotypes survive less often, so that they are under-represented among the offspring counted. A statistical method, the **chi-square test**, helps a geneticist decide whether a gap between observed and expected counts is due to sampling, or is so large that the assumptions behind the expected ratio should be re-examined. The calculation is not needed here, only the purpose of the test.

Dominance is one relationship between alleles, and there are others. In **incomplete dominance** each allele adds to the trait, and the heterozygote lies between the two homozygotes. Carnations with an allele for red petals and an allele for white petals have pink petals. The alleles stay distinct, so two heterozygotes cross to give offspring in the 1:2:1 ratio of genotypes, one of each homozygote to two of the heterozygote.

In **codominance** a heterozygote expresses both alleles at the same time, and is not an intermediate between them. The ABO gene has three common alleles, $I^A$, $I^B$ and $i$. A person with $I^A I^B$ has both A and B antigens on the blood cells and so has type AB blood. The $i$ allele makes neither antigen and is recessive to the other two, so $I^A i$ gives type A, $I^B i$ gives type B and $ii$ gives type O.

reveal.text: Under incomplete dominance the phenotypic ratio matches the genotypic ratio of 1:2:1.
Parents of types A and B who are both heterozygous can have a child of any of the four types.

lead.text: Two genes can be followed in one cross. When one locus is crossed on its own, three quarters of the offspring show the dominant trait and one quarter the recessive trait. If the two loci assort independently during gamete formation, the product rule gives the share of each combination. Three quarters times three quarters is 9/16 of the offspring dominant at both loci, three quarters times one quarter is 3/16 dominant at only one locus, and likewise 3/16 at only the other, and one quarter times one quarter is 1/16 recessive at both.

afterFigure.text: The four classes are written A_B_, A_bb, aaB_ and aabb, where the underscore stands for either allele. They come out in the ratio **9:3:3:1**, provided the loci assort independently, among other conditions. The square in the figure shows the sixteen equally likely pairings of gametes and the class each one gives.

lead.text: Some dihybrid crosses give a ratio other than 9:3:3:1, and 15:1, 9:7, 12:3:1 and 9:3:4 all occur. Each of these can be made by adding together some of the four classes of 9:3:3:1, and each points to an interaction between the two genes. A common interaction is **epistasis**, in which the phenotype of one locus masks that of another, so that fewer than the usual four classes are seen.

In Labrador retrievers the B locus controls how well melanin is made: B_ hair is black and bb hair is brown. A second locus, E, controls whether any pigment is deposited in the hair, and at least one E allele is needed. Every dog that is ee is pale yellow whatever its B genotype, so ee masks the B locus. The classes eeB_ and eebb now look alike, and 9:3:3:1 becomes 9 black, 3 chocolate and 4 yellow. A masking that depends on a recessive genotype is called recessive epistasis. A dominant allele can do the masking as well, and then the ratio is 12:3:1.

steps.headline: Two Labrador retrievers heterozygous at both coat-colour loci have 160 pups, with invented counts of 88 black, 33 chocolate and 39 yellow. Which ratio fits?

workedSteps.text: Count the phenotype classes. There are three, not four, so two of the four classes of 9:3:3:1 have merged, which points to one locus masking the other.
Pick the ratio. Black needs B_ and at least one E, chocolate is bb with at least one E, and yellow is ee at any B genotype, so the pattern is 9:3:4, which merges the classes eeB_ and eebb.
Work out the expected counts. The parts add up to 16, so each part is 160 ÷ 16 = 10 pups, and 9:3:4 expects 90 black, 30 chocolate and 40 yellow.
Compare. The observed 88, 33 and 39 differ from 90, 30 and 40 by 2, 3 and 1 pups, a scatter that sampling can produce, so the counts fit 9:3:4 and recessive epistasis.

steps.headline: Two squash plants heterozygous at both fruit-colour loci give 160 fruits, with invented counts of 121 white, 29 yellow and 10 green. Which ratio fits?

workedSteps.text: In squash, a dominant allele A at one locus blocks all pigment, so fruit with A are white, and at the other locus B_ gives yellow fruit and bb gives green fruit. The cross gives three classes, so two of the four classes of 9:3:3:1 have merged.
Pick the ratio that fits the sizes of the three classes.
Work out the expected count for the largest class.
The expected counts are 120 white, 30 yellow and 10 green. The observed 121, 29 and 10 differ by 1, 1 and 0 fruits, so the counts fit 12:3:1, which is dominant epistasis.

lead.text: Some genes follow a different pattern because they lie on a sex chromosome. Most X-linked genes have no counterpart on the Y chromosome, so a male has a single copy and is **hemizygous** for them. The white gene of the fruit fly lies on the X chromosome. A fly with the mutant allele $w^-$ has white eyes and the normal allele $w^+$ gives red eyes. The mutant allele is recessive, so a heterozygous female has red eyes, a homozygous mutant female has white eyes, and a male has red or white eyes according to the one allele he has.

The definitive test for a sex-linked gene is a pair of **reciprocal crosses**. A male and a female with different phenotypes are crossed, and then the cross is repeated with the phenotypes reversed between the sexes. When the two crosses disagree, and sons and daughters differ in phenotype, sex linkage is the usual cause. For a gene on an autosome the two crosses would give the same result.

afterFigure.text: In the first cross every offspring has red eyes. In the reciprocal cross the daughters have red eyes and the sons have white eyes, because each son receives his only X from his mother and his Y from his father.

diagram.alt: Two crosses for the white-eye gene of the fruit fly. A red-eyed female crossed with a white-eyed male gives red-eyed sons and daughters. A white-eyed female crossed with a red-eyed male gives red-eyed daughters and white-eyed sons.
diagram.caption: Reciprocal crosses for an X-linked gene give different results. Circles are females and squares are males.

reveal.text: Identical results from reciprocal crosses, in both sexes, are what an autosomal gene predicts, and any difference between them points to sex linkage.
When the number of classes matches the ratio and the gaps are small, the simplest reading is that the ratio holds and the loci do not interact.

lessons.orientation: Infer parent genotypes and the relationship between genes from offspring counts: test cross, incomplete dominance and codominance, 9:3:3:1 and its modified forms, and sex linkage from reciprocal crosses.
lessons.nextAction: Work out how often two linked genes are separated in the offspring.

blocks.text: A Punnett square turns the genotypes of two parents into a prediction about their offspring. A breeder can use it the other way round: a pea plant with purple flowers is crossed with a white-flowered plant, and a count of the offspring shows which alleles the purple parent carries.

A count is never exactly the predicted ratio, so reading it means judging which prediction it fits best. That judgement tells you the genotype of a parent, how the alleles of one gene relate, whether two genes interact, and whether a gene lies on a sex chromosome.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to infer parent genotypes and gene interactions from the counts in a cross.
intro.whyItMatters: Counts of offspring are how breeders and geneticists find out what the parents carry.

recap.keyIdea: Counts of offspring point to genotypes and to how genes act, once the number of classes is matched to a ratio and the gaps from the expected counts are judged to be small.

blocks.text: A test cross to a homozygous recessive reveals a parent's genotype, incomplete dominance and codominance change what the heterozygote looks like, and two independent loci give 9:3:3:1. When one locus masks another, classes merge into 9:3:4 or 12:3:1, and a gene on the X chromosome shows itself when reciprocal crosses differ.

To read a count, count the classes, pick the ratio, work out the expected counts, compare them with the observed ones and then decide whether sampling alone explains the gaps. The chi-square test is the tool for that last judgement.

recap.nextHook: Genes that lie close together on one chromosome do not assort independently, and the next lesson reads that from the counts too.

lessons.title: Linked genes and recombination

lead.text: Independent assortment works because the pairs of chromosomes line up at random during meiosis, so the way one pair divides says nothing about how another pair will divide. Two genes on different chromosomes therefore produce all four combinations of their alleles in equal numbers. Two genes on the same chromosome behave differently, since each allele travels with the chromosome that carries it, and the two genes can come apart only if that chromosome first swaps a piece with its partner.

afterFigure.text: The place a gene occupies on a chromosome is its **locus**, and alleles at loci that lie close together on one chromosome tend to be inherited together. This is called **linkage**, and it is where Mendel's second law fails for genes that sit close together. Geneticists turn it into a tool, because how strongly two genes are linked shows how far apart they sit, which lets them place genes along a chromosome in a process called genetic mapping.

diagram.alt: Two views of chromosomes carrying genes. In the first, gene 1 with alleles A and a sits on one pair of chromosomes and gene 2 with alleles B and b on another pair. In the second, both genes sit on a single pair, A with B on one chromosome and a with b on the other.
diagram.caption: Two genes on separate chromosomes are dealt out independently. Two genes on one chromosome travel together. Use the buttons to compare.

lead.text: Take a dihybrid whose chromosomes carry A with B on one strand and a with b on the other. If nothing is exchanged between the genes, every gamete receives one of those two original combinations, AB or ab, and these are the **parental** gametes. A gamete carrying Ab or aB has a combination that neither chromosome held, and it is called **recombinant**. Recombinants arise when a crossover exchanges pieces between the two chromosomes in the stretch between the genes.

A crossover involves two of the four chromatids present at that stage of meiosis, so the other two pass on unchanged, and a meiosis with a crossover between the genes makes two parental gametes and two recombinant ones, as the second view of the figure shows.

afterFigure.text: The **recombination frequency** is the recombinant gametes divided by all the gametes counted. Unlinked genes give about 50 percent, and about 50 percent is also the most that can be observed for any two genes. The more room there is between two genes on one chromosome, the more often a crossover falls in it, so the frequency rises from 0 percent for genes too close to be separated towards that ceiling.

diagram.alt: Four chromatids drawn as vertical strands, two from each chromosome of a pair, carrying alleles A and B on the left pair and a and b on the right pair. With no crossover the four gametes are AB, AB, ab and ab. With a crossover between the genes the middle two strands swap their lower halves and the four gametes are AB, Ab, aB and ab.

lead.text: The genotype AaBb does not say which alleles share a chromosome. A dihybrid whose parents were AABB and aabb received AB on one chromosome and ab on the other, an arrangement called **coupling**. A dihybrid whose parents were AAbb and aaBB received Ab on one chromosome and aB on the other, an arrangement called **repulsion**, yet its genotype is the same AaBb.

afterFigure.text: The arrangement decides which gametes count as parental, because the parental gametes are always the two combinations that the dihybrid's parents handed down. In coupling the parental gametes are AB and ab and the recombinants are Ab and aB, and in repulsion the roles are swapped. The genotype of one generation is therefore not enough to count recombinants, and you also need the genotypes of the generation before it.

diagram.alt: Two chromosomes of a dihybrid AaBb drawn side by side. In coupling, one carries A and B and the other a and b, and the parents were AABB and aabb. In repulsion, one carries A and b and the other a and B, and the parents were AAbb and aaBB.

reveal.text: Whether a gamete counts as recombinant depends on what the dihybrid's own parents supplied, which is why the arrangement has to be settled before any counting.

lead.text: A test cross lets you count the dihybrid's gametes directly. The recessive partner aabb can pass on only a and b, so each offspring shows by its phenotype which combination the dihybrid supplied. The Online Open Genetics textbook works through an example in mice, in which short-tailed brown mice (aaBB) are crossed with long-tailed white mice (AAbb). Every dihybrid then carries aB on one chromosome and Ab on the other, so the parental gametes are aB and Ab. Of 120 offspring from the test cross, 48 are short and brown and 42 long and white, the two parental classes, while 13 are short and white and 17 long and brown, the two recombinant classes.

afterFigure.text: The recombination frequency is the recombinants over all the offspring, (13 + 17) ÷ 120, which is 30 ÷ 120 or 25 percent. That is below the 50 percent that unlinked genes give, so the tail and fur genes are linked. The classification came first and the division second, and a wrong arrangement would have put the wrong classes in the numerator.

diagram.alt: A table of four offspring classes from the mouse test cross with their numbers: short brown 48, long white 42, short white 13, long brown 17. The second view adds the gamete each offspring received and whether it is parental or recombinant, and the calculation 30 out of 120 is 25 percent.
diagram.caption: The two largest classes are the parental ones. Use the buttons to see them classified.

steps.headline: A dihybrid from AABB and aabb parents is test-crossed, and the 100 offspring include 38 AaBb, 44 aabb, 9 Aabb and 9 aaBb. What is the recombination frequency?

workedSteps.text: The parents were AABB and aabb, so the dihybrid carries AB on one chromosome and ab on the other, which is coupling.
Gametes AB and ab give AaBb and aabb offspring. Gametes Ab and aB give Aabb and aaBb offspring, so those two classes are the recombinants.
The total is all four classes added together.
Divide the recombinants by the total.
Eighteen percent is well below 50 percent, so the genes are linked, and the two large classes are the parental ones.

steps.headline: A dihybrid from AAbb and aaBB parents is test-crossed, and the 200 offspring include 87 Aabb, 83 aaBb, 16 AaBb and 14 aabb. What is the recombination frequency?

workedSteps.text: The parents were AAbb and aaBB, so the dihybrid carries Ab on one chromosome and aB on the other, which is repulsion.
Say which two classes are the recombinants.
Say what the recombinants come to as a percentage of the total.
The largest classes are the dominant-recessive ones this time, and the genes are still linked. The arrangement, and not the look of a class, says which classes are parental.

lead.text: Here the first line is done for you and the next two are yours.

Crossovers fall at random along a chromosome, so genes that sit farther apart are separated more often, and the recombination frequency grows roughly in step with the distance between them. Geneticists therefore give that distance in **map units**, also called **centiMorgans** (cM) after Thomas Hunt Morgan, and a recombination frequency of 1 percent is about 1 cM. The mouse genes above, at 25 percent, are about 25 cM apart. The approximation holds well while the frequency is below about 30 percent, and map distance goes on to reflect the amount of DNA between genes only roughly, since in the plant Arabidopsis 1 cM is about 150,000 base pairs, which holds about 50 genes.

Distances are measured for one pair of genes at a time, and combining pairs gives an order. Suppose three genes P, Q and R show 6 cM between P and Q, 9 cM between Q and R, and 15 cM between P and R. The longest distance equals the sum of the other two, 6 + 9 = 15, so P and R are the ends and Q lies between them.

afterFigure.text: A map shows order and spacing and nothing about which end of the chromosome P is at.

diagram.alt: Three genes P, Q and R. The distances are P to Q 6 cM, Q to R 9 cM and P to R 15 cM. The second view places the genes on a line with Q between P and R, 6 cM from P and 9 cM from R.
diagram.caption: The longest distance is the sum of the other two, which fixes the middle gene. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: Whichever gene is not in the longest pair is the one in the middle, and a check is that its two distances add up to the longest.

lead.text: The match between frequency and distance fails for genes far apart, for a reason the figure shows. Between two distant genes a second crossover is likely as well, and two crossovers return the original combination to the strand. The gamete then looks parental and is not counted as a recombinant, though the chromosome was cut twice.

afterFigure.text: Observed frequencies between distant genes therefore underestimate how many crossovers took place. With enough of them, genes at opposite ends of a long chromosome behave as if they were unlinked, which is why some chromosomes more than 100 cM long still give a frequency of only 50 percent between genes at their tips. A frequency near 50 percent cannot say whether two genes are on different chromosomes or far apart on the same one.

diagram.alt: A pair of chromosomes with genes A and B, and the strand a gamete receives after crossovers. After one crossover between the genes the strand carries A and b, a recombinant. After two crossovers the strand carries A and B, the parental combination, although two exchanges took place.
diagram.caption: A second crossover cancels the first as far as the two genes can tell. Use the buttons to compare.

reveal.text: Under the assumed arrangement the parental classes are the small ones, which gives 800 recombinants out of 1,000. A result above 50 percent shows the assumption was wrong. The dihybrid carried AB and ab, the recombinants are the classes of 98 and 102, and the frequency is 20 percent.
The sum of two short distances is a better guide than one long measurement, because double crossovers hide recombination more often over long stretches.

lessons.orientation: Compute a recombination frequency from test-cross counts, decide whether two genes are linked, and convert it to a map distance, taking account of which arrangement the parents carried.
lessons.nextAction: Read a family tree, rule inheritance patterns in or out, and work out a carrier chance.

blocks.text: Mendel's second law says that the alleles of different genes are dealt out independently. For a dihybrid, an individual heterozygous at two genes, that gives a precise prediction: when it is test-crossed to an individual homozygous recessive at both genes, the four kinds of offspring turn up in equal numbers.

The Online Open Genetics textbook works through a test cross in mice, scored for tail length and fur colour, with 120 offspring. Independent assortment predicts 30 of each kind. The counts in the example are 48, 42, 13 and 17, so two kinds are far commoner than the other two, and some pairs of genes evidently do not come apart as freely as Mendel's did.

diagram.alt: Two bar charts of a test cross of 120 mice offspring in four kinds. Independent assortment predicts 30 in each kind. The cross gave 48 short brown, 42 long white, 13 short white and 17 long brown.
diagram.caption: The two bars on the left of the second view are far above the 30 that independent assortment predicts, and the two on the right are far below it. Use the buttons to switch views.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to sort test-cross offspring into parental and recombinant classes, work out a recombination frequency, and read it as a distance between genes.
intro.whyItMatters: The same counting places genes along a chromosome, which is how a genetic map is built.

recap.keyIdea: Genes close together on one chromosome are inherited together unless a crossover separates them, and the recombination frequency, counted once the parents' arrangement is settled, measures how far apart they are.

blocks.text: Two genes on one chromosome stay together except when a crossover falls between them, and the share of recombinant offspring in a test cross grows with their distance, up to about 50 percent. Which offspring are recombinant depends on the arrangement the dihybrid inherited, so you settle coupling or repulsion first and then count.

A frequency in percent is about the same number of map units, a good approximation for short distances. Over long stretches double crossovers go uncounted, so frequencies cannot pass about 50 percent and distances fall short of the sum of their parts.

recap.nextHook: A family tree can show how a condition passes down, and the next lesson reads one to rule inheritance patterns in or out and to work out a carrier chance.

lessons.title: Reading a pedigree

lead.text: A pedigree draws one trait through one family. Circles are females and squares are males, a line between two people joins them as partners, and lines running down lead to their children. Each generation sits on its own row, numbered with roman numerals, and each person in a row has a number, so II-3 is the third person in the second generation. A filled symbol marks a person who has the trait. A half-filled symbol marks a **carrier**, a person with no symptoms who has one copy of a recessive allele and can pass it on, although a pedigree often cannot show who the carriers are. The affected person who brought the family to a geneticist's attention is the **proband**, marked with an arrow.

afterFigure.text: A pedigree records what relatives remember and what doctors diagnosed, so errors creep in, and some people who carry a variant never show the trait. The examples here assume that every pedigree is accurate, and the last screens return to what that assumption leaves out.

diagram.alt: The symbols of a pedigree: an unaffected square for a male, an unaffected circle for a female, a filled square for a person with the trait, a half-filled circle for a carrier, a filled circle with an arrow for the proband, and two partners with a line down to a child in the next generation.

lead.text: Which pattern a pedigree follows depends on where the gene sits and whether its allele is dominant or recessive. An autosomal dominant condition shows with one copy of the allele, so every affected person must have an affected parent. An autosomal recessive condition needs two copies, so two unaffected parents who each carry one copy can have an affected child. A father gives his X chromosome to every daughter and to no son, and a mother gives X to children of either sex, and the two X-linked patterns follow from that. A Y-linked trait passes from father to son only, and a mitochondrial one comes through the egg, so only mothers pass it on.

afterFigure.text: The table gives the one feature that most quickly separates each pattern from the rest. Use these rules to rule patterns out. One person who breaks a rule removes a pattern for good, whereas a family that follows a rule is only consistent with it.

diagram.alt: A table of six modes of inheritance and the feature that identifies each: autosomal dominant, an affected parent for every affected person; autosomal recessive, unaffected parents can have an affected child; X-linked dominant, no affected son from an affected father; X-linked recessive, an affected daughter needs an affected father; Y-linked, father to son only; mitochondrial, mothers only.
diagram.caption: Each pattern leaves one feature that is quick to check in a family tree.

lead.text: Once a condition is known to be autosomal recessive, the parents of an affected child must both be carriers, since each passed on one copy of the allele. A [[Punnett square|A grid of the equally likely pairings of two parents' gametes. Met in 'What could the offspring inherit?' in Biology: Cells to Ecosystems.]] of two carriers has four boxes, AA, Aa, Aa and aa, so each of their children has probability 1/4 of being affected, 1/2 of being an unaffected carrier, and 1/4 of being neither. The first figure shows it as 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 for the affected child, because each parent passes on the recessive allele with probability 1/2.

A different question arises for a child who is already known to be unaffected. The four boxes were equally likely, but the pedigree has excluded the aa box, so three boxes remain, and two of the three are Aa. An unaffected child of two carriers is therefore a carrier with probability **2/3**, and not 1/2, which would be the probability before anything is known about the child.

afterFigure.text: Chances that must all happen together are multiplied, which is the product rule, and chances of alternatives are added, which is the sum rule. Every calculation that follows uses those two rules.

steps.headline: II-3 and an unrelated partner plan a family, and 1 in 25 people of European ancestry carry the cystic fibrosis allele. What is the chance of an affected child?

workedSteps.text: II-3 is unaffected and both her parents are carriers, so she is a carrier with probability 2/3.
Her partner is unrelated, so his chance is the population's carrier frequency.
Two carriers pass on the allele to a child with probability 1/4, and the child is affected only if all three events hold.
Multiply the three chances.
The chance is 1 in 150. The general population's chance is 1 in 2,500, so a sibling with the condition raises it about seventeen-fold.

lead.text: The family in Pedigree A is invented. The figure of 1 in 25 comes from the textbook, and it holds for people of European ancestry.

workedSteps.text: I-1 and I-2 are unaffected and have an affected daughter, so both are carriers of an autosomal recessive allele.
Say how likely II-2 is to be a carrier.
His partner carries no copy, so III-1 can receive the allele only from II-2, who passes it on with probability 1/2 if he is a carrier.
Say how likely III-1 is to be a carrier.

lead.text: Pedigree B follows a condition through three generations. I-1 is an affected man and his wife I-2 comes from outside the family, so she is assumed to carry no copy of the allele. Every daughter of I-1 receives his X chromosome, so II-1 and II-2 are carriers for certain, whatever the family tree looks like, and the second view marks them. His son II-3 receives his Y chromosome and therefore cannot have the trait from him, which is why a father never passes an X-linked recessive trait to a son.

A carrier daughter passes either of her X chromosomes to a child with probability 1/2, so each of her sons is affected with probability 1/2, as III-1 is. Her daughters receive their father's X as well, and if it is normal they are unaffected, so a woman is affected only when her father is affected and her mother carries the allele.

afterFigure.text: Counting affected men against affected women is a weak guide in a family of a few people. The transmission rules do better: an affected daughter of unaffected parents rules out X-linked recessive, and an affected father with an affected son rules out X-linked dominant.

reveal.text: A woman who is a carrier for certain, with a partner carrying no copy, has sons that are affected half the time and daughters that are carriers half the time and never affected.

lead.text: Pedigree C shows a dominant pattern. The condition appears in all three generations and every affected person has an affected parent. II-1 is an affected man whose son III-1 is also affected, and since an affected father passes his Y chromosome to a son, that transmission rules out X-linked dominant and leaves autosomal dominant. Dominant conditions are usually rare, so an affected person is usually heterozygous, because otherwise both parents would need to have the same rare condition.

An affected parent does not always have an affected child. II-3 is affected and both her children are unaffected, which makes the trait look as though it skips a generation. If she is heterozygous, each child escapes the allele with probability 1/2, and both do with probability 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. That is far from rare in a small family, so an unaffected generation does not argue against a dominant condition.

afterFigure.text: A recessive condition skips generations because carriers are unaffected, and a dominant one can seem to skip because of chance, so a skipped generation does not by itself identify the pattern.

steps.headline: Families that share more than genes

lead.text: A condition can run in a family for reasons that have nothing to do with inherited variants. Relatives often share a home, a diet and exposure to the same toxins, and a condition that all of them develop can then look inherited when it is not. Different causes can also give similar symptoms in different patients, some genetic and some not.

A pedigree has limits of its own. It records what relatives recall and what doctors diagnosed, so some of it is wrong, and some carriers never show the trait. A mode of inheritance only makes sense once a genetic cause is plausible, so the first question about a cluster in one family is whether the family shares something other than genes.

reveal.text: Clusters in a household are a reason to ask about shared exposures before asking about alleles.

lessons.orientation: Decide which modes of inheritance a pedigree allows, rule modes out from specific features, and work out a carrier probability by chaining the Mendelian chances through the family.
lessons.nextAction: Say what penetrance, expressivity and heritability each mean, and use them on a trait with many causes.

blocks.text: A genetic counsellor is shown a family. Two parents with no sign of cystic fibrosis have a daughter who has it, and a son and another daughter who do not. The unaffected daughter is planning a family and wants to know how likely it is that her own child will have the condition. The family is invented, but the question is a real one in counselling.

The answer depends on how the condition is inherited and on what is known about her partner. A family tree, called a pedigree, puts that evidence on one page. The tree is read first, to see which patterns of inheritance could produce it and which cannot, and the chances are worked out afterwards.
