intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to rule modes of inheritance in or out from a pedigree, and work out a carrier chance by multiplying chances along the family.
intro.whyItMatters: Counsellors use exactly this reasoning to tell a family how likely a condition is in a child.

recap.keyIdea: A pedigree rules modes of inheritance out through the features that each leaves, and a carrier chance is found by multiplying the chances along the family, remembering that an unaffected child of two carriers is a carrier with probability 2/3.

blocks.text: Unaffected parents with an affected child rule out both dominant modes, an affected daughter of an unaffected father rules out X-linked recessive, and a father who passes a trait to his son rules out X-linked dominant. Once a mode is settled, the carrier chance for an unaffected relative comes from the Punnett square with the affected box removed, and the chain of chances is multiplied.
Each pregnancy has the same chance as the last, and a cluster of cases in a family is not yet evidence of inheritance until shared exposures are set aside.

recap.nextHook: Pedigrees follow one gene through one family, but many traits depend on several genes and the environment, and the next lesson separates penetrance, expressivity and heritability.

lessons.title: Traits with many causes

lead.text: A person's trait comes from the genotype and the environment together, so the same genotype can lead to different outcomes. Two terms describe the gap. **Penetrance** is the proportion of people with a particular genotype who show the matching trait, so a genotype with a penetrance of 100 percent always shows and one below 100 percent has carriers who never develop it. **Expressivity** is how much the trait varies among those who do show it. Both arise from chance, from the environment and from variants in other genes.

The eight carriers in the opening figure had a penetrance of 5 out of 8, and their signs ranged from mild to severe, which is broad expressivity. The two properties are independent, as the four views of the figure show.

afterFigure.text: BRCA1 and BRCA2 are the usual example of reduced penetrance: many people with a variant in one of these genes develop cancer during their lifetime, but some do not, and doctors cannot predict which. Marfan syndrome shows variable expressivity. People with it usually carry a variant in FBN1, yet the signs range from a mild tall, thin build with long fingers to life-threatening complications of the heart and blood vessels.

diagram.alt: Four rows of eight circles for people with the same genotype. Complete penetrance and narrow expressivity: all eight show alike. Incomplete penetrance and narrow expressivity: five show alike and three do not show. Complete penetrance and broad expressivity: all eight show, from mild to severe. Incomplete penetrance and broad expressivity: five show, from mild to severe, and three do not.

reveal.text: A variant with reduced penetrance raises the chance of the condition without fixing it. The woman is still a carrier at raised risk, and she can still pass the variant on.

lead.text: Penetrance and expressivity describe what a single variant does. Most common traits and diseases depend on many variants at once, each with a modest effect, together with the environment, and a trait of that kind is called **polygenic**. Height is the standard case. More than 700 variants that affect it have been found, and more are expected. A few rare variants have dramatic effects, such as variants in the FGFR3 gene that cause achondroplasia, a rare condition marked by short stature, but for most people height is controlled by a combination of variants with modest effects plus a smaller contribution from nutrition and other environmental factors.
Because so many variants are involved, children receive different combinations of them from the same parents, so siblings differ in height, and the height of one child is hard to predict.

afterFigure.text: Common conditions such as obesity, heart disease and type 2 diabetes have no single genetic cause either. They are influenced by many genes together with lifestyle and environment, and a condition with many contributing causes is called complex, or multifactorial. Such conditions often cluster in families without a clear pattern of inheritance, and the family's shared environment makes their genetic part hard to isolate.

reveal.text: A polygenic trait runs in families, because relatives share many of the variants, and still differs between siblings, because each child receives a different combination of them.

lead.text: **Heritability** is a statistic, written $h^2$, that says how much of the variation in a trait among the people in a population goes with genetic differences among them. It runs from 0 to 1. The language a person speaks has a heritability of zero, since genes do not decide it, and many single-gene conditions, such as phenylketonuria, have a high heritability. Most complex traits fall in the middle, which suggests that genes and environment both contribute to the differences among people.

It has historically been estimated from twins. Identical twins have nearly identical DNA, and fraternal twins share about half of theirs on average. If a trait is more alike in identical twins than in fraternal twins who grew up in the same environment, genes probably play an important part, and comparing the two kinds of pair gives an estimate of the heritability.

afterFigure.text: An estimate describes a single population living in a single environment, and it can shift when conditions do. A heritability of 0.7 therefore means that 70 percent of the differences in the trait among people in that population go with genetic differences. It does not mean that 70 percent of one person's trait is caused by their genes.

reveal.text: The figure of 0.7 describes how differences in the trait are shared out among people in one population and one environment, and says nothing about the causes in any one person.

lead.text: Three further cautions follow from the definition. Heritability does not say which genes or which environmental influences are involved, or how important each is. A trait can be **familial**, shared by members of a family, without being heritable: the language spoken tends to be shared in families, yet it has no genetic contribution. And heritability says nothing about how easy it is to change a trait. Hair colour has a high heritability, and it is easy to change with dye.

The figure shows how a high heritability and a large change can sit together. In the second view everyone's value has moved up by the same amount, as a better environment might move it for everybody, so the average has risen while the differences among people, and the share of them that goes with genes, are what they were. The MedlinePlus page on height says something similar of real families: studies of immigrant families show that moving to a country with better food, healthcare and employment can have a substantial effect on the height of the next generation.

lessons.orientation: Say what penetrance, expressivity and heritability each mean, and decide from a case whether a pattern points to one gene with incomplete penetrance, to many genes plus environment, or to a shared environment.
lessons.nextAction: Count alleles in a population, use Hardy-Weinberg proportions to estimate carriers, and read a departure from them.

blocks.text: MedlinePlus Genetics notes that many carriers of a variant in BRCA1 or BRCA2 will develop cancer in their lifetime and some will not, and that doctors cannot predict which. A variant, it seems, does not fix what happens to the person who carries it.

The figure shows the same thing for an invented condition. Eight people carry one variant, five of them show the condition, and among those five the signs range from mild to severe. Several different quantities describe the gap between a genotype and a trait, and they are easy to confuse.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to tell penetrance, expressivity and heritability apart, and say what a heritability figure does and does not mean for one person.
intro.whyItMatters: Claims about the genes behind height or disease usually rest on these three ideas.

recap.keyIdea: Penetrance is whether a genotype shows, expressivity is how strongly, and heritability is a statistic about differences among people in one population, so none of them splits one person's trait into a genetic share and an environmental one.

blocks.text: Penetrance counts the carriers who show a trait, expressivity describes how much it varies among those who do, and both come from chance, the environment and other genes. Most common traits are polygenic, with many variants of modest effect and the environment contributing as well.

Heritability says how much of the variation among people in one population goes with genetic differences. It does not say which genes are involved, it is not the genetic share of one person's trait, a familial trait need not be heritable, and a trait with a high heritability can still be changed by the environment.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from families to whole populations, and shows how many carriers a rare recessive condition implies.

lessons.title: Hardy-Weinberg as a null model

lead.text: A population's genes can be described by how common each allele is. For a gene with two alleles, A and a, write **p** for the frequency of A and **q** for the frequency of a. Together they account for every copy of the gene, so $p + q = 1$. To find them you count alleles and not people, because each person has two copies: a homozygote contributes two copies of one allele and a heterozygote one copy of each. The Online Open Genetics textbook counts a sample of 500 people with 320 AA, 160 Aa and 20 aa. Their 1,000 copies of the gene hold 2 × 320 + 160 = 800 copies of A and 2 × 20 + 160 = 200 copies of a.

afterFigure.text: So $p = 800 / 1{,}000 = 0.8$ and $q = 200 / 1{,}000 = 0.2$. The frequency of an allele is a different quantity from the frequency of a genotype, and the difference is the factor of two for homozygotes.

reveal.text: Counting copies and not people is what makes the frequency comparable between populations, whatever their sizes.

lead.text: Given the allele frequencies, you can predict how alleles will pair up in the next generation. If mating is random with respect to the gene, a gamete carrying A meets another carrying A with probability $p \times p$, and in the same way the four pairings of the Punnett square have probabilities $p^2$, $pq$, $pq$ and $q^2$. The two middle pairings give the same genotype, so the expected genotype frequencies are $p^2$ for AA, $2pq$ for Aa and $q^2$ for aa. They add up to $(p + q)^2 = 1$, and the formula is called the **Hardy-Weinberg formula**.

For the sample of 500 people, with $p = 0.8$ and $q = 0.2$, it gives 0.64, 0.32 and 0.04, and 0.64 × 500 = 320, 0.32 × 500 = 160 and 0.04 × 500 = 20. The expected counts match the observed ones exactly, so that sample is already in Hardy-Weinberg proportions.

afterFigure.text: Two further facts follow. The allele frequencies stay the same from one generation to the next, since each generation's gametes carry the same mixture of A and a. And a population that begins with other genotype proportions reaches the Hardy-Weinberg ones after a single generation of random mating, and keeps them afterwards.

lead.text: The Hardy-Weinberg proportions describe what happens when nothing acts on a gene except the random pairing of gametes. They hold when mating is random with respect to the gene, when no genotype survives or reproduces better than another, when individuals neither enter nor leave the population, when no new alleles arise by mutation, and when the population is large enough that chance does not shift the frequencies. Few natural populations meet every condition, yet large populations of many species, humans included, come close for many genes.

That makes the formula a **null model**, a baseline for what to expect if none of those forces acts, so that a departure from it points to one of them. Hardy wrote his paper to debunk the view that a dominant allele would tend to become more common simply by being dominant, and the formula shows it does not: dominance changes which genotypes show the trait and leaves the allele frequencies where they were.

afterFigure.text: One distinction needs care. $p^2$ is the frequency of the AA genotype, whereas a dominant trait shows in both AA and Aa, so the proportion of people with the dominant trait is $p^2 + 2pq$.

reveal.text: The dominant trait is shown by everyone except the aa homozygotes, so the proportion can also be found as 1 minus $q^2$.

lead.text: The formula also runs backwards. A recessive condition affects only people with two copies of the allele, so the proportion affected is $q^2$, and $q$ is its square root. Carriers are the heterozygotes, $2pq$. When the allele is rare, $p$ is almost 1, so $2pq$ is almost $2q$, and the carrier frequency is about twice the square root of the incidence.

The square shows why that is so much larger than the incidence. For a rare allele the aa corner is tiny, while the two strips of heterozygotes beside the large AA block are many times bigger. The textbook figures for cystic fibrosis in people of European ancestry show the same gap, about 1 in 2,500 affected and about 1 in 25 carriers.

afterFigure.text: Carriers outnumber affected people by about a hundred to one, so most copies of a rare recessive allele sit in carriers, where the condition cannot show. That helps to explain why selection against a recessive condition does not remove its allele quickly, since recessive alleles can survive at low frequencies even under selection.

steps.headline: A recessive condition affects about 1 in 2,500 births in people of European ancestry. How common are carriers of the allele?

workedSteps.text: Only people with two copies are affected, so the incidence is $q^2$.
Take the square root to find the allele frequency.
The two alleles account for every copy, so $p$ is what remains.
Carriers are the heterozygotes, which have frequency $2pq$.
That is about 1 in 25.5, close to the textbook's figure of about 1 in 25, so roughly 4 percent of these people carry the allele.

steps.headline: A recessive condition affects 1 in 10,000 births. About what proportion of people carry one copy of the allele?

workedSteps.text: The incidence is $q^2$.
Say what the allele frequency is.
The two alleles account for every copy, so $p$ is what remains.
Say how common carriers are.

lead.text: The first line is done, and the two lines with blanks are yours.

A sample rarely matches the proportions exactly, and a clear departure is information. To read one, take the allele frequency from the counts, work out the expected genotype counts, and compare. Fewer heterozygotes than $2pq$ predicts, with both kinds of homozygote in excess, is the usual signature of non-random mating. Inbreeding raises homozygosity for every gene, because relatives are more likely to carry the same alleles. Pooling groups that have different allele frequencies has the same effect, as the figure shows, because each group alone is in the proportions and the mixture is not.

In the figure, village 1 has $p = 0.9$ and village 2 has $p = 0.5$, and each is in Hardy-Weinberg proportions. Pooling equal numbers of people from both gives AA 0.53, Aa 0.34 and aa 0.13, an allele frequency of 0.7, and the proportions that frequency expects are 0.49, 0.42 and 0.09. The heterozygotes are 0.08 short.

afterFigure.text: A departure says that something is acting and does not say what. Selection and non-random choice of mates both change genotype proportions, and in real genotype data a deviation can also be a sign of an error in genotyping, so more evidence has to decide. The reverse needs care too: proportions that fit say nothing about other genes or other generations.

reveal.text: The direction of the gap matters: a deficit of heterozygotes points to non-random mating or pooled groups, and another pattern in the counts would point elsewhere.

lead.text: For a gene on the X chromosome the proportions differ between the sexes. A man has one X, so he is affected whenever he carries the allele, and the proportion of affected men is $q$. A woman has two X chromosomes and is affected only with two copies, so the proportion of affected women is $q^2$.

Red-green colour blindness in western European men affects about 1 in 12, which gives $q$ of about 0.083. The formula predicts $q^2 = 0.007$ for women, and the observed figure is about 1 in 200, or 0.005, which is close to the Hardy-Weinberg proportions.

reveal.text: Because a woman needs the allele on both X chromosomes, the condition is much rarer in women than in men, as in red-green colour blindness.

lessons.orientation: Work out allele and genotype frequencies from counts, use Hardy-Weinberg proportions to estimate how many carriers a rare recessive condition implies, and read a departure from those proportions as evidence about mating, selection or sampling.
lessons.nextAction: Decide whether chance, selection, a bottleneck or a founder event best explains an allele pattern.

blocks.text: Cystic fibrosis affects about 1 in 2,500 people of European ancestry, yet about 1 in 25 of them are carriers, a hundred carriers for every person with the condition. Nobody found that figure by testing everyone. It follows from a formula that rests on how alleles pair up when mates are chosen at random.
The same formula gives a baseline for the question of whether anything is acting on a gene, because a population that departs from it is telling you something.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to count alleles from genotypes, estimate how many carriers a rare recessive condition implies, and read a departure from Hardy-Weinberg proportions.
intro.whyItMatters: The same arithmetic tells a counsellor how common carriers are and tells a population geneticist when something is acting on a gene.

recap.keyIdea: Allele frequencies give the genotype proportions $p^2$, $2pq$ and $q^2$ under random mating, and because few things in nature are random, a departure from those proportions points to something acting on the gene.

blocks.text: Counting copies of the gene gives the allele frequencies, with homozygotes counted twice, and the proportions $p^2$, $2pq$ and $q^2$ follow when mating is random and nothing else acts. For a rare recessive condition the incidence is $q^2$, so carriers number about twice its square root, far more than the affected people.

A deficit of heterozygotes suggests inbreeding or pooled groups, and any departure says that something is acting without saying what. For a gene on the X chromosome, men are affected at $q$ and women at $q^2$.

recap.nextHook: The proportions assume a large population, and the next lesson asks what chance and selection do when it is small.

lessons.title: Chance and selection in populations

lead.text: A jar holds 20 marbles, ten red and ten blue, and each colour stands for one allele of a gene. To make the next generation you draw a marble at random, put a new marble of the same colour in a second jar, and repeat until the second jar holds 20. Unless it holds exactly ten of each colour, the frequencies have shifted, although nothing favours either colour. A change of this kind, made by chance in the frequency of an existing allele, is called **genetic drift**.

Repeat the draw with each new jar and the numbers wander, sometimes towards red and sometimes towards blue. If one generation draws no red marbles at all, red is lost for good and blue is **fixed**, so that every later generation is entirely blue. The figure follows five such sequences for jars of 20 marbles and for jars of 200. In the 20-marble runs, three of the five reached a single colour within 40 generations, and in the 200-marble runs none did.

afterFigure.text: In small populations fixation can happen in a few generations. A lost allele cannot be replaced by chance, so drift pushes a population towards uniformity over time, although it has no direction of its own and follows only the arithmetic of chance. Only mutation or migration can bring a lost allele back.

diagram.alt: Five lines for each of two computer simulations of a jar of red and blue marbles, starting at half red, followed for 40 generations. With 20 marbles the lines wander widely and three of the five reach 0 or 1 and stay there. With 200 marbles the lines stay close to one half.
diagram.caption: One computer simulation. The dots mark where a line reached all blue or all red. Use the buttons to compare the two sizes.

reveal.text: Drift acts in every population, and it is a matter of degree: the fewer copies of an allele there are, the larger the chance swings.

lead.text: The marbles can be replaced by an exact count. A very large colony of bacteria is split evenly between two alleles, A and B, which are neutral, meaning that they do not affect survival or reproduction. The drop they live in shrinks until it can feed only four of them, and which four survive is random. Because the colony is so large, each survivor carries A with probability 1/2 whoever else survived, so each of the 16 possible combinations of four survivors has probability 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/16. Counting them by the number that carry A gives 1, 4, 6, 4 and 1 combinations.

afterFigure.text: Only six combinations hold two A and two B, so an even split has probability 6/16 = 0.375, and an uneven split has probability 10/16. An even split, the only outcome in which the allele frequencies are unchanged, is less likely than a change, and in two of the 16 combinations one allele is lost altogether. A population that contracts sharply to a few survivors in this way is called a **bottleneck**, and here the frequencies have changed by chance alone.

diagram.alt: A bar chart of the 16 equally likely combinations of four bacteria carrying alleles A and B, grouped by the number carrying A: none 1, one 4, two 6, three 4, four 1. Two A and two B is 6 of 16, any other mix is 10 of 16, and one allele lost altogether is 2 of 16.
diagram.caption: The even split is the largest single group and still less likely than all the others together.

reveal.text: Counting combinations works for any number of survivors, and the chance that one allele is lost shrinks quickly as the number grows.

lead.text: A bottleneck leaves a random sample of the alleles, whatever the cause of the shrinkage. In a true bottleneck the chance of survival is random and owes nothing to any inherent genetic advantage, so allele frequencies can change radically, independently of selection. In Illinois the greater prairie chicken fell from roughly 100 million birds in 1900 to roughly 50 in the 1990s, because of hunting and loss of habitat, and DNA from birds of the middle of the century and of the 1990s shows a steep fall in genetic variation over the last few decades.

A **founder effect** is a bottleneck of a particular kind: a small group splits off and forms a new population. Its alleles are a random sample that can misrepresent the original population, as the figure illustrates with invented numbers.

afterFigure.text: A well-documented case is the Amish colony that settled in Pennsylvania in 1744. Two of its members carried the same recessive allele, the one behind Ellis-van Creveld syndrome, and the colony stayed fairly insular, so after many generations of inbreeding the syndrome is far more common among the Amish than among people in general.

diagram.alt: Two rows of circles for copies of a gene. The source population has 100 copies of which 2 carry a rare allele, 2 percent. A colony founded by 20 people has 40 copies of which 2 carry the allele, 5 percent.
diagram.caption: Invented numbers for illustration. A small founding group can carry an allele at a share quite unlike the source's.

reveal.text: A founder effect needs nothing but a small group and chance, so it is the explanation to rule out before evidence of selection is sought.

lead.text: Selection, unlike drift, has a direction. It favours alleles whose effects raise survival or reproduction, lowers the frequency of alleles with unfavourable effects, and ignores neutral ones, while drift acts on frequencies without regard to what the alleles do. In nature the two always act together, and either can only work on the variation that mutation supplies.

Drift matters most when an allele is present in few copies, because the law of large numbers makes chance swings larger then. It can overwhelm weak selection, and while an advantageous allele is rare it is almost as likely to be lost by drift as a neutral one. Selection against a recessive allele has a further limit. The allele survives at low frequencies in carriers, where it does not show, and so it is not easily removed.

Selection can also keep a harmful allele. If a carrier does better than people with two copies of the allele or none at all, selection holds both alleles in the population, and the carrier's edge is called **heterozygote advantage**. The sickle cell allele is the well-established case. People with the benign sickle trait resist malaria, because in a carrier infected red cells sickle and are removed from the blood, which limits the infection. People with two copies typically die of sickle cell disease unless they have advanced medical care, and people with none are likelier to die of malaria.

The theory makes a prediction that can be checked. The allele is most frequent where malaria has been, and often still is, a serious problem. About 1 in 10 African Americans carries it, since their recent ancestors came from regions with heavy malaria. As effective antimalarial treatment spreads, the frequency of the allele is expected to fall, provided that treatments for sickle cell disease stay unavailable or only partly effective.

reveal.text: A good test is a prediction that could fail. Here the prediction is that carriers resist the infection, and the clearest failure is carriers being no better off.

lead.text: Cystic fibrosis is more common than any other genetic disease in people of European descent, with about 1 in 25 carriers, and that suggested carriers might have an advantage. Mice were used to test whether carriers resist cholera, and the results appeared in 1994: carrier mice had less secretory diarrhoea than mice with no copy, so for a time it seemed that cholera resistance explained why the carrier state is so frequent. Cholera, though, began killing Europeans only long after the allele's frequency was established. A human study then found that carriers were indistinguishable from non-carriers, and the earlier data had come from mice alone.

Other ideas have been put forward, among them resistance to tuberculosis and a respiratory advantage for early Europeans moving north, and the textbook notes speculation that the common allele, ΔF508, may give carriers some advantage.

afterFigure.text: The Wikipedia article on heterozygote advantage says that, as of 2016, what selective pressure lies behind the high frequency of cystic fibrosis alleles remained unclear, and unbiased drift could account for it instead of an advantage. The careful statement is that the question is open: selection and drift are both possible, and evidence about carriers is what would choose between them.

reveal.text: A result in a model organism is a reason to look in people. It is not an answer, and a null result in one study does not hand the question to the rival explanation either.

lessons.orientation: Decide whether chance, selection, a bottleneck or a founder event is the better explanation for a change in allele frequency or an unusually common allele, and say what evidence would separate the explanations.
lessons.nextAction: Read a genetic test result, say what it can and cannot tell the person, and state a risk fairly.

blocks.text: About 1 in 25 people of European descent carry an allele for cystic fibrosis, and about 1 in 10 African Americans carry the sickle cell allele, although two copies of either one cause serious disease. A common harmful allele asks for an explanation, and there are two obvious candidates: carrying one copy might give an advantage that selection favours, or the allele might have become common by chance.
Chance is easy to underestimate, because it has no purpose and leaves no obvious sign, so the first step is to see how much it can do on its own, starting from a small calculation.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose between chance, selection, a bottleneck and a founder event as the explanation for an allele pattern, and say what evidence would decide.
intro.whyItMatters: It is how you judge claims about why a disease allele is common in one group of people.

recap.keyIdea: Chance changes allele frequencies at random, and more so when few copies are present, so a common allele needs evidence of selection before selection is the explanation, and the evidence has to come from carriers.

blocks.text: Drift changes frequencies by chance and has no direction. It acts in every population and most strongly in small ones, where an allele can be lost or fixed in a few generations. A bottleneck or a founder event leaves a random sample of alleles, which can leave an allele common without any selection.

Selection has a direction and can hold a harmful allele when carriers do better, as with the sickle cell allele and malaria. To choose between selection and drift you need a prediction that could fail, such as carriers doing better against the infection, and a result in mice does not settle the question for people, as the cystic fibrosis case shows.

recap.nextHook: Chance and selection shape what a population carries, and the next lesson asks what a genetic test can tell a person who has taken one.

lessons.title: What a genetic test tells you

lead.text: A genetic test is chosen to answer one question, and the common tests differ mainly in how much of the genome they read. A **targeted single variant test** looks for one specific change in one gene, usually a change already known to cause a disorder, and it is the natural choice for a relative of someone whose variant has been found. A single gene test reads the whole of one gene for any change in it, so it fits a suspected condition that many different variants of that gene can cause. A **gene panel** reads several genes at once, and it is used when symptoms fit a wide array of conditions.

When those tests find nothing, or when the cause is unclear from the start, **exome sequencing** reads the parts of the genome that code for proteins, and genome sequencing reads all of the DNA. The figure orders the five by how much they read.

afterFigure.text: Some tests do not read gene sequences at all. A chromosomal test finds large changes, such as a missing or extra chromosome or a missing piece of one, a gene expression test shows which genes are active in a cell, and a biochemical test measures the amount or activity of a protein or enzyme that a gene makes. The tests that consumers can order directly usually check a set of specific variants in particular genes, which makes them closer to a targeted test than to a full reading of each gene.

reveal.text: Exome and genome sequencing are often more cost and time effective than running several single gene or panel tests one after another, which is one reason they are used when the cause is unclear.

lead.text: In a positive result the laboratory has found a change in the gene, chromosome or protein under examination. Depending on why the test was done, that can confirm a diagnosis, show that a person is a carrier, or point to a raised risk of disease. A predictive test that comes back positive usually cannot give the exact risk, and it often cannot say whether symptoms will appear, how severe they will be or how the disorder will progress. The National Cancer Institute makes the same point about BRCA changes: a positive result cannot tell whether or when a person will develop cancer, and some people who inherit a harmful change never do.

A negative result means that the laboratory found no change known to affect health in what it examined, and what that is worth depends on the case, as the two women in the opening show. When a close relative is known to carry a particular harmful BRCA change and the laboratory knew to look for it, a negative result is clear: the woman did not inherit that change and cannot pass it to her children. She still has the cancer risks of the general population, and her family history may place her higher. When no harmful variant is known in the family, a negative result adds nothing to what her family history and other risk factors already showed, and many tests cannot detect every change that can cause a disorder.

A laboratory that finds a variant also places it in one of five classes, judged from the research done so far on how likely the variant is to cause disease. A **pathogenic** variant is responsible for disease, with ample research supporting the link, and a likely pathogenic variant *probably* is, although there is not enough research to be certain. At the other end a benign variant is not responsible for disease, with ample research disproving the link, and a likely benign variant probably is not. In the middle sits the **variant of uncertain significance**, written VUS, whose role in disease can be neither confirmed nor refuted because the research is too thin or because it conflicts.

afterFigure.text: The classes describe the state of the evidence on the day of the report, so a variant's class can change as research accumulates, and variants are re-evaluated from time to time. Each variant is judged on its own: a gene linked to a disease does not make every variant in it pathogenic, and a variant pathogenic for one disease may be harmless for another. For BRCA tests the National Cancer Institute reports that most variants of uncertain significance are reclassified as benign once more data become available.

reveal.text: A variant of uncertain significance can move in either direction as research accumulates, so a clinician returns to the classification from time to time.

lead.text: A positive result is usually followed by a risk figure, and how the figure is stated decides what a person takes from it. For ovarian cancer the National Cancer Institute gives lifetime risks of about 39% to 58% for women who carry a harmful BRCA1 change and 13% to 29% for those with a BRCA2 change, against about 1.1% for women in the general population. Each percentage is an **absolute risk**, the chance that a woman in that group develops the cancer during her lifetime, and the figure pictures each one as a count out of 100 women.

afterFigure.text: The same figures support two statements that answer different questions. Compared with the general population, 39% to 58% against 1.1% is roughly 35 to 53 times as high, and that ratio is the **relative risk**, which says how much larger one risk is than another. In absolute terms, 100 less 58 and 100 less 39 leave 42 to 61 of every 100 BRCA1 carriers who are not expected to develop ovarian cancer. A fair account of the result gives both: the risk is many times the average, and for a large share of carriers the cancer does not occur.

steps.headline: A harmful BRCA2 change carries a 5% to 10% lifetime risk of pancreatic cancer, against about 1.7% in the general population. How should that risk be stated?

lead.text: These are the National Cancer Institute's figures, and each is an absolute risk for one group.

workedSteps.text: Write the two absolute risks side by side: carriers first, then the general population.
Divide each end of the carrier range by the general figure, to say how many times larger the risk is.
Now take the carriers' side. Of 100 carriers, 5 to 10 are expected to develop pancreatic cancer, and the rest are not.
Put the ratio and the count into one sentence that overstates neither.

lead.text: A laboratory can detect a variant perfectly and the test can still tell a person little, because three separate questions are involved. **Analytical validity** asks whether the test accurately shows that a particular variant is present or absent. **Clinical validity** asks how closely that variant is tied to having, lacking or being at risk of a particular disease. **Clinical utility** asks whether the result can guide decisions about diagnosis, treatment, management or prevention.

In the United States the CLIA standards cover how laboratories perform tests, the qualifications of their staff and their quality control, and they are designed to ensure analytical validity. They do not address clinical validity or clinical utility. The Food and Drug Administration requires information about clinical validity for some tests, particularly those that can influence a person's medical care, and test takers, health care providers and insurers often judge utility. For tests sold directly to the public the position is less clear, because some providers are not CLIA-certified and many such tests are not regulated by the FDA.

reveal.text: The FDA looks at clinical validity for some tests, particularly those that can influence a person's medical care, so a CLIA certificate and FDA review answer different questions.

steps.headline: What wide tests miss and add

lead.text: Reading more of the genome does not remove the limits. Exons, the stretches of genes that provide instructions for proteins, are thought to make up about 1 percent of a person's genome. Most known disease-causing changes lie in exons, which makes [[exome sequencing|Reading the protein-coding parts of the genome. Met earlier in this lesson.]] an efficient first look, but changes outside the exons can alter gene activity and protein production and cause disorders, and exome sequencing would miss them. A negative exome result therefore means that no explanation was found in the exons. Genome sequencing reads all of the DNA, and both methods find many more changes than a single gene test does, so the significance of much of what they find is unknown.

A wide test can also return a **secondary finding**, a variant in a gene unrelated to the reason for the test. ACMG, a United States professional college for medical genetics and genomics, recommended in its 2021 update that laboratories report variants in a list of 73 genes, chosen because the conditions they cause can be recognised early and acted on. People having exome or genome sequencing can opt out of receiving those results, and [[variants of uncertain significance|Variants whose role in disease can be neither confirmed nor refuted. Met earlier in this lesson.]] in the 73 genes are not reported.

reveal.text: The National Cancer Institute recommends genetic counselling for people who use direct-to-consumer testing, to help them understand the results and to make sure the most suitable test was done.

lessons.orientation: Read a genetic test result: say which question the test was built to answer, what a positive, negative or uncertain result does and does not tell this person, and how to state a risk figure fairly.
lessons.reviewLabel: What a genetic test tells you
lessons.nextAction: Compute an odds ratio from allele counts and explain why a genome-wide scan needs a significance threshold of $5 \times 10^{-8}$.

blocks.text: Two women each take a test for harmful changes in the BRCA genes, and each is told that the result is negative. The first has a sister who is known to carry a particular harmful change in BRCA1, and the laboratory was told to look for that change. The second has no known family variant, so her test had no particular change to look for.

The report uses the same word for both, and a clinician will read the two results quite differently. A result answers only the question its test was built to ask, so the first thing to settle about any genetic test is what it was looking for.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what a genetic test result does and does not tell a person, and to state a risk figure fairly.
intro.whyItMatters: Reading a result for what it can show spares a person false reassurance and needless alarm.

recap.keyIdea: A genetic result answers only the question its test was built to ask, so reading one means asking what was looked for, what was found and how the risk is stated.

blocks.text: You saw that the same word, negative, is clear for a woman tested for a known family variant and adds little for a woman with no known variant, and that a [[variant of uncertain significance|A variant that cannot be confirmed to play a role in disease. Met earlier in this lesson.]] is usually reclassified as benign, with care following family history until then. You stated BRCA risks as a ratio and as a count, and you kept apart the accuracy of a laboratory, the link between a variant and a disease, and the usefulness of a result.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson reads a genome-wide scan, in which a million SNPs are compared at once and a strict threshold decides which results count.

lessons.title: Genome scans and risk scores

steps.headline: Cases, controls and the odds ratio

lead.text: The usual design is a case-control study. One large group of people has the disease, and they are the **cases**. Another large group of similar people does not, and they are the **controls**. Every person is genotyped at [[SNPs|Single-base variants found in at least 1 percent of people. Met in 'Genes, variants and the rest of the genome'.]] spread across the genome, typically a million or more, and for each SNP the question is whether one allele is more frequent among the cases. The answer is reported as an **odds ratio**, together with a p-value.

Take an invented SNP with alleles T and C. Allele T is counted 600 times among the cases and 500 times among the controls, and allele C 400 times among the cases and 500 times among the controls. The odds ratio for T is the ratio of two ratios: the first compares the cases' count of T with the controls' (600 to 500), the second compares the cases' count of C with the controls' (400 to 500), and the odds ratio divides the first by the second.

afterFigure.text: An odds ratio of 1 means the allele is as frequent among the cases as among the controls, and a value above 1 means it is more frequent among the cases. Real scans find small effects. The median odds ratio per risk SNP is about 1.33 and only a few exceed 3.0, so the 1.5 of this example is above the median for a scan.

diagram.alt: A table of invented allele counts: allele T 600 in cases and 500 in controls, allele C 400 in cases and 500 in controls. The second view works out the odds ratio for allele T as 600 over 500, which is 1.2, divided by 400 over 500, which is 0.8, giving 1.5.

Work out the two ratios, A over B and X over Y, and divide the first by the second.
Read the result against what scans usually find.

steps.headline: A bar set by the number of tests

lead.text: The arithmetic behind the opening question decides how strict a scan has to be. A p-value below 0.05 turns up by chance in about 1 test in 20, so a million tests at that cut-off flag about $0.05 \times 1{,}000{,}000 = 50{,}000$ SNPs even if none of them is linked to the disease. Genome-wide studies therefore require $p < 5 \times 10^{-8}$, and at that level the same million tests are expected to give $5 \times 10^{-8} \times 1{,}000{,}000 = 0.05$ chance hits, which is a chance hit in about one scan in twenty.

The threshold depends on how many tests are made. It does not shrink for a larger effect or loosen for a smaller study. Scans also guard against false positives in other ways: they first analyse a discovery group and then check their best SNPs in an independent validation group, and they account for the geographic and ethnic background of participants. Many variants differ in frequency between populations, so a difference in ancestry between cases and controls can produce a false signal.

reveal.text: Scans guard against chance results by checking their most significant SNPs in an independent validation group before treating them as findings.

lead.text: Once every SNP has a p-value, the results are drawn as a **Manhattan plot**. Each dot is one SNP, placed from left to right by its position along the chromosomes, and its height is the negative logarithm of its p-value, so a smaller p-value stands higher. The threshold becomes a horizontal line at about 7.3, because $-\log_{10}(5 \times 10^{-8})$ is 7.3, and only dots above it count as significant. Nearby SNPs tend to be inherited together, so a real signal rises as a stack of dots and not as a single one, and the stacks give the plot its skyline.

afterFigure.text: In the invented plot the highest stack is on chromosome 6, a second clears the line on chromosome 11, and one on chromosome 2 stops short of it, so it does not count however far it stands above the dots around it. The second view enlarges the stack on chromosome 6. The SNP at its top has the strongest association in the region, which is a different matter from being the variant that affects the disease. A genotyping chip reads only a sample of the variants in a region and relies on nearby variants travelling together, so the top SNP may simply be tagging along with a causal variant that is not on the chip at all.

An associated region can hold hundreds of variants across several genes. **Fine-mapping** narrows them to a set that is likely to include the causal variant, and it needs dense coverage, very good genotypes and large samples, which is why it is done less often than the scan.

A tall stack on chromosome 6 and a shorter one on chromosome 11 rise above the line, and a stack on chromosome 2 stops below it. The second view enlarges the stack on chromosome 6, marks the top SNP, and shows a causal variant near gene B that is not on the chip.

reveal.text: A stack that reaches the line is where the work starts: replication in a second group and fine-mapping come before anyone names a causal variant.

lead.text: A single SNP from a scan explains only a small share of the risk of a common disease, so researchers add many of them up. A **polygenic score** summarises the effects of many variants in one number, calculated as a weighted sum of the trait-associated alleles a person carries, with the weights taken from the results of scans. For a disease it is called a polygenic risk score. Across a population the scores form a bell curve, with most people near the middle and a few in each tail.

afterFigure.text: What a score gives is a rank. It tells you how a person's risk compares with that of other people, which is a relative risk, and it is built from scans that compared cases with controls. It carries no baseline, the risk that an average person faces, and no timeframe, the period over which a risk is counted. To state an absolute chance the score has to be combined with a baseline for a given population and period, and even then the figure is a probability that cannot say whether one person will develop the disease.

diagram.alt: A bell curve of polygenic scores with the low tail shaded green and labelled lower relative risk, the middle labelled most people, and the high tail shaded orange and labelled higher relative risk. A note says that a score gives no baseline risk and no time period.
diagram.caption: A score places a person on the curve. The curve says nothing about how large the risk is in absolute terms.

steps.headline: An invented score doubles a person's relative risk for conditions P and Q, whose average lifetime risks are 10 in 100 and 0.5 in 100. What follows for each?

workedSteps.text: The score is a relative statement: the person's risk is twice the average for each condition.
Multiply the average by 2 to turn the relative risk into an absolute one. Start with condition P.
Do the same for condition Q.
Compare how much the absolute risk has changed for each condition.

reveal.text: Wikipedia adds that a person's genetic liability does not change over a lifespan, and that the risk arising from it has to be read in the context of environmental factors.

lead.text: Predictive power is often summarised by the area under the ROC curve, written **AUC**, which runs from 0 to 1, and a larger value means better prediction. A 2018 coronary disease score built from about 120,000 British people reached an AUC of about 0.64 from genetic information alone, and about 0.80 once age and sex were added. For hypothyroidism the figures were about 0.71 and about 0.78. Most scores are not predictive enough to diagnose, and they are more useful beside other information such as age, body mass index and smoking status.

An average can hide a useful case. A score that is weak across a whole population may still predict well for people at the extremes: in a landmark study of cardiovascular disease, people in the top 1% of scores had a lifetime risk above 10%, comparable to that of people with rare variants that cause it.

Scores also depend on whose genomes built them. In 2021 most of the available data still came from people of European ancestry, which is why scores generally perform better in that ancestry, and the National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI) says that their accuracy may be valid and useful only for European ancestry populations at present. Some causal variants are shared between ancestries, and researchers are calling for new scans in more diverse groups.

reveal.text: The source says that more diverse biobanks are needed to spread the benefits of score-based medicine more evenly.

lessons.orientation: Read a genome-wide association result: compute and interpret an odds ratio, explain the strict significance threshold, say why a top SNP need not be causal, and turn a polygenic score into relative and absolute risk without overclaiming.
lessons.nextAction: Choose between end joining, a repair template and a base editor for a stated editing goal, and say what can go wrong.

blocks.text: A landmark study of 2005 compared 96 people with age-related macular degeneration, a common form of blindness, with 50 healthy people, and it found two single-nucleotide polymorphisms, or SNPs, whose alleles were more frequent in one group than in the other. Both lay in a gene that makes complement factor H, a protein that helps regulate inflammation, and the finding was unexpected.

A scan today reads a million or more SNPs in every participant and asks the same question of each one: is an allele more frequent in the people with the disease than in similar people without it? A scan that asks one question a million times changes what a single answer is worth.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to compute an odds ratio, explain the genome-wide threshold, read a Manhattan plot, and say what a polygenic score does and does not tell a person.
intro.whyItMatters: Reports that a SNP or a score is linked to a disease rest on these steps, and each one is easy to misread.

recap.keyIdea: A genome-wide scan finds regions associated with a disease by testing a million SNPs against a strict threshold, and a polygenic score turns the results into a relative rank that gives no absolute chance on its own.

blocks.text: You computed an odds ratio from allele counts and saw why a cut-off of 0.05 would flag about 50,000 SNPs by chance in a scan of a million. You read a [[Manhattan plot|A plot of the negative logarithm of each SNP's p-value along the genome. Met earlier in this lesson.]] as a set of regions, because the top SNP of a stack may only be tagging along with the causal variant, and you turned an invented relative risk of 2 into very different absolute risks for two conditions. You also weighed what AUC values and the ancestry of the data say about how far a score can be trusted.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson turns from reading the genome to changing it, and asks which editing route fits a goal and what can go wrong.

lessons.title: Editing a genome

lead.text: Genome editing uses the same two parts as the bacterial system. The **guide RNA** carries a target sequence of 20 bases, which can be written to match any chosen site, and it also attaches to the Cas9 enzyme. Where the guide matches the DNA, Cas9 cuts it. The guide is a separate molecule from Cas9, so a new target needs only a new guide.

afterFigure.text: Cas9 has a second requirement that the guide cannot change. It recognises a short sequence beside the target, called the **PAM**, and for the Cas9 most often used the PAM is the sequence NGG. That sequence is short and unspecific. In the human genome it turns up about once in every 8 to 12 base pairs, which works out to a few hundred million sites across about 3 billion bases, so the PAM cannot pick out one gene. The 20-base match does that, and the two together give the system its specificity, which is high but not perfect.

reveal.text: Engineered versions of Cas9, shortened or stabilised guides and computer tools that predict a guide's specificity are all used to reduce off-target effects.

steps.headline: Three ways to finish the job

lead.text: A cut is repaired by the cell's own machinery, and the route the cell takes decides what the edit is. When the cell simply rejoins the ends, by a process called end joining, the repair often leaves random deletions or insertions at the cut, and these can disrupt the gene. The result is a **knockout**: the gene stops working, though the researcher cannot choose how. When the researcher supplies a repair template, a piece of DNA that matches the sequence on either side of the cut and carries the sequence wanted, the cell can use it to repair the break by homology-directed repair. The result is a **knock-in**, a chosen sequence placed at an exact site, and the template has to be designed for each application.

afterFigure.text: A **base editor** avoids the break. Cas9 is fused to an enzyme that changes one base directly, such as C to T or A to G, so the DNA is changed without cutting it and no donor template is required. Base editors can edit only point mutations, so they suit a single-base change and nothing larger.

reveal.text: Where a single base has to change and no template is supplied, the choice is a base editor, and the choice shifts to a template once a longer chosen sequence is wanted.

lead.text: Each part of the system can fail. Off-target effects, which are changes at sites other than the intended one, have serious consequences for a cell's genome, so researchers have engineered Cas9 variants and guides that reduce them. Delivery is a second problem. Cas9 and its guide come from bacteria, so cells can mount an immune response against them, and a virus used to carry them has a small capacity while the Cas9 gene is large, which led researchers to take smaller versions of Cas9 from other bacteria. Delivery can also damage cells, and sometimes the damage kills them.

afterFigure.text: An edit may also fail to reach every copy. A 2015 report of editing in non-viable human embryos described changing only some of the intended genes, with off-target changes in others. In 2018 a researcher said that he had edited two human embryos so that CCR5, a gene whose protein HIV uses to get into cells, would stop working. He reported that the twin girls born from the embryos had working copies of CCR5 as well as disabled ones. That state is called **mosaicism**: the cells of one individual carry different versions of a gene. People widely judged the work to be unethical, dangerous and premature.

steps.headline: Edits that stay and edits that could be inherited

lead.text: Casgevy was the first drug approved anywhere that uses CRISPR gene editing. The United Kingdom's medicines regulator approved it in November 2023 to treat sickle-cell disease and beta thalassemia, and the United States Food and Drug Administration approved it in December 2023. It acts on genes in a patient's own blood stem cells. That makes it a **somatic** edit: the changes are made in body cells, they stay within certain tissues, and they do not pass to the next generation.

Edits to egg or sperm cells, or to an embryo, can be inherited by later generations, and they are called **germline** edits. An international summit on human gene editing in 2015 drew the same distinction: in somatic cells the effects of an edit are limited to a single individual, while in germline cells the changes can be inherited by descendants. MedlinePlus reports that germline and embryo editing are against the law in the US and many other countries, on grounds of ethics and safety. Its page carries no date, so the law as it stands today needs checking.

lessons.orientation: Choose and critique a genome-editing approach for a stated goal: which repair route gives a knockout and which a precise change, what a guide RNA must match, what can go wrong, and what changes when the edited cells are germline.
lessons.nextAction: Say what an epigenetic mark is and judge a claim about it by which generation is first free of direct exposure.

blocks.text: Bacteria defend themselves against viruses with a system that keeps short pieces of each virus's DNA. When the same virus attacks again, the bacteria make RNA from those pieces, the RNA finds and attaches to the matching viral DNA, and an enzyme such as Cas9 cuts that DNA apart.

Researchers adapted the system by writing a guide of their own, a short RNA that attaches to a chosen target in a cell's DNA and brings Cas9 to cut it there. Cutting is the easy part of editing. What follows the cut decides the result, and that is largely left to the cell.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to choose an editing route for a goal, say what can go wrong, and tell an edit that stays in one person from one that could be inherited.
intro.whyItMatters: A report that an edit worked depends on the route used, on what else changed, and on which cells carry the change.

recap.keyIdea: Cas9 cuts where a guide RNA matches, the cell's repair route decides what the edit is, and whether the edited cells are body cells or germline decides who can inherit it.

blocks.text: You chose between end joining, a repair template and a base editor for different goals, and saw that the 20-base match aims the cut because a PAM turns up every 8 to 12 base pairs. You met off-target changes, delivery problems and [[mosaicism|The cells of one individual carry different versions of a gene. Met earlier in this lesson.]] as limits on an edit, and kept a somatic edit apart from one that could be inherited. You also settled an apparent disagreement between two sources by checking when each was written.

recap.nextHook: The next lesson weighs a different kind of claim, about marks on the genome that change gene activity without changing the sequence.

lessons.title: Weighing epigenetic claims

steps.headline: Marks on top of the sequence

lead.text: An **epigenetic mark** is a chemical modification attached to DNA or to the proteins it wraps around, and it affects whether a gene is on without changing a single base of the sequence. The best known is **DNA methylation**, in which small chemical groups called methyl groups are attached to the building blocks of DNA. A gene that carries methyl groups is turned off, and no protein is made from it. A second kind is **histone modification**: DNA is wrapped around histone proteins, and chemical groups added to or removed from the histones change how tightly it is wrapped, which affects whether the gene can be turned on. All the marks in a genome together make up its epigenome.

These marks do real work. They help each cell make only the proteins its function needs, they are maintained from cell to cell when cells divide, and they differ among people, among tissues and even among cells of one tissue. Environmental influences such as diet and exposure to pollutants can affect them, and errors, such as marking the wrong gene, can alter gene activity and have been found to relate to cancers, metabolic disorders and degenerative disorders. These effects are not permanent changes to the DNA, so on their own they cannot be selected in an evolutionary context.

In a female mammal one of the two X chromosomes is chosen at random in each cell and marked for inactivation, and the mark is maintained when the cell divides, so a patch of cells descended from one cell has the same X switched off. A cat that is [[heterozygous|Carrying two different alleles of the same gene. Met in 'What could the offspring inherit?' in Biology: Cells to Ecosystems.]] for an orange and a black coat colour allele on its X chromosomes shows the result. Patches of skin cells have different X chromosomes inactivated, which gives the mottled coat called tortoiseshell. Every cell has the same DNA sequence, and the patches differ only in which X is active.

afterFigure.text: **Imprinting** is a second well-supported case. For some genes the mark depends on which parent supplied the copy, because the mother and the father give different epigenetic patterns to particular places in the genome through their germ cells. The best-known human example is a deletion of part of chromosome 15, which produces Angelman syndrome or Prader-Willi syndrome depending on whether the deleted chromosome came from the child's mother or her father. The deletion is the same in both, and the parent of origin makes the difference.

steps.headline: Why inheritance is hard to show

lead.text: Whether marks pass from one generation to the next is a separate question from whether they exist, and in mammals the evidence is hard to gather. Epigenetic marks are erased twice in the life cycle: just after fertilisation, and again in the developing primordial germ cells, which are the precursors of eggs and sperm. A mark can be inherited only if it escapes both erasures. Some rare sites do escape, and parental imprinting arises in part because some maternal DNA methylation escapes the first erasure. The inheritance of a mark acquired through the environment is called **transgenerational epigenetic inheritance**.

The erasures are one reason these studies are disputed. Another is that exposure and inheritance are hard to separate: the mother's uterine environment and the care a baby receives after birth can produce effects that look inherited. Marks that are inherited also tend to fade, since most multigenerational epigenetic traits reported in other organisms are gradually lost over several generations.

steps.headline: The first generation free of exposure

lead.text: Call the exposed person F0, her children F1, their children F2, and so on. Exposure reaches further than the person exposed, because the germ cells inside a person are exposed as well. A father's sperm are exposed along with him, so the children conceived from them are exposed through their origin, and F2 is the first generation whose cells never met the exposure. A pregnant mother exposes her fetus, F1, and the germ cells that fetus carries, which will form F2, so her first generation with no direct exposure is F3.

afterFigure.text: That counting is the reason for the proposed criteria for showing transgenerational inheritance in mammals. The effect has to appear in a generation entirely free from direct exposure, which is F2 or later for paternal exposure and F3 or later for maternal exposure, and the study should also show that the mark persists in the germline and in the tissue where the effect appears and should exclude differences in the DNA sequence.
An effect seen in F1 or F2 after a mother was exposed in pregnancy is therefore an effect of exposure in the womb, called **fetal programming**, and is not yet evidence of inheritance.

steps.headline: Pregnant women went hungry in the Dutch hunger winter, and effects were reported in their children and grandchildren. Does that show epigenetic inheritance?

lead.text: During the Dutch hunger winter of 1944 and 1945, babies exposed in the third trimester were smaller than babies born in the previous year, and a raised risk of metabolic and cardiovascular disease was reported in them and in their children.

workedSteps.text: Label the generations: the pregnant women are F0 and the babies they carried are F1.
workedSteps.math: F0: pregnant women, F1: their babies

workedSteps.text: A baby's germ cells are present before birth. Decide who counts as directly exposed.
Decide which generation is the first with no direct exposure.
Decide what a raised risk in the babies' children shows.

reveal.text: In the same study, diabetes mortality in the grandchildren rose when food had been plentiful, and Wikipedia describes the findings as suggesting inheritance, which is as far as an observational study can take them.

steps.headline: What a study has to show

lead.text: Even an effect in an unexposed generation needs more before it counts as inheritance. The proposed framework asks that the mark persist in the germline and in the tissue where the effect appears, that differences in the DNA sequence be excluded by sequencing the genome, and that the study use controls such as in vitro fertilisation and cross-fostering, which separate transmission through the germ cells from the womb and from early care. Human studies are observational and rarely supply these. A 2026 review of studies of trauma in populations exposed to war and genocide found that the reported methylation differences in parents and children were inconsistent, and it concluded that human observational studies cannot establish inheritance or causality. The samples are small, the designs are cross-sectional, and biological transmission cannot be told apart from what a family shares in its surroundings and culture.

Within one lifetime the evidence is clearer. A study of 40 pairs of healthy identical twins aged 3 to 74 found that the epigenetic differences between the two members of a pair grow with age, although their DNA sequences are the same, so time and environment do alter the epigenome. That is a finding about a single lifetime and says nothing about inheritance. Wikipedia also reports that two writers have advised caution against pseudoscientific claims, made outside the field, that people can alter their genes and their health through mind control.

reveal.text: The supported statements describe what marks do within one body or one lifetime, and the others claim effects that carry across generations or that have no evidence behind them.
To support the inheritance claim, a study would need the effect in the first generation free of direct exposure and the mark in the germline.

lessons.orientation: Say what epigenetic marks are and do, separate what is well supported (cell identity, X inactivation, imprinting, change with age) from what is contested (transgenerational inheritance in humans), and judge a claim by which generation is first free of direct exposure.
lessons.nextAction: You can now say what an epigenetic mark is, sort a claim into what is well supported and what is not established in humans, and find the first generation free of direct exposure.

blocks.text: A bone-forming cell and a muscle cell in the same person carry the same DNA sequence, and each makes only the proteins that its job needs. Epigenetics studies how cells regulate which genes are active while leaving that sequence unchanged, and in the cases where it is best understood the evidence is strong.
Claims about epigenetics reach much further, to the effects of famine on grandchildren, of trauma on children and of habits on a person's genes, and the evidence behind them varies a great deal.

intro.promise: By the end you'll be able to say what epigenetic marks do, sort claims about them by the evidence, and find the first generation free of direct exposure.
intro.whyItMatters: Epigenetic claims in the news range from well established to unsupported, and a few questions about the evidence tell them apart.

recap.keyIdea: Epigenetic marks change how a gene is used without changing its sequence, and a claim that an effect is inherited has to show it in a generation that was never directly exposed.

blocks.text: You met marks that are well supported, X inactivation in a tortoiseshell cat, imprinting on chromosome 15 and the growing differences between identical twins, and you saw why inheritance across generations is hard to show: marks are erased twice, and the exposure of a pregnant mother reaches her fetus and its germ cells. You counted generations for a famine and for a paternal study, and weighed a wellness claim and a study design against the criteria.

questions.prompt: Suppose a single-base difference between two people fell at a position chosen at random along the DNA. Using the figures above, where is it most likely to fall?
hints: Which kind of place covers more of the DNA, protein-coding sequence or the rest?
A position chosen at random lands in each kind of place in proportion to how much DNA that kind covers.

acceptedIdeas: Outside protein-coding sequence, because about 99 percent of the DNA is noncoding
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Outside protein-coding sequence, because about 99 percent of the DNA is noncoding

choices.label: Inside a gene that makes a protein, because genes are what differ between people
Outside protein-coding sequence, because about 99 percent of the DNA is noncoding
Equally often inside and outside protein-coding sequence, because either is possible

questions.onCorrect: A random position falls in noncoding DNA about 99 times in 100, so most differences are not in protein-coding sequence.

misconceptions.feedback: Protein-coding sequence is only about 1 percent of the DNA, so a position chosen at random seldom lands in it.
Either place is possible, but the two cover very different amounts of DNA, so they are not equally likely.

questions.prompt: An invented headline reads: 'Your DNA differs from everyone else's at millions of places.' A person carries 4 to 5 million SNPs among about 3 billion bases. What does that number say about how alike two people are?
hints: Compare the number of SNPs with the 3 billion positions they are spread over.
Work out roughly what share 5 million is of 3 billion before deciding whether it is large.

acceptedIdeas: Two people match at over 99 percent of their bases, because millions is a small share of 3 billion
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two people match at over 99 percent of their bases, because millions is a small share of 3 billion

choices.label: Two people match at about 99 percent of their bases, because about 1 percent of positions differ
Two people differ mainly inside protein-coding genes, because those are the DNA that varies
Two people match at over 99 percent of their bases, because millions is a small share of 3 billion
Two people are quite unlike at the DNA level, because millions of differences is a very large number

questions.onCorrect: Under 0.2 percent of positions differ, which fits with more than 99 percent of bases being the same in all people.

misconceptions.feedback: One percent of 3 billion bases would be 30 million positions, several times the 4 to 5 million SNPs a person carries.
Most SNPs lie in the DNA between genes, and protein-coding sequence is only about 1 percent of the genome, so the differences are not mainly in genes.
A count means little without the total it comes from, and millions of positions out of 3 billion is under 0.2 percent.

questions.prompt: An invented health leaflet on sickle cell disease says that people with the condition 'have the sickle cell gene'. The gene HBB gives the instructions for beta-globin, a part of the haemoglobin inside red blood cells. Which correction of the leaflet is most accurate?
hints: Ask whether the gene itself or a version of it is what differs between people.
Beta-globin is part of the haemoglobin carried in red blood cells, and everyone has red blood cells.

acceptedIdeas: Everyone has the HBB gene, and the disease comes from a variant that changes how the gene works
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Everyone has the HBB gene, and the disease comes from a variant that changes how the gene works

choices.label: Only people with the disease have the HBB gene, because other people make haemoglobin without it
People with the disease carry an extra gene that other people do not have
A person with one copy of the variant has no HBB gene left, so cannot make beta-globin
Everyone has the HBB gene, and the disease comes from a variant that changes how the gene works

questions.onCorrect: The leaflet's phrase is a shortcut. The difference lies in the variant, not in having the gene.

misconceptions.feedback: Haemoglobin includes beta-globin, which HBB codes for, so everyone has the gene. What differs between people is the version of it.
No extra gene is involved. The condition arises from a variant in a gene that everyone has.
A variant changes one version of a gene and does not remove the gene, and people typically have two copies of each gene.

questions.prompt: A student reads that a variant lies inside an intron and says that it cannot matter, because introns are removed before a protein is made. The intron contains an enhancer for the gene it sits in. What is the best reply to the student?
hints: Ask what an enhancer does and whether that depends on the intron being removed from the RNA.
Regulatory elements are noncoding DNA, and introns are noncoding too.

acceptedIdeas: The enhancer still acts on the gene, so a variant in the intron may change how much protein is made
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The enhancer still acts on the gene, so a variant in the intron may change how much protein is made

choices.label: The student is right, because only the exons of a gene can be affected by any variant inside it
The variant must change an amino acid, because it lies within the boundaries of the gene itself
The enhancer still acts on the gene, so a variant in the intron may change how much protein is made

questions.onCorrect: Regulatory elements such as enhancers can sit in introns, so a variant there can change how the gene is controlled.

misconceptions.feedback: A variant can fall anywhere in the DNA, and regulatory elements such as enhancers can lie in introns, so a change there can matter.
Amino acids are read from exons, and an intron is removed before a protein is made, so a variant in an intron is not read as a codon.

questions.prompt: A study finds that a SNP lying in the DNA between two genes is more common in people who have a particular disease. What is the most reasonable first reading of the finding?
hints: The SNP lies between genes. Which parts of the map could it still be useful for?
SNPs can serve as markers, and some noncoding DNA controls genes.

acceptedIdeas: It marks a region worth examining, since the SNP may act as a marker or lie in a regulatory element
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It marks a region worth examining, since the SNP may act as a marker or lie in a regulatory element

choices.label: The SNP must change an amino acid in a protein, since it is more common in people who have the disease
It marks a region worth examining, since the SNP may act as a marker or lie in a regulatory element
The finding is probably a mistake, since the DNA between genes is junk and cannot affect anything

questions.onCorrect: A marker leads researchers to a region. Finding what in that region matters is a further step.

misconceptions.feedback: A SNP between genes does not lie in protein-coding sequence, so it cannot itself change an amino acid.
Noncoding DNA was once called junk, but at least some of it controls genes, and SNPs there can act as markers, so the finding deserves a closer look.

questions.prompt: Six single-base changes are found in different places in the DNA. What can a change in each place do?
hints: Ask first which part of the genome the change falls in, and then what that part does.
Regulatory elements affect how much protein is made, while the coding part decides the amino acids.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Promoter and enhancer changes can change when or how much protein is made, the microRNA gene change can alter that RNA, the codon change can alter an amino acid, and the changes between genes and inside the quiet intron most likely have no effect.

bins.label: Can change when or how much protein is made

items.label: A change in the promoter of a gene, just ahead of where the gene is read
items.explanation: A promoter is a regulatory element, so a change there can alter how much of the protein is made.

items.label: A change in an enhancer that lies far from the gene it helps to activate

misconceptions.feedback: Changes that keep the frame can matter too, since a missing or replaced amino acid can alter how the protein folds or works.
A deletion shifts the frame only when the number of bases removed is not a multiple of three, and three bases keep the frame.

questions.prompt: A protein works only as a dimer made of two subunits that pair at random. A mutant allele makes subunits that join normal ones and disable the dimer. In a heterozygote, half the subunits made are mutant. Which statement about the dimers is right?
hints: A dimer is fully normal only if both of its subunits are normal.
Half the subunits are normal. What is the chance that both subunits of one dimer are?

acceptedIdeas: Fewer than half are fully normal, because a dimer needs both of its subunits normal
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Fewer than half are fully normal, because a dimer needs both of its subunits normal

choices.label: Fewer than half are fully normal, because a dimer needs both of its subunits normal
Half of the dimers are fully normal, because half of the subunits are normal
More than half are fully normal, because one normal subunit is enough for a dimer

questions.onCorrect: A dimer is normal only when both of its subunits are, so the share of normal dimers falls below the share of normal subunits.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts subunits and not dimers. A dimer takes two subunits and is normal only if both are, so the share of normal dimers is smaller than the share of normal subunits.
A mutant subunit disables the dimer it joins, so a dimer with one normal subunit and one mutant one does not work.

questions.prompt: Haemoglobin C has lysine, Lys, in place of glutamic acid, Glu, at position 6 of beta-globin. Suppose the codon for Glu at that position is GAA. Which single-base change gives Lys?
hints: Find the codons for Lys in the table, and see which of them is one base away from GAA.
A change to a codon for the same amino acid, or to a stop codon, does not give Lys.

acceptedIdeas: GAA to AAA
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: GAA to AAA

choices.label: GAA to GAG
GAA to GUA
GAA to AAA
GAA to UAA

questions.onCorrect: Lys is named by AAA, which differs from GAA at the first base only.

misconceptions.feedback: GAG also names Glu, so the amino acid would be unchanged.
GUA names Val, which is the replacement in sickle cell haemoglobin and not Lys.
UAA is a stop codon, so the chain would end there.

questions.prompt: A person who carries one null allele of a gene and one normal allele is affected, because one working copy makes too little product. What word names this property of the gene?
hints: The affected person still has one normal copy. What does it fail to do?
The lesson also named the opposite case, in which one working copy is enough.

acceptedIdeas: haploinsufficient
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The gene is haploinsufficient.
