questions.onCorrect: A haploinsufficient gene needs two working copies, so a null allele in one copy shows as a dominant effect.

misconceptions.feedback: Haplosufficient is the opposite: one working copy is enough, so a null allele is recessive.

questions.prompt: A null allele of an enzyme gene is recessive: people with one null allele and one normal allele are healthy. What best explains this?
hints: A carrier has one working copy. Ask what that copy can supply.
Some genes need both copies to make enough product, so the explanation cannot be about every gene.

acceptedIdeas: One working copy makes enough enzyme for a normal phenotype
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: One working copy makes enough enzyme for a normal phenotype

choices.label: The mutant allele is switched off in carriers, so the normal copy stands alone
The normal copy repairs the mutant protein, so the carrier's enzyme works
Null alleles of every gene are recessive, whatever the gene
One working copy makes enough enzyme for a normal phenotype

questions.onCorrect: For most genes one normal allele supplies enough product, so a loss of function in the other allele is recessive.

misconceptions.feedback: The mutant allele still exists in carriers, and no switching off is needed. The normal copy alone is enough for most genes.
A null allele makes no active product to repair, and a normal copy does not mend another allele's protein.
Some genes are haploinsufficient, and for those a null allele is dominant, so the rule is not true of every gene.

questions.prompt: Two deletions inside the coding sequence of one gene remove 12 bases and 14 bases. Which is more likely to change every amino acid after the deletion?
hints: Count how many whole codons each deletion could remove.
A deletion keeps the frame only if the number of bases lost is a multiple of three.

acceptedIdeas: The 14-base deletion, because 14 is not a multiple of three and so shifts the frame
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The 14-base deletion, because 14 is not a multiple of three and so shifts the frame

choices.label: The 12-base deletion, because it removes more bases from the coding sequence than the other
The 14-base deletion, because 14 is not a multiple of three and so shifts the frame
Both equally, because each of them removes bases from the coding sequence of the gene

questions.onCorrect: Fourteen is not a multiple of three, so that deletion shifts the frame and changes the codons after it.

misconceptions.feedback: The size of a deletion does not decide the effect on the frame. Twelve is a multiple of three, so the frame is kept.
The two differ in whether the number of bases is a multiple of three, which decides whether the frame shifts.

questions.prompt: A purple-flowered pea plant is crossed to a white-flowered plant, aa. Of the 50 offspring, 22 are purple and 28 are white. Which statement about the purple parent is best supported?
hints: What genotype must a white-flowered offspring have, and which alleles did it receive from which parent?
If the purple parent were AA, could any offspring be white?

acceptedIdeas: It is Aa, because white offspring need an a from each parent, and counts scatter around 1:1
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It is Aa, because white offspring need an a from each parent, and counts scatter around 1:1

choices.label: It cannot be told, because the counts are not exactly 25 purple and 25 white, as 1:1 would give
It is Aa, because white offspring need an a from each parent, and counts scatter around 1:1
It is AA, because an Aa parent would give mostly purple offspring, three for each white one

questions.onCorrect: White offspring show that the purple parent carries a, and counts near 1:1 fit Aa.

misconceptions.feedback: Exact counts are not expected. Counts scatter around the predicted ratio, and the white offspring already settle the genotype.
A cross of Aa with aa gives equal numbers of the two classes, because the tester gives only a. The three to one ratio belongs to a cross of two heterozygotes.

questions.prompt: In an invented beetle species, one allele gives a dark shell, another gives a pale shell, and a beetle with one of each has a grey shell, so the alleles show incomplete dominance. Two grey beetles are crossed and give 400 offspring. About how many are grey?
hints: Write the cross as Aa by Aa and list the genotypes of the offspring.
The genotypes come out AA, Aa and aa in the ratio 1:2:1, and only one of them is grey.
Take the grey share of the 400 offspring.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Two heterozygotes give offspring in the genotype ratio 1:2:1, and only the heterozygote is grey, so half of the 400, which is 200, are grey.

questions.onCorrect: Half of the offspring are heterozygous, and the heterozygote is the grey beetle.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share showing the dominant trait when one allele is fully dominant. Here the heterozygote looks different from both homozygotes.
That is the share of each homozygote, one quarter. The heterozygote is the grey beetle, and it is half of the offspring.

questions.prompt: A woman of blood type A and a man of blood type B have a child of type O. What does this show about the parents?
hints: Which genotype gives type O, and what must each parent have passed on?
Types A and B can each hide a recessive allele.

acceptedIdeas: Each parent carries an $i$ allele, so both are heterozygous for the ABO gene
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each parent carries an $i$ allele, so both are heterozygous for the ABO gene

choices.label: One parent must really be type AB, because type O needs a third allele
The child has a new variant, because type O cannot come from parents of types A and B
Each parent carries an $i$ allele, so both are heterozygous for the ABO gene

questions.onCorrect: Type O is $ii$, so each parent passed on an $i$, which a type A or a type B person can carry.

misconceptions.feedback: Each parent shows one type and can still carry a hidden $i$. An AB parent would show both antigens.
Type O is $ii$, and a parent of type A ($I^A i$) or B ($I^B i$) can pass on an $i$, so no new variant is needed.

questions.prompt: In Labrador retrievers heterozygous at the B and E loci, the yellow class takes two of the four classes of the 9:3:3:1 ratio. Why does it take two?
hints: What does the ee genotype do to pigment, and does it matter what the B locus carries?
Ask which two of the four genotype classes include ee.

acceptedIdeas: Every ee pup is yellow whatever it carries at the B locus, so the classes eeB_ and eebb merge
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Every ee pup is yellow whatever it carries at the B locus, so the classes eeB_ and eebb merge

choices.label: Every ee pup is yellow whatever it carries at the B locus, so the classes eeB_ and eebb merge
Yellow pups carry a third allele at the B locus, which adds to the ratio from the other classes
Only eebb pups are yellow, so the extra yellow pups must have been counted wrongly

questions.onCorrect: The ee genotype blocks pigment at any B genotype, so two classes look the same.

misconceptions.feedback: No third allele is needed. The ee genotype alone stops pigment being deposited, whatever the B locus carries.
Every ee pup is yellow, whether it is B_ or bb, so both classes are yellow and the count is not a mistake.

questions.prompt: Two squash plants heterozygous at both fruit-colour loci give 160 fruits, with invented counts of 121 white, 29 yellow and 10 green. Which ratio fits the three classes best?
hints: Compare the size of each class with the expected shares of 16.
Three classes fit more than one ratio, so use the sizes of the classes to choose.

acceptedIdeas: 12:3:1, since the white class is about three quarters of the total
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 12:3:1, since the white class is about three quarters of the total

choices.label: 9:3:4, because that ratio has three classes, and three classes appear
12:3:1, since the white class is about three quarters of the total
9:3:3:1, because the two loci assort independently of each other

questions.onCorrect: The white class is 121 of 160, about 12 parts in 16, which points to 12:3:1.

misconceptions.feedback: Three classes fit 9:3:4 as well as 12:3:1, but 9:3:4 expects about 90 in the first class and 40 in the last, far from 121 and 10.
A ratio of 9:3:3:1 has four classes, and only three appear, so one locus is masking the other.

questions.prompt: For 160 fruits in the ratio 12:3:1, how many are expected to be white?
hints: Add the parts of the ratio to find the total number of parts.
Divide the 160 fruits by the total number of parts to get the size of one part.
The white class is the one with 12 parts.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The ratio has 16 parts, so each part is 10 fruits, and the white class has 12 parts, which is 120 fruits.

questions.onCorrect: Each of the 16 parts is 10 fruits, so the white class of 12 parts has 120.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the size of the largest class in 9:3:4. This ratio has 12 parts in the largest class.
That is the total number of fruits. The white class has 12 of the 16 parts.

questions.prompt: In an invented rodent species with XX females and XY males, a pure-breeding long-tailed female is crossed to a pure-breeding short-tailed male, and a pure-breeding short-tailed female to a pure-breeding long-tailed male. Both crosses give only long-tailed sons and daughters. What do the results suggest?
hints: Compare the two crosses. Do they differ, and do sons differ from daughters within a cross?
A sex-linked gene gives different results in reciprocal crosses, or different results in the two sexes.

acceptedIdeas: The gene is most likely on an autosome, because both crosses give the same result in both sexes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The gene is most likely on an autosome, because both crosses give the same result in both sexes

choices.label: The gene is on the X chromosome, because every offspring shows the long-tailed trait in both crosses
The gene is on the Y chromosome, because the sons in the second cross resemble their father
The gene is most likely on an autosome, because both crosses give the same result in both sexes

questions.onCorrect: Reciprocal crosses with the same result in both sexes point to an autosomal gene.

misconceptions.feedback: A gene on the X chromosome would usually give different results in reciprocal crosses, or in sons and daughters. Here nothing differs.
A gene on the Y chromosome passes only from father to son, and the daughters here are long-tailed as well, so the gene is not on the Y.

questions.prompt: An invented cross of two plants heterozygous at both loci gives 320 offspring in four phenotypic classes of 183, 58, 62 and 17. What do the counts suggest?
hints: Work out the counts that 9:3:3:1 expects for 320 offspring, and compare them with the observed counts.
Masking would merge classes, so ask how many classes appear.

acceptedIdeas: Four classes near 180, 60, 60 and 20 fit 9:3:3:1, so the loci assort independently
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Four classes near 180, 60, 60 and 20 fit 9:3:3:1, so the loci assort independently

choices.label: Four classes near 180, 60, 60 and 20 fit 9:3:3:1, so the loci assort independently
The counts are not exactly 180, 60, 60 and 20, so one locus must be masking the other locus
The smallest class is below 20, so the double recessive offspring must be dying young in the cross

questions.onCorrect: Expected counts of 180, 60, 60 and 20 differ from the observed ones by two or three offspring, which sampling can explain.

misconceptions.feedback: Real counts scatter around the expected ones. Masking would merge classes, so fewer than four would appear, and here there are four.
A gap of three offspring from an expected twenty is the kind of scatter that sampling gives, so no loss of a class is needed to explain it.

questions.prompt: In an invented plant, a flower is purple only when the plant has a dominant allele at both of two loci, and is white in every other genotype. Two plants heterozygous at both loci give 640 offspring, 358 purple and 282 white. Which ratio fits?
hints: Which of the four classes of 9:3:3:1 are purple here, and which are white?
Add up the white parts of each ratio and compare the counts it expects for 640 offspring with 358 and 282.

acceptedIdeas: 9:7, because the purple class is A_B_ alone and the other three classes merge as white
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 9:7, because the purple class is A_B_ alone and the other three classes merge as white

choices.label: 15:1, because a dominant allele at either locus is enough to make a flower purple
9:7, because the purple class is A_B_ alone and the other three classes merge as white
3:1, because two phenotypes appear and a dominant trait shows in three quarters
9:3:4, because a recessive genotype at one locus masks the other locus

questions.onCorrect: Only the A_B_ class is purple, which is 9 parts in 16, and the other three classes together make 7 parts. For 640 offspring that expects 360 purple and 280 white, close to 358 and 282.

misconceptions.feedback: A ratio of 15:1 would give about 600 purple and 40 white. Here both loci need a dominant allele, and the white class is far larger than 40.
A ratio of 3:1 would give about 480 purple and 160 white, and it describes one locus. Here two loci act together, so the purple class is 9 parts in 16.
A ratio of 9:3:4 has three classes, and only two appear here. The three classes that lack a dominant allele at one locus or at both look alike.

questions.prompt: In turkeys the females are ZW and the males are ZZ. A brown male crossed to a bronze female gives bronze sons and brown daughters, and a bronze male crossed to a brown female gives only bronze offspring. What explains the two results?
hints: Which parent gives a daughter her Z chromosome, and which gives her W?
Bronze is dominant. Work out the genotypes of the sons and the daughters in the first cross.

acceptedIdeas: The gene lies on the Z chromosome, so a daughter receives her only copy from her father
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The gene lies on the Z chromosome, so a daughter receives her only copy from her father

choices.label: The gene lies on the W chromosome, so every daughter resembles her mother in phenotype
The gene lies on the Z chromosome, so a daughter receives her only copy from her father
The gene lies on an autosome, but the bronze allele is dominant only in the males

questions.onCorrect: A daughter's single Z comes from her father, so reciprocal crosses give daughters different phenotypes.

misconceptions.feedback: In the first cross the daughters are brown and their mother is bronze, so the daughters do not resemble the mother.
An autosomal gene would give the same result in reciprocal crosses, and nothing here says that dominance differs between the sexes.

questions.prompt: A breeder has the counts from a cross of two plants heterozygous at two loci. Put the steps of reading them in order, the first at the top.
hints: The number of classes narrows the choice of ratio before anything else can be done.
Expected counts need a ratio and a total, and a comparison needs both the expected and the observed counts.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Count the classes, pick the ratio, work out the expected counts, compare them with the observed counts, and then decide whether the gaps are only sampling.

items: Count the phenotype classes among the offspring
Pick the ratio that has that number of classes and a similar pattern of sizes
Work out the expected count for each class from the total number of offspring
Compare the observed counts with the expected counts
Decide whether sampling alone explains the gaps, and name the gene interaction if so

questions.onCorrect: The classes point to a ratio, the ratio gives expected counts, and comparing them with the observed counts shows whether the ratio fits.

questions.prompt: A dihybrid AaBb is test-crossed with aabb, and the two genes assort independently. Of 200 offspring, how many do you expect to be aabb?
hints: A test cross to aabb gives four kinds of offspring, one for each kind of gamete the dihybrid can make.
Independent assortment makes those four kinds of gamete equally likely.
Divide the 200 offspring between the four kinds.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The dihybrid makes AB, Ab, aB and ab gametes in equal numbers, so each kind of offspring is a quarter of the total: 200 ÷ 4 = 50.

questions.onCorrect: Independent assortment gives all four kinds of offspring equally, so a quarter of the 200 are aabb. Counts that depart from that point to something else.

misconceptions.feedback: That would be half the offspring. The aabb offspring come from one of four equally likely gametes.
That is a percentage. The question asks how many of the 200 offspring.

questions.prompt: Two pure-breeding lines, AAbb and aaBB, are crossed, and the dihybrid offspring are used in a test cross. Which gametes from the dihybrid are recombinant?
hints: Work out what each pure-breeding line can pass on.
The dihybrid carries on its two chromosomes exactly the gametes of its parents.

acceptedIdeas: AB and ab, which neither of the pure-breeding lines had
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: AB and ab, which neither of the pure-breeding lines had

choices.label: Ab and aB, the combinations the two lines handed down
AB and ab, which neither of the pure-breeding lines had
None, because pure-breeding parents never give recombinants

questions.onCorrect: The dihybrid carries Ab and aB, so AB and ab are new combinations, and they are the recombinants.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are the parental gametes. The AAbb line could pass on only Ab and the aaBB line only aB, so Ab and aB are what the dihybrid inherited.
Pure-breeding parents make the dihybrid's arrangement certain. They do not stop the dihybrid's own chromosomes from exchanging pieces.

questions.prompt: Why are the Aabb and aaBb offspring the recombinants in this cross?
hints: Start from the arrangement the dihybrid had.
Compare each class of offspring with the two combinations the parents handed down.

acceptedIdeas: The dihybrid received AB and ab, so Ab and aB are combinations neither of its chromosomes carried
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The dihybrid received AB and ab, so Ab and aB are combinations neither of its chromosomes carried

choices.label: The dihybrid received AB and ab, so Ab and aB are combinations neither of its chromosomes carried
They are the two smallest classes of offspring, and the smallest classes are always the recombinants
They carry the recessive allele of one gene only, and a lone recessive allele marks recombination

questions.onCorrect: AB and ab are what the dihybrid inherited, so gametes carrying Ab or aB are new combinations.

misconceptions.feedback: Small size is a usual result and not the rule. The parents' arrangement decides which classes are recombinant.
Recessive alleles appear in parental and recombinant classes alike, and aabb is a parental class in this cross.

questions.prompt: Which two classes of offspring are the recombinants?
hints: The dihybrid carried Ab and aB, so write down which offspring come from those gametes.
The recombinant gametes are the other two combinations.

acceptedIdeas: AaBb and aabb, which come from the AB and ab gametes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: AaBb and aabb, which come from the AB and ab gametes

choices.label: Aabb and aaBb, the two largest classes of offspring
AaBb and aabb, which come from the AB and ab gametes
Aabb and aabb, taking one class from each pair of gametes

questions.onCorrect: The dihybrid carried Ab and aB, so AB and ab gametes are the new combinations, and they give AaBb and aabb offspring.

misconceptions.feedback: Those come from the Ab and aB gametes that the AAbb and aaBB parents handed down, so they are the parental classes.
Aabb is parental, since it comes from an Ab gamete, so this pair mixes a parental class with a recombinant one.

questions.prompt: Add the two recombinant classes and divide by the total number of offspring. What is the recombination frequency, in percent?
hints: Add the numbers in the two recombinant classes.
The total is the sum of all four classes.
Divide the first by the second and write the result as a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The recombinants are 16 + 14 = 30 of 200 offspring, so 30 ÷ 200 = 0.15, or 15 percent.

questions.onCorrect: Thirty recombinants among 200 offspring is 15 percent, which marks the genes as linked.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share of parental offspring, 170 of 200. The frequency counts the recombinants.
That is the number of recombinants. The frequency divides it by the 200 offspring.

questions.prompt: Three genes show these distances: X to Y 9 cM, X to Z 5 cM and Z to Y 4 cM. Which gene lies between the other two?
hints: Find the longest distance. Its two genes are the ends of the stretch.
The gene left over should sit between them, with its two distances adding up to the longest.

acceptedIdeas: Z, because 5 and 4 add up to the 9 cM between X and Y
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Z, because 5 and 4 add up to the 9 cM between X and Y

choices.label: X, because it is the first gene named in the question
Y, because it is one end of the longest distance
Z, because 5 and 4 add up to the 9 cM between X and Y
Distances in pairs cannot fix the order of three genes

questions.onCorrect: The longest distance, 9 cM, is the sum of 5 and 4, so X and Y are the ends and Z is between them.

misconceptions.feedback: The position in a list says nothing about the map. The longest distance, 9 cM, is between X and Y, so those are the ends.
Y is one end of the longest distance, 9 cM, and ends do not lie between the others.
Here they can: when one distance equals the sum of the other two, the gene those two share is in the middle.

questions.prompt: A dihybrid is test-crossed. Of 1,000 offspring, 412 are AaBb, 388 are aabb, 98 are Aabb and 102 are aaBb. Someone assumes the dihybrid carried A with b on one chromosome and a with B on the other. What recombination frequency would that assumption give?
hints: With A and b together, the parental gametes are Ab and aB. Which offspring classes do they give?
Everything else is recombinant under that assumption. Is the result a possible recombination frequency?

acceptedIdeas: 80 percent, above the ceiling, so that arrangement is wrong
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 80 percent, above the ceiling, so that arrangement is wrong

choices.label: 20 percent, from the two smaller classes of offspring
50 percent, which would show that the genes are unlinked
80 percent, above the ceiling, so that arrangement is wrong
No figure, because AaBb alone does not show the arrangement

questions.onCorrect: Aabb and aaBb would be the parental classes, 200 of 1,000, leaving 800 recombinant offspring, which is 80 percent and cannot occur, since 50 percent is the most observed.

misconceptions.feedback: That figure comes from reading AaBb and aabb as parental. The assumption in the question makes Aabb and aaBb the parental classes instead.
The counts are 800 against 200, nowhere near an even split, so this assumption cannot give 50 percent.
The assumed arrangement does fix the classes, so a figure follows from it. That figure turns out to be impossible, and that is what exposes the mistake.

questions.prompt: In an invented cross, genes X and Z show a recombination frequency of 12 percent and genes Z and Y show 14 percent, which puts Z between X and Y. Measured directly, X and Y show 24 percent, less than the 26 percent that 12 + 14 gives. What explains the shortfall?
hints: A frequency counts gametes that differ from the parental combination at the two genes.
Ask what a gamete looks like if two crossovers happened between the genes.

acceptedIdeas: Some meioses have two crossovers between them, which look parental and are missed
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Some meioses have two crossovers between them, which look parental and are missed

choices.label: Map distances always add exactly, so the cross between X and Y was scored wrongly
Some meioses have two crossovers between them, which look parental and are missed
Z cannot lie between X and Y, because the distances do not add up exactly
Frequencies above 20 percent are measured in different units from the smaller ones

questions.onCorrect: Two crossovers between X and Y restore the parental combination, so those gametes go uncounted and the measured frequency is below the sum.

misconceptions.feedback: Map distances add only approximately. They are most reliable for short stretches, and the longer the stretch, the more it falls short.
The order stands: 24 is close to 12 + 14. A small shortfall over the longer stretch is the usual pattern, so it does not overturn the order.
Percent recombinants and map units are used the same way at every distance. What changes is how many crossovers go uncounted.

questions.prompt: Pure-breeding tall white plants (TTrr) are crossed with pure-breeding short red plants (ttRR), and the dihybrid offspring are test-crossed. Of 500 offspring, 247 are tall white, 213 short red, 22 tall red and 18 short white. What is the recombination frequency, in percent?
hints: Work out which gametes the dihybrid received from its parents, and which phenotypes they give in the test cross.
The recombinant offspring are the two classes that those gametes do not give.
Add the recombinants, divide by 500 and give a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The dihybrid carries Tr and tR, so the tall white and short red offspring are parental. The recombinants are 22 + 18 = 40 of 500, which is 8 percent.

questions.onCorrect: The dihybrid received Tr and tR, so the tall red and short white offspring are the recombinants: 40 of 500, which is 8 percent.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share of parental offspring, 460 of 500. The frequency counts the recombinants.
That counts 22 recombinants only. Both recombinant classes count.

questions.prompt: In a test cross of a dihybrid, 249 of the 500 offspring are recombinant. What does that support?
hints: Work out the frequency: recombinants over total.
Which kinds of gene pair give a frequency of about 50 percent?

acceptedIdeas: The genes are on different chromosomes, or far apart on one chromosome
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The genes are on different chromosomes, or far apart on one chromosome

choices.label: The genes are tightly linked, because so many offspring are recombinant
The genes are on different chromosomes, or far apart on one chromosome
The counts must be wrong, because a frequency cannot reach 25 percent

questions.onCorrect: The frequency is 249 ÷ 500, nearly 50 percent, the value for genes on different chromosomes and for genes far apart on one chromosome.

misconceptions.feedback: Tight linkage gives few recombinants. A frequency near 50 percent is what independent assortment gives.
Frequencies run up to about 50 percent, and about 50 percent is the expected value for genes that assort independently.

questions.prompt: A map has gene W at its left end. Distances between pairs of genes are W to X 8 cM, X to Y 5 cM, W to Y 13 cM, Y to Z 9 cM, X to Z 14 cM and W to Z 22 cM. Put the genes in order from W.
hints: The longest distance fixes the far end. Which gene is at the opposite end from W?
Check each gene's distance from W against the distances between the genes on either side of it.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its place
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: W to Z is the longest distance at 22 cM, so Z is the far end. The distances from W are X 8, Y 13 and Z 22, and each gap adds up: 8 + 5 + 9 = 22.

questions.onCorrect: The distances from W grow along the map, and the gaps between neighbours add up to the longest distance: 8 + 5 + 9 = 22 cM.

questions.prompt: Two unaffected carriers of a recessive allele have a child. What is the probability that the child is affected?
hints: Each carrier passes on the recessive allele with probability 1/2.
The child is affected only if it receives the recessive allele from both parents.
Chances of events that must both happen are combined by the product rule.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each parent passes on the recessive allele with probability 1/2, and both must do so: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

questions.onCorrect: A recessive condition needs the allele from both parents, and each carrier passes it on half the time, so the chance is 1/4.

misconceptions.feedback: Half is the chance that the child is a carrier. An affected child needs the allele from both parents.
That is the chance that the child is not affected. The question asks for the affected chance.

questions.prompt: In Pedigree A two unaffected parents have an affected daughter. Which mode of inheritance fits?
hints: Dominant modes need an affected parent. Does either parent here have the trait?
A daughter receives one X chromosome from her father. What would that mean for an X-linked recessive trait?

acceptedIdeas: Autosomal recessive, passed on from two carrier parents
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Autosomal recessive, passed on from two carrier parents

choices.label: Autosomal dominant, passed on from an unaffected parent
X-linked recessive, passed on from an unaffected father
Autosomal recessive, passed on from two carrier parents
X-linked dominant, passed on from an unaffected mother

questions.onCorrect: Both parents are unaffected, which rules out the dominant modes, and an affected daughter rules out X-linked recessive, so autosomal recessive is the mode that fits.

misconceptions.feedback: A dominant condition needs an affected parent, and I-1 and I-2 are both unaffected.
An affected daughter needs an affected father, because she receives one of her X chromosomes from him, and I-1 is unaffected.
This also needs an affected parent. Neither parent is affected.

questions.prompt: In Pedigree A, II-2 and II-3 are both unaffected, and their parents are both carriers. What is the probability that both II-2 and II-3 are carriers?
hints: Work out the chance that one unaffected child of two carriers is a carrier.
Each child's genotype is decided separately, so the chances for the two children combine by the product rule.
Multiply the chance for II-2 by the chance for II-3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each unaffected sibling is a carrier with probability 2/3, and the two are independent, so 2/3 × 2/3 = 4/9, about 0.44.

questions.onCorrect: Each of the two is a carrier with probability 2/3, and the genotypes of siblings are independent, so the chances multiply to 4/9.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance for one sibling. Both must be carriers, and the two chances multiply.
That is the chance that a child of two carriers is affected. These siblings are known to be unaffected.

questions.prompt: Why are the three chances multiplied and not added?
hints: Ask whether any one of the three events would be enough to give an affected child.
Compare the product rule with the sum rule in the previous screen.

acceptedIdeas: The child is affected only if all three events happen together, and chances of joint events are multiplied
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The child is affected only if all three events happen together, and chances of joint events are multiplied

choices.label: The child is affected only if all three events happen together, and chances of joint events are multiplied
The three chances describe alternatives, so they are added to give the total chance of an affected child
Multiplying keeps the answer small, so the estimate errs on the safe side for the family counselled

questions.onCorrect: An affected child needs II-3 to be a carrier, the partner to be a carrier, and the child to receive the allele from both, so the chances multiply.

misconceptions.feedback: Alternatives are added, as in rolling a five or a six on one throw. Here the three events are not alternatives, since each has to hold.
The rule follows from the events and not from a wish for a safe estimate. The answer is small because three things must all hold.

questions.prompt: II-2 is unaffected, and his parents are both carriers. What is the probability that II-2 is a carrier?
hints: His parents are both carriers, since they have an affected child.
Remove the genotype that would make him affected from the four equally likely ones.
Count how many of the genotypes that remain are Aa.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The four equally likely genotypes are AA, Aa, Aa and aa, and II-2 is not aa, so two of the three remaining are Aa: 2/3.

questions.onCorrect: Among the three genotypes an unaffected child can have, two are Aa, so he is a carrier with probability 2/3.

misconceptions.feedback: Half is the chance before the family's evidence is used. II-2 is known to be unaffected, so the aa box is excluded.
That is the chance that a child of two carriers is affected. II-2 is unaffected.

questions.prompt: If II-2 is a carrier, a child receives his recessive allele with probability 1/2. What is the probability that III-1 is a carrier?
hints: III-1 is a carrier only if II-2 is a carrier and he passes the allele on.
Combine the carrier chance for II-2 with the chance of passing it on.
Both events must happen, so the chances multiply.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: II-2 is a carrier with probability 2/3 and passes the allele on with probability 1/2, so III-1 is a carrier with probability 2/3 × 1/2 = 1/3.

questions.onCorrect: Both things must hold, so 2/3 × 1/2 = 1/3.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance of inheriting the allele from a known carrier. II-2 is a carrier with probability 2/3 only, and the chances multiply.
That is the chance that II-2 himself is a carrier. III-1 must also receive the allele from him.

questions.prompt: A woman's father has an X-linked recessive condition. Her partner is unaffected and carries no copy of the allele. What should the counsellor expect for their children?
hints: A woman receives her father's X chromosome. What does that say about her?
A son receives his mother's X, and a daughter receives one X from each parent.

acceptedIdeas: Half the sons are affected and none of the daughters
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Half the sons are affected and none of the daughters

choices.label: All the sons and half the daughters are affected
Half the children are affected, sons and daughters alike
Half the sons are affected and none of the daughters
No child is at risk, because the woman herself is unaffected

questions.onCorrect: She is a carrier for certain, so each son is affected with probability 1/2, and each daughter receives her father's normal X and is unaffected.

misconceptions.feedback: She has one copy of the allele, so a son has an even chance of receiving it and not a certainty. A daughter receives her father's normal X from the partner.
A daughter always receives the partner's X, which carries no copy of the allele, so she is not affected.
Her father passed her his X, so she is a carrier, and each of her sons has an even chance of receiving the allele.

questions.prompt: A couple have one child with an autosomal recessive condition. What is the chance that their next child is affected?
hints: Ask whether anything about the first child changes how the parents' gametes are dealt out.
Each pregnancy is a new draw from the same two carriers.

acceptedIdeas: 1 in 4, the same chance as for their first child
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 1 in 4, the same chance as for their first child

choices.label: Nil, because they have already had their affected child
1 in 16, because two births in a row must both be affected
1 in 4, the same chance as for their first child
1 in 2, because the first child shows both parents carry the allele

questions.onCorrect: Each pregnancy is a fresh draw from the same two carriers, so the chance of an affected child stays at 1 in 4.

misconceptions.feedback: A first affected child does not use up the risk. Both parents are carriers, so every pregnancy carries the same chance.
The first child's outcome is already known, so only the next child's chance is left, and it does not depend on the first.
Both parents are carriers, but a child is affected only if it receives the allele from both, which has chance 1/2 × 1/2.

questions.prompt: Four members of one household have the same illness, and a test of their water supply finds contamination. What should a counsellor conclude before drawing a pedigree?
hints: What do the four people share besides their genes?
A mode of inheritance only makes sense once a genetic cause is plausible.

acceptedIdeas: A shared environment could explain it, so a genetic cause is not yet shown
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A shared environment could explain it, so a genetic cause is not yet shown

choices.label: It is autosomal dominant, since it appears in several members of one family
It is mitochondrial, since all of the family members live in the same household
A shared environment could explain it, so a genetic cause is not yet shown
It is autosomal recessive, since it has skipped no generation in the family

questions.onCorrect: Relatives share exposures as well as genes, so contaminated water is a competing explanation, and the mode of inheritance can wait.

misconceptions.feedback: Several affected people in one family do not by themselves show a dominant allele. The household also shares a possible cause that is not genetic.
Sharing a household has nothing to do with the mother's mitochondria. A mode of inheritance has yet to be shown.
Recessive conditions are the ones that tend to skip generations, and anyway the question of mode comes after the question of cause.

questions.prompt: In an invented family, a man, his son and his granddaughter, the son's daughter, all have a condition. Their partners are unaffected and come from outside the family. Which mode of inheritance fits best?
hints: Does each affected person have an affected parent?
Look for a father who passes the trait to a son, and say what that rules out.

acceptedIdeas: Autosomal dominant, since each affected person has an affected parent
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Autosomal dominant, since each affected person has an affected parent

choices.label: X-linked dominant, since an affected woman is among the family members
Autosomal dominant, since each affected person has an affected parent
Autosomal recessive, since the condition appears in several people
Mitochondrial, since it passes down through the generations

questions.onCorrect: Every affected person has an affected parent, and the father-to-son step rules out the X-linked modes, so autosomal dominant fits.

misconceptions.feedback: The man's son is affected, and a father gives a son his Y chromosome, so X-linked dominant is ruled out.
That would need each partner from outside to carry the allele too, which is unlikely for a rare condition. A recessive pedigree also tends to show fewer affected people.
A mitochondrial trait comes from the mother, and here the granddaughter's affected parent is her father.

questions.prompt: An unaffected woman has a brother with an autosomal recessive condition, and her parents are unaffected. Her partner comes from a population where about 1 in 40 people carry the allele (an invented condition). What is the chance that their child is affected, as 1 in how many?
hints: Work out the chance that the woman is a carrier, given that she is unaffected and her parents are carriers.
Multiply by the partner's carrier chance, and then by the chance that two carriers have an affected child.
Write the final chance as a fraction with 1 on top and read off the denominator.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: She is a carrier with probability 2/3, her partner with probability 1/40, and two carriers have an affected child with probability 1/4: 2/3 × 1/40 × 1/4 = 1/240.

misconceptions.feedback: That leaves out the woman's chance of being a carrier. She is unaffected and her parents are carriers, which makes it less than certain.
That leaves out the 1/4, the chance that two carriers pass the allele on to the same child.
A woman with an affected brother and unaffected parents is a carrier with probability 2/3, and not 1/2.

questions.prompt: This sentence is from a genetics textbook, where AD stands for autosomal dominant. A patient has ALS and no relatives with the condition. What does the extract support?
hints: Read which share of cases the extract says are inherited, and which share are sporadic.
A share across many patients says what is typical. It does not settle what is true of one patient.

acceptedIdeas: That is not unusual, since most cases are sporadic and not inherited
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That is not unusual, since most cases are sporadic and not inherited

choices.label: That is not unusual, since most cases are sporadic and not inherited
The case must be sporadic, so the question of inheritance is closed
ALS is mostly dominant, so the family history is probably incomplete

extracts.text: approximately 5-10% of cases are inherited in an AD pattern, while the majority of the remaining cases appear to be sporadic, in other words, not caused by a mutation inherited from a parent.
extracts.who: Nickle and Barrette-Ng, Online Open Genetics, section 5.4 (CC BY-SA 3.0)

questions.onCorrect: Most ALS cases are sporadic, so a patient with no affected relatives fits the common pattern, though a share of cases are inherited.

misconceptions.feedback: The extract gives a share of cases and cannot settle one patient. About 5 to 10 percent are inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern.
The extract says the reverse: only 5 to 10 percent of cases are inherited in that pattern, and most of the rest are sporadic.

questions.prompt: In the figure, eight people carry the same variant of an invented condition, and five of them show it. Which statement is best supported?
hints: Count how many of the eight carriers show the condition and how many do not.
Ask what the figure would look like if the variant fixed the outcome for every carrier.

acceptedIdeas: Carrying the variant does not settle who shows it, since five of the eight do and three do not
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carrying the variant does not settle who shows it, since five of the eight do and three do not

choices.label: The variant is harmless, because three of the eight carriers show no sign of it
The three carriers without signs will develop it later, because a variant fixes the outcome
Carrying the variant does not settle who shows it, since five of the eight do and three do not
The condition cannot be genetic, because the variant is found in people who do not show it

questions.onCorrect: The same variant gives different outcomes in different people, so carrying it raises the chance of the condition without settling who is affected.

misconceptions.feedback: Five of the eight carriers do show the condition, so the variant is not harmless. It raises the chance of the condition without fixing the outcome.
Nothing in the figure says that the three will develop it. A variant does not fix who shows a condition, and doctors cannot predict which carriers will.
A variant can be part of the cause and still be found in people with no sign of the condition, so its presence in some healthy people does not rule out a genetic cause.

questions.prompt: A woman carries a high-risk variant in BRCA2 and is still free of cancer at 60. Which statement is accurate?
hints: A variant that raises risk is different from a variant that guarantees disease.
Ask what the cancer-free carrier tells you about the proportion of carriers who develop it.

acceptedIdeas: Many carriers develop cancer but not all do, so the variant has reduced penetrance
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Many carriers develop cancer but not all do, so the variant has reduced penetrance

choices.label: The test must have been wrong, since every carrier of such a variant develops cancer
Many carriers develop cancer but not all do, so the variant has reduced penetrance
The variant is harmless in her, so her risk is now the same as that of anyone else
She cannot pass the variant on to her children, since it has not caused cancer in her

questions.onCorrect: Penetrance is the proportion of carriers who show the trait, and for BRCA variants it is below 100 percent, so a cancer-free carrier is expected.

misconceptions.feedback: Many carriers develop cancer and some do not. A cancer-free carrier does not show that the test was wrong.
She still has the variant, and her risk stays raised. Having no cancer so far does not remove the variant.
Passing on a variant does not depend on whether it has caused disease in the carrier.

questions.prompt: In an invented family, two brothers who grew up in the same home differ in adult height by 12 cm. Which explanation fits what is known about height?
hints: How many variants influence height, and how large is the effect of each?
Two children of the same parents do not receive the same set of variants.

acceptedIdeas: They received different combinations of the many variants that affect height
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They received different combinations of the many variants that affect height

choices.label: One brother must carry a single variant of large effect, as in achondroplasia
They received different combinations of the many variants that affect height
Height is not inherited, because brothers from the same parents can differ
The environment of two brothers in one home cannot differ in any way

questions.onCorrect: With hundreds of variants of modest effect, each child draws a different combination from the same parents, so siblings differ.

misconceptions.feedback: Single variants with large effects cause rare conditions. Most of the variation in height among healthy people comes from many variants with modest effects.
Children usually grow up about as tall as their parents because they inherit variants from them. Different combinations explain why siblings still differ.
Nutrition and health in childhood can differ even in one home, and anyway environment is only part of the story.

questions.prompt: A study reports a heritability of 0.7 for a trait in one population. Which statement is correct?
hints: Heritability is a statement about differences among people in a population.
Check each option for a claim about one person, about particular genes, or about whether the trait can change.

acceptedIdeas: 70 percent of the variation in that population's trait goes with genetic differences
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: 70 percent of the variation in that population's trait goes with genetic differences

choices.label: 70 percent of each person's trait in that population is caused by that person's genes
Seven genes are responsible for the trait in that population, whatever the environment
70 percent of the variation in that population's trait goes with genetic differences
The trait cannot be changed by the environment, in that population or any other

questions.onCorrect: A heritability of 0.7 is a statement about variation: 70 percent of the differences among people in that population go with genetic differences.

misconceptions.feedback: Heritability describes variation among people. It does not split any one person's trait into a genetic share and an environmental one.
Heritability gives no information about which genes are involved, or about how many.
Heritability says nothing about how easily a trait changes. A trait with high heritability can still respond to the environment.

questions.prompt: In one population an invented measurement, trait X, has a heritability of 0.9. A school meals scheme raises the average value of X by ten units, and the spread among children stays as it was. Does this show that the heritability estimate was wrong?
hints: Heritability is about differences among people. Did the differences change?
Ask what a heritability of 0.9 says about how easily the trait can be changed.

acceptedIdeas: No, since a better environment for everyone can raise the average and leave the spread
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, since a better environment for everyone can raise the average and leave the spread

choices.label: Yes, since with a heritability of 0.9 the environment could have had no effect at all
No, since a better environment for everyone can raise the average and leave the spread
No, since the meals scheme must have changed the genes that the children inherited
Yes, since a heritability can be measured only after any environmental change is over

questions.onCorrect: Heritability concerns the spread among people, which stayed the same, so a shift in the average is no contradiction.

misconceptions.feedback: A high heritability does not mean that the trait cannot change. It describes how differences among people relate to genetic differences in the environment as it was.
A change in diet does not alter the DNA that children inherited. The average moved because the environment moved, with the genes as they were.
A heritability is estimated in one population and one environment at a time, and it can change if circumstances change, but it can be measured before a change too.

questions.prompt: Heart disease clusters in a family, with no clear pattern of inheritance. Which comparison would best separate genetic causes from a shared household?
hints: Identical twins share almost all their DNA, and fraternal twins share half on average.
Both kinds of twin pair grew up in a shared home, so the home is a constant across the comparison.

acceptedIdeas: Compare identical and fraternal twins who grew up together
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Compare identical and fraternal twins who grew up together

choices.label: Count how many relatives in the family are affected
Compare identical and fraternal twins who grew up together
Measure the trait only in the oldest generation of the family
Test one family member for one gene and generalise from the result

questions.onCorrect: If identical twins are more alike than fraternal twins in the same environment, the difference points to genes.

misconceptions.feedback: Counting affected relatives cannot tell genes from shared habits, since relatives share both.
The oldest generation shares the same two kinds of influence as the rest, so measuring it alone separates nothing.
One gene in one person says little about a condition that depends on many genes and on lifestyle.

questions.prompt: Which idea describes each of these invented cases best?
hints: Ask whether the case is about who shows a trait, how strongly it shows, or differences among people in a population.
A trait shared by relatives need not have anything to do with their genes.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Penetrance: the 12 carriers and the 10 people with one genotype. Expressivity: the two brothers. Heritability: the town and the twins. Familial, not heritable: the religion and the well.

items.label: Of 12 people who carry a variant of an invented gene, 9 develop the condition
items.explanation: The case counts who shows the trait among the carriers, which is penetrance.

items.label: Two brothers share an invented variant: one has a faint rash and the other severe blistering
items.explanation: Both show the trait and differ in how strongly, which is expressivity.

items.label: In one town, 0.6 of the differences in an invented measurement go with genetic differences
items.explanation: It is a share of variation among people in one population, which is heritability.

items.label: An invented trait is much more alike in identical twins than in fraternal twins raised together
items.explanation: Comparing the two kinds of twins is how heritability is estimated.

items.label: Everyone in a family follows the same religion
items.explanation: It is shared in the family but has no genetic contribution, so it is familial and not heritable.

items.label: Four people in a household fall ill after drinking from the same well
items.explanation: The household shares an exposure, which makes the illness familial without being inherited.

items.label: Only 3 of 10 people who have the same genotype show any sign of a trait
items.explanation: A genotype that shows in some carriers and not others has incomplete penetrance.

questions.onCorrect: Each case asks a different question: who shows the trait, how strongly, how much variation goes with genes, or whether sharing a family says anything about genes.

questions.prompt: A MedlinePlus page on height says this. What is the most careful way to read the estimate?
hints: The sentence is about an estimate for people in general. Is it about one person's height, or about differences?
Check each option for a claim about one person, or about whether height can change.

acceptedIdeas: About 80 percent of the differences in height among people go with genes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 80 percent of the differences in height among people go with genes

choices.label: Each person's height is 80 percent made by their genes and 20 percent by food
About 80 percent of the differences in height among people go with genes
Height cannot be changed by nutrition, since it is so largely genetic
A child's height can be predicted to within 20 percent from the child's genes

extracts.text: Scientists estimate that about 80 percent of an individual’s height is determined by the DNA sequence variations they have inherited
extracts.who: MedlinePlus Genetics, "Is height determined by genetics?" (US National Library of Medicine, public domain)
extracts.kind: A health information page from a US government library

questions.onCorrect: Read as a heritability estimate, the figure says that about 80 percent of the differences in height among people go with genetic differences.

misconceptions.feedback: That reads a population statistic as a share of one person's height. A heritability does not split an individual's trait into parts.
A high heritability gives no information about how easily a trait changes, and the same page says nutrition and health matter.
The page says the opposite: because so many variants are involved, a given child's height is hard to predict.

questions.prompt: A man and his two adult children all have type 2 diabetes. The family asks whether the condition is inherited in the way cystic fibrosis is. What is the best reply?
hints: Type 2 diabetes is a common condition, and common conditions rarely have one cause.
Ask whether a single gene and a clear pattern of inheritance would be expected.

acceptedIdeas: It depends on many genes and on lifestyle, so it clusters without a clear pattern
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It depends on many genes and on lifestyle, so it clusters without a clear pattern

choices.label: Yes, it follows a dominant pattern, since a parent and both children are affected
It depends on many genes and on lifestyle, so it clusters without a clear pattern
No, since common conditions have no genetic part and are caused by lifestyle alone
Yes, it is recessive, since both children must have inherited it from carriers

questions.onCorrect: Type 2 diabetes is influenced by many genes and by lifestyle, so it runs in families without following one clear pattern.

misconceptions.feedback: Three affected people in a family do not show a single-gene dominant pattern. Common conditions cluster in families for many reasons.
Nearly all conditions have some genetic component. Diabetes involves many genes together with lifestyle and environment.
A recessive pattern would need a specific single-gene explanation, and a condition caused by many factors does not have one.

questions.prompt: In a population, half the copies of a gene are A and half are a, and gametes join at random. What is the probability that a child is Aa?
hints: Write the four ways the two gametes can pair: AA, Aa, aA and aa.
Each gamete carries A or a with probability 1/2, and the two gametes are independent.
Add the probabilities of the pairings that give a heterozygote.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The child is Aa if the egg is A and the sperm a, or the egg a and the sperm A, and each pairing has probability 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4, so the total is 1/2.

questions.onCorrect: Two of the four equally likely pairings give Aa, so half of the children are heterozygous.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the chance of one particular pairing, such as AA. Aa can arise in two ways, A from the mother or A from the father.
That is the chance of at least one A, which includes AA as well as Aa.

questions.prompt: A sample of 320 people has 200 AA, 80 Aa and 40 aa. What is the frequency of allele A?
hints: Each person has two copies of the gene. How many copies are there in all?
Count the copies of A: two from each AA and one from each Aa.
Divide the copies of A by all the copies.
questions.onCorrect: The 640 copies of the gene hold 480 copies of A, so the frequency of A is 0.75.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the share of people who are AA, 200 of 320. The allele frequency counts copies of the gene, with homozygotes counted twice.
That is the share of people with at least one A, 280 of 320. The frequency counts copies of A among all copies.

questions.prompt: A population is in Hardy-Weinberg proportions, with $p = 0.7$ and $q = 0.3$. What proportion of people show the dominant trait?
hints: People with the dominant trait are AA or Aa.
Work out the frequency of each of those two genotypes and add them.
Check your answer by subtracting the frequency of aa from 1.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: AA is $0.7^2 = 0.49$ and Aa is $2 \times 0.7 \times 0.3 = 0.42$, so the dominant trait shows in 0.49 + 0.42 = 0.91.

questions.onCorrect: AA and Aa together make 0.49 + 0.42 = 0.91, which is 1 minus the 0.09 of people who are aa.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the frequency of AA only. Aa people show the dominant trait as well.
That is the frequency of the allele A. The proportion of people showing the trait is a genotype frequency.
That is the frequency of Aa only. AA people show the dominant trait as well.

questions.prompt: Why are carriers counted as $2pq$ and not as $pq$?
hints: Think of the Punnett square and count the boxes that hold one A and one a.
The two middle boxes give the same genotype.

acceptedIdeas: The Aa pairing can arise two ways, A from the mother and a from the father or the reverse
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The Aa pairing can arise two ways, A from the mother and a from the father or the reverse

choices.label: Carriers have two copies of the rare allele, so the frequency $q$ is counted twice, once for each
The Aa pairing can arise two ways, A from the mother and a from the father or the reverse
The factor 2 corrects for the allele being rare, so it would drop out for a common allele

questions.onCorrect: The Aa genotype fills two of the four boxes of the square, each with chance $pq$, so its frequency is $2pq$.

misconceptions.feedback: A carrier has one copy of the rare allele. A person with two copies is affected, and that is the $q^2$ class.
The factor 2 comes from the two orders in which the alleles can pair. It is there for any allele frequency.

questions.prompt: Take the square root to find the allele frequency $q$.
hints: The incidence is $q^2$, so $q$ is the number whose square is the incidence.
A square root of 0.0001 is a number you can check by squaring it.
Try squaring your answer to see whether you get back to the incidence.
questions.onCorrect: The square root of 0.0001 is 0.01, so the allele frequency is 1 in 100.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the incidence, $q^2$. The allele frequency is its square root.
Check by squaring: 0.001 squared is 0.000001, not 0.0001.

questions.prompt: Work out the carrier frequency $2pq$ and say it as 1 in how many people.
hints: Multiply $2 \times 0.99 \times 0.01$.
Divide 1 by the result to say it as 1 in how many.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: $2pq = 2 \times 0.99 \times 0.01 = 0.0198$, and $1 \div 0.0198$ is about 50.5, so about 1 in 50.

questions.onCorrect: Carriers are 2 × 0.99 × 0.01 = 0.0198 of the population, about 1 in 50.

misconceptions.feedback: That is $1/q$, which counts the allele copies and leaves out the factor of 2 for the two ways of pairing.
That is the incidence of the condition, 1 in 10,000, which counts only people with two copies.

questions.prompt: In the sample of 320 people with 200 AA, 80 Aa and 40 aa, the allele frequency is $p = 0.75$, and Hardy-Weinberg proportions would give 180 AA, 120 Aa and 20 aa. What is the best reading of the observed counts?
hints: Compare the observed and expected count in each of the three classes.
Which classes are above their expected count, and which is below?

acceptedIdeas: Heterozygotes are 40 short and homozygotes are in excess, which fits inbreeding or pooling
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Heterozygotes are 40 short and homozygotes are in excess, which fits inbreeding or pooling

choices.label: The sample is in equilibrium, since the allele frequency comes out as a round figure of 0.75
There are too many heterozygotes, which would point to selection in their favour in this sample
Heterozygotes are 40 short and homozygotes are in excess, which fits inbreeding or pooling
The counts must have been miscounted, since a sample should match the formula almost exactly

questions.onCorrect: Heterozygotes are 40 below their expected 120 and both homozygote classes are above, which is the signature of non-random mating.

misconceptions.feedback: A round allele frequency says nothing about genotype proportions. The observed counts differ from the expected ones in every class.
The observed 80 is below the expected 120, so heterozygotes are in deficit, not in excess.
A sample need not match exactly, but errors are only one possible cause. The pattern, with too few heterozygotes, is what non-random mating produces.

questions.prompt: An invented X-linked recessive condition affects 1 in 20 men. What do Hardy-Weinberg proportions predict for women, as 1 in how many?
hints: For a gene on the X, the proportion of affected men is the allele frequency $q$.
A woman is affected only with two copies of the allele.
Square $q$ and say the result as 1 in how many.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: $q = 1/20 = 0.05$, so affected women are $q^2 = 0.0025$, which is 1 in 400.

questions.onCorrect: With $q = 1/20$, women are affected at $q^2 = 1/400$, far less often than men.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the figure for men. Women need two copies of the allele, so they are affected less often.
That doubles $q$ and does not square it. A woman is affected only if both her X chromosomes carry the allele.

questions.prompt: A recessive condition in an invented population affects 1 in 40,000 births. About how many people in the population carry one copy of the allele, as 1 in how many?
hints: The incidence is $q^2$, so find $q$ first.
The carrier frequency is $2pq$, and $p$ is $1 - q$.
Divide 1 by the carrier frequency to say it as 1 in how many.
questions.onCorrect: The square root gives $q = 0.005$, and carriers are $2pq \approx 0.00995$, about 1 in 100.

misconceptions.feedback: That is $1/q$, which leaves out the factor of 2 for the two ways the alleles can pair.
That is the incidence of affected people. Carriers are far more common.

questions.prompt: A sample of 300 people has 126 AA, 96 Aa and 78 aa. The allele frequency is $p = 0.58$, so Hardy-Weinberg proportions would give about 101 AA, 146 Aa and 53 aa. What does the sample suggest?
hints: Compare each observed count with its expected count and note the direction of each gap.
A deficit of heterozygotes with an excess of both homozygotes has well-known causes.

acceptedIdeas: There are too few heterozygotes, which fits non-random mating or pooled groups
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: There are too few heterozygotes, which fits non-random mating or pooled groups

choices.label: It is in Hardy-Weinberg proportions, since the two allele frequencies add up to 1
There are too many heterozygotes, which points to inbreeding in the population
There are too few heterozygotes, which fits non-random mating or pooled groups
Selection must be removing heterozygotes, since the homozygotes are in excess

questions.onCorrect: Heterozygotes number 96 against 146 expected, with both homozygote classes above expectation, which fits non-random mating or pooled groups.

misconceptions.feedback: The allele frequencies add up to 1 for any sample. The genotype counts are what differ from the expected ones.
The observed 96 is well below the expected 146, so there are too few heterozygotes. Inbreeding gives that deficit.
Selection can change proportions, but so can inbreeding and pooling. The counts alone do not say which, and they point first to non-random mating.

questions.prompt: A researcher finds that one gene in a large, randomly mating population fits Hardy-Weinberg proportions exactly. What can she conclude?
hints: The formula is a baseline for one gene in one population.
Check each option for a claim about other genes, or about what the proportions would show for an allele that harms health.

acceptedIdeas: That nothing acts on this gene strongly enough to shift the proportions
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That nothing acts on this gene strongly enough to shift the proportions

choices.label: That the population is not evolving at any of the genes in its genome
That the dominant allele will go on becoming more common over time
That nothing acts on this gene strongly enough to shift the proportions
That the allele has no effect on health, since it is not being selected

questions.onCorrect: Fitting the proportions for one gene says that no force is acting strongly enough to shift them for that gene, and it says nothing more than that.

misconceptions.feedback: Proportions for one gene say nothing about other genes, and they do not rule out forces too weak to show in one sample.
The formula shows that frequencies stay as they are, and dominance does not make an allele spread.
Proportions in a sample say nothing about effects on health. A harmful recessive allele can sit in proportions too.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is tossed four times. Which statement is correct?
hints: List the sequences of heads and tails, for example HHTT and HTHT. How many are there in all?
Count how many of those sequences hold exactly two heads.

acceptedIdeas: Getting some other number of heads is more likely than getting exactly two
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Getting some other number of heads is more likely than getting exactly two

choices.label: Exactly two heads is the most likely outcome, so it is more likely than all the others together
Getting some other number of heads is more likely than getting exactly two
Every number of heads from none to four is equally likely, since the coin is fair

questions.onCorrect: Of the 16 equally likely sequences, 6 hold exactly two heads and 10 do not, so some other count is more likely than two heads.

misconceptions.feedback: Two heads is the likeliest single count, but the other counts together are more likely. Two heads is 6 of the 16 equally likely sequences.
A fair coin makes every sequence equally likely, but some counts come from more sequences than others. One head can arise four ways and four heads only one.

questions.prompt: Two populations each begin with allele A at frequency 0.5, one of 40 individuals and one of 4,000, and neither is under selection. Which shows the larger random change in allele frequency in a generation?
hints: Think of the figure: which jar's lines wandered farther?
Averaging over more draws smooths out chance.

acceptedIdeas: The population of 40, since few copies of the gene make chance swings larger
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The population of 40, since few copies of the gene make chance swings larger

choices.label: The population of 4,000, since more individuals give chance more events to act on
The population of 40, since few copies of the gene make chance swings larger
Both equally, since drift does not depend on how many individuals there are
Neither, since a change in allele frequency means that selection is at work

questions.onCorrect: The magnitude of drift per generation is larger when allele copies are few, so the population of 40 shows the bigger random swing.

misconceptions.feedback: With more copies of the gene, the random ups and downs average out, so the frequency stays closer to where it started.
Drift does depend on size. The magnitude of the change in a generation is larger when allele copies are few.
Selection is not needed. A change by chance alone is exactly what drift is.

questions.prompt: A drop of a very large colony, in which neutral alleles A and B are equally common, shrinks until it can feed only three bacteria, and which three survive is random. Compared with the four survivors of the lesson, how likely is it that all three carry the same allele?
hints: Each survivor carries A or B with probability 1/2. What does each extra survivor add to the chances that both alleles appear?
With four survivors, two of the 16 combinations had every survivor alike. Would a smaller group have a larger or a smaller share like that?

acceptedIdeas: More likely, because fewer survivors give the other allele fewer chances to appear
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: More likely, because fewer survivors give the other allele fewer chances to appear

choices.label: Equally likely, because each survivor carries either allele with probability one half
Less likely, because a smaller group is easier to keep evenly mixed
More likely, because fewer survivors give the other allele fewer chances to appear

questions.onCorrect: With fewer survivors the other allele has fewer chances to turn up, so a group of three is more often all one allele than a group of four.

misconceptions.feedback: Each survivor is a fifty-fifty draw, but the chance that every survivor matches depends on how many survivors there are, and it rises as the group gets smaller.
A smaller group is less likely to hold both alleles, because each survivor is one more chance for the other allele to appear, and there are fewer survivors.

questions.prompt: In an invented case, a recessive disease allele has a frequency of 0.30 in an isolated colony founded by 12 people, and 0.01 on the mainland they came from. What is the best first explanation?
hints: How many copies of the gene could 12 founders carry, and what does a sample that small do to a rare allele?
Ask which explanation needs the fewest extra assumptions.

acceptedIdeas: A founder effect, as 12 founders are only a small random sample of the mainland
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A founder effect, as 12 founders are only a small random sample of the mainland

choices.label: Selection favours the allele on the island, since the allele is common there now
A founder effect, as 12 founders are only a small random sample of the mainland
A higher mutation rate on the island has made the allele common in the colony
The mainland measurement must be wrong, since both populations should match

questions.onCorrect: A small founding group is a random sample of the source's alleles, and it can leave a rare allele far more common without any extra assumption.

misconceptions.feedback: An allele that causes a disease needs evidence of some advantage before selection is proposed, and no such evidence is given.
Mutation changes frequencies very slowly, so it could not take an allele from 0.01 to 0.30 in the life of a colony.
Populations descended from one source can differ, and a small founding sample is a standard reason, so no error need be assumed.

questions.prompt: Heterozygote advantage is proposed to explain why an allele is common in a region with a certain infection. Which finding would count against the proposal?
hints: The proposal predicts that carriers do better against the infection. What result would contradict that prediction?
A finding that the proposal explains cannot also count against it.

acceptedIdeas: Carrier children in the region catch the infection as often as non-carriers
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carrier children in the region catch the infection as often as non-carriers

choices.label: The allele is common in the regions where the infection is also common today
Carrier children in the region catch the infection as often as non-carriers
The allele's frequency falls where the infection is treated effectively
Infected red cells of carriers are cleared from the blood quickly

questions.onCorrect: The proposal predicts carrier resistance, so carriers catching the infection as often and as severely as others contradicts it.

misconceptions.feedback: That pattern is what the proposal explains. It supports the idea and cannot test it.
A fall where the infection no longer acts is what the proposal predicts, so it supports the idea.
Quick clearing of infected cells would be a way for carriers to resist infection, so it supports the idea.

questions.prompt: An invented variant, v, is common among people on an island. Mice with one copy of the matching variant survive an infection better than mice with none, but a study of islanders finds that carriers and non-carriers are equally affected by the infection. What should you conclude about why v is common?
hints: What does a result in mice show about people, and what does a study of people show?
Ask whether the evidence rules out every selective explanation, or only the one that was tested.

acceptedIdeas: The mouse result does not show a human advantage, so selection against chance stays open
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The mouse result does not show a human advantage, so selection against chance stays open

choices.label: The infection explains it, since mice and humans share the gene in question
The mouse result does not show a human advantage, so selection against chance stays open
Drift alone must explain it, since the human study found no advantage for carriers
Carriers of v can have no effect on health, since islanders show no difference in this infection

questions.onCorrect: A mouse result does not establish a human advantage, and a null human result does not prove drift, so the question stays open.

misconceptions.feedback: A result in mice does not settle a question about people, and the human study found no advantage.
Missing evidence for one explanation does not prove another. Other advantages, or an earlier selection pressure, are still possible.
The study looked at one infection. Carriers could differ in other ways that it did not measure.

questions.prompt: Six bacteria survive, drawn at random from a very large colony in which neutral alleles A and B are equally common. A student says that three A and three B is the likeliest outcome, so the frequencies will most probably stay at one half. What is the best reply?
hints: How many of the equally likely combinations give three and three, and how many give something else?
Compare the even split with all the uneven splits taken together.

acceptedIdeas: Three and three is the likeliest split, yet uneven splits together are likelier, so a shift is expected
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Three and three is the likeliest split, yet uneven splits together are likelier, so a shift is expected

choices.label: Three and three is the likeliest split, yet uneven splits together are likelier, so a shift is expected
The student is right, since the likeliest outcome is the one that will most probably be seen
Frequencies cannot change, since neutral alleles have no effect on which bacteria survive
Every count of A from none to six is equally likely, since each survivor is chosen at random

questions.onCorrect: An even split is the single likeliest outcome and is still outweighed by the uneven ones, so chance alone usually shifts the frequencies and sometimes loses an allele.

misconceptions.feedback: A single outcome can be the likeliest and still be less likely than all the others together, and the uneven splits outnumber the even one.
Neutral alleles do not change who survives, but a small random sample of the colony need not match the colony. That is how chance alone changes frequencies.
The combinations are equally likely, but the counts are not, because many combinations give three A and few give none or six.

questions.prompt: In an invented case, a town was founded 200 years ago by 15 settlers. A recessive disorder allele has a frequency of 0.12 in the town and 0.005 in the region the settlers came from, and the disorder shortens life. Which evidence would best separate a founder effect from selection favouring carriers?
hints: Selection favouring carriers makes a prediction about carriers. What is it?
A founder effect predicts no advantage for carriers at all. What would you measure to tell the two apart?

acceptedIdeas: Whether carriers in the town leave more surviving children than non-carriers
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Whether carriers in the town leave more surviving children than non-carriers

choices.label: How many people in the town have the disorder at the present day
Whether carriers in the town leave more surviving children than non-carriers
Whether the allele is also found in the region that the settlers had come from
How large the town is today compared with the region the settlers left

questions.onCorrect: Selection favouring carriers predicts that carriers do better, so comparing the children that carriers and non-carriers leave is the evidence that discriminates.

misconceptions.feedback: The count of affected people follows from the allele frequency under either explanation, so it separates nothing.
That is already known, since the region has it at 0.005, and either explanation allows it.
Today's size says little about the 15 founders and does not distinguish chance from selection.

questions.prompt: In the 19th century over-hunting severely reduced the numbers of the northern elephant seal. Its genetic variation is now lower than that of the southern elephant seal, which was hunted much less. What is a sharp fall of this kind in a population's size called?
hints: The animals that survived were a small random sample of the population.
Think of the narrow neck of a bottle.

acceptedIdeas: bottleneck
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A population bottleneck: the survivors of a sharp fall in numbers carry only a random sample of the alleles.

questions.onCorrect: A sharp fall in numbers leaves a small random sample of the alleles, which is why the northern elephant seal shows less variation than the southern.

misconceptions.feedback: A founder effect is a small group splitting off to form a new population. Here the whole population shrank.
Drift is the chance change in allele frequency that follows. The event itself, a sharp fall in numbers, has a name of its own.

questions.prompt: Both reports say negative. Which woman's result gives the clearer answer about whether she carries a harmful change?
hints: Ask what each laboratory was looking for.
Think about what a test can say when the change it is hunting for is already known, and what it can say when it is not.

acceptedIdeas: The first woman's, because the laboratory knew exactly which change it was looking for
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The first woman's, because the laboratory knew exactly which change it was looking for

choices.label: The second woman's, because a test of whole genes covers every change that could matter
Both are equally clear, because a negative result means the same thing in every case
The first woman's, because the laboratory knew exactly which change it was looking for
