questions.onCorrect: A laboratory told which change to look for can say clearly that the change is absent. Without a known family variant, a negative result adds little to what the family history already shows.

misconceptions.feedback: Many tests cannot detect every change that can cause a disorder, so even a test of whole genes can miss a variant. With no known family variant, her negative result leaves her risk where her family history put it.
What a negative result is worth depends on what the laboratory was asked to find and on what is known in the family, so the same word carries different information in the two cases.

questions.prompt: Six patients are each offered a genetic test. Which kind of test suits each one best?
hints: Start by asking whether the variant or the gene is already known, and how many genes could explain the symptoms.
Two of the cases are about something other than the order of bases in a gene.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The brother's case is a targeted single variant test. The single gene case and the many-conditions case are a single gene test and a gene panel. The child with two negative tests needs exome or genome sequencing. The missing chromosome piece and the enzyme activity are chromosomal and biochemical tests.

items.label: A man whose brother has a known harmful variant wants to know whether he inherited it
items.explanation: The variant is already known, so the laboratory needs to look only for that change.

items.label: A doctor wants to confirm one suspected condition that many different variants of a single gene can cause
items.explanation: A single gene test reads the whole gene for any change in it.

items.label: A child's symptoms fit a wide array of conditions, each caused by variants in different genes
items.explanation: A panel reads several genes at once, which suits symptoms with many possible genetic causes.

items.label: A child has had a single gene test and a panel test, and both found nothing
items.explanation: When narrower tests have not given a diagnosis, the widest net is the next step.

items.label: A clinician suspects a condition caused by a missing piece of a chromosome
items.explanation: A chromosomal test finds large changes such as deleted segments, which a gene-by-gene reading does not target.

items.label: A clinician suspects an enzyme deficiency and wants to measure how active the enzyme is
items.explanation: A biochemical test studies the amount or activity of a protein, and does not read the DNA.

questions.onCorrect: The known variant needs only a targeted look, the wide net is kept for an unclear cause, and some questions are about whole chromosomes or about proteins.

questions.prompt: A woman's panel finds a BRCA2 variant of uncertain significance. Her mother and aunt both had ovarian cancer, and no harmful variant has been found in the family. A colleague suggests treating the result as a mild positive. What is the best reply?
hints: The source says what management of risk should rest on while the variant is unclassified.
Ask which of the four replies stays within what the evidence can support.

acceptedIdeas: Plan her care from her family history and other risk factors, since the variant remains unsettled
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Plan her care from her family history and other risk factors, since the variant remains unsettled

choices.label: Plan her care from her family history and other risk factors, since the variant remains unsettled
Treat it as harmful, because a variant that cannot be ruled out should be handled as pathogenic
Repeat the test on a second sample, because an uncertain result means the laboratory made an error
Set the result aside, because a variant of uncertain significance is the same as a negative result

extracts.text: Most often, as more data become available VUS are reclassified as being benign (do not increase cancer risk). Until a VUS is reclassified, whether as harmful or benign, management of cancer risk should be based on family history and other risk factors.
extracts.who: National Cancer Institute, BRCA fact sheet (US government, public domain)
extracts.kind: A fact sheet from a US government cancer institute

questions.onCorrect: The variant is neither harmful nor cleared, so her mother's and aunt's cancers stay the guide to her risk until research reclassifies it.

misconceptions.feedback: Most variants of uncertain significance are later reclassified as benign, so treating one as harmful goes beyond what the evidence shows.
A variant of uncertain significance is a real finding whose meaning is unknown, and repeating the same test cannot settle what the change does.
Until it is reclassified the variant is neither cleared nor confirmed, and her family history still counts when her risk is assessed.

questions.prompt: About 5% to 10% of people with a harmful BRCA2 change develop pancreatic cancer in their lifetime, against about 1.7% of the general population. Roughly how many times the general risk is the carrier range?
hints: Divide the lower end of the carrier range by 1.7, then the upper end.
Both results are single digits.

acceptedIdeas: Roughly 3 to 6 times
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Roughly 3 to 6 times

choices.label: Roughly 3 to 6 times
About 30 to 60 times
About 1.5 to 3 times

questions.onCorrect: Five and ten divided by 1.7 give about 2.9 and 5.9, so the carrier range is roughly 3 to 6 times the general risk.

misconceptions.feedback: That moves the decimal point one place. Five divided by 1.7 is nearly 3, and ten divided by 1.7 is nearly 6.
That is too low. Ten divided by 1.7 is nearly 6, and five divided by 1.7 is nearly 3.

questions.prompt: Of every 100 people with a harmful BRCA2 change, 5 to 10 are expected to develop pancreatic cancer in their lifetime. How many of the 100 are expected not to?
hints: Subtract the number who develop it from 100.
Subtract each end of the range in turn, and remember that the larger number lost gives the smaller number left.

acceptedIdeas: About 90 to 95
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 90 to 95

choices.label: About 5 to 10
About 90 to 95
About 98 to 99

questions.onCorrect: A hundred less 10 and 100 less 5 leave 90 to 95 carriers who are not expected to develop pancreatic cancer.

misconceptions.feedback: Those are the people who are expected to develop it. The question asks about the rest.
That takes away the general population's 1.7% instead of the carrier range of 5% to 10%.

questions.prompt: Which sentence states the pancreatic cancer risk of a BRCA2 carrier fairly?
hints: A fair sentence uses the ratio you found and the count you found.
Check each sentence for words that turn a risk into a certainty or that play a raised risk down.

acceptedIdeas: Carriers have several times the general risk, yet most are not expected to develop it
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Carriers have several times the general risk, yet most are not expected to develop it

choices.label: Carriers will develop pancreatic cancer, at several times the rate of everyone else
The absolute risk is low, so carrying the change makes little difference to a person's health
Carriers have several times the general risk, yet most are not expected to develop it

questions.onCorrect: The ratio says how much larger the risk is, and the count says how many carriers are affected. A fair statement keeps both.

misconceptions.feedback: The figures are 5% to 10%, so most carriers do not develop it. Saying carriers will develop it turns a risk into a certainty.
A risk several times the general figure is a real difference even when the count is small, so the ratio belongs in the statement too.

questions.prompt: A company's brochure says that its genetic test for a disease risk is run in a CLIA-certified laboratory, so a high-risk result can be trusted to predict disease. What does the certification cover?
hints: Match the phrase in the source, analytical validity, to one of the three questions in the lesson.
Ask which questions the source says the standards leave untouched.

acceptedIdeas: How accurately the laboratory detects the variant, with nothing said about whether it predicts disease
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: How accurately the laboratory detects the variant, with nothing said about whether it predicts disease

choices.label: The strength of the link between the variant and the disease, since the standards review the research behind each test
Whether the result would change care, since the standards require every approved test to be useful
How accurately the laboratory detects the variant, with nothing said about whether it predicts disease

extracts.text: By controlling the quality of laboratory practices, CLIA standards are designed to ensure the analytical validity of genetic tests. CLIA standards do not address the clinical validity or clinical utility of genetic tests.
extracts.who: MedlinePlus Genetics, "How can I be sure a genetic test is valid and useful?" (US National Library of Medicine, public domain)
extracts.kind: A health information page from a US government library

questions.onCorrect: The certificate speaks to accuracy of detection. Whether the variant predicts disease, and whether the result helps care, are separate questions.

misconceptions.feedback: The standards govern how a laboratory works. They do not examine the evidence that links a variant to a disease, which is the question of clinical validity.
Usefulness to care is clinical utility, which the standards also leave out. Test takers, health care providers and insurers are often the ones who judge it.

questions.prompt: A woman whose aunt had ovarian cancer buys a direct-to-consumer test, and her report says that no harmful variants in BRCA1 or BRCA2 were found. What can she fairly conclude?
hints: Recall what direct-to-consumer tests usually look at: whole genes, or selected variants?
A negative result is a statement about what the test examined.

acceptedIdeas: The test found none of the variants it checks, and a harmful change it does not check for is still possible
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The test found none of the variants it checks, and a harmful change it does not check for is still possible

choices.label: The test found none of the variants it checks, and a harmful change it does not check for is still possible
She carries no harmful change in either gene, so her aunt's cancer is no reason to see a clinician or a counsellor
The test must be wrong, because a family history of ovarian cancer should always produce a positive result

extracts.text: People should also be aware that because some DTC tests do not test for every harmful change in the two genes, it is possible that someone could have a harmful change in BRCA1 or BRCA2 that the DTC test doesn’t detect.
extracts.who: National Cancer Institute, BRCA fact sheet (US government, public domain)
extracts.kind: A fact sheet from a US government cancer institute

questions.onCorrect: A test that checks selected variants can say only that those variants were not found. It cannot clear the rest of the gene.

misconceptions.feedback: The test checked selected variants, so it cannot rule out the others, and her family history is still worth discussing with a clinician or a genetic counsellor.
A negative report does not show an error. The test may check only some variants, and a family history carries its own information whatever the report says.

questions.prompt: Among men in the general population, about 0.1% develop breast cancer by age 70, against 1.8% to 7.1% of men with a harmful BRCA2 change. Which sentence states the risk for a man with that change most fairly?
hints: Divide each end of the carrier range by 0.1 to see how much larger it is than the general figure.
Then read the carrier figures on their own, as a number out of 100.

acceptedIdeas: Far above the general rate, though fewer than 1 in 10 carriers is expected to develop it by 70
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Far above the general rate, though fewer than 1 in 10 carriers is expected to develop it by 70

choices.label: Low enough that carrying the change makes little real difference to a man's chance of breast cancer
Far above the general rate, though fewer than 1 in 10 carriers is expected to develop it by 70
High enough that a man with the change should expect to develop breast cancer before he is 70

questions.onCorrect: The ratio is roughly 18 to 71 times the general figure, and the highest carrier figure is still below 10 in 100, so both statements belong together.

misconceptions.feedback: The carrier range is roughly 18 to 71 times the general figure, so the change does make a large difference in relative terms.
The upper figure is 7.1 in 100, so most carriers do not develop it by 70. A raised risk is different from an expected outcome.

questions.prompt: A child has seizures with no known cause. Exome sequencing finds no variant that explains them. What does that negative result tell her doctors?
hints: Think about which parts of the genome an exome test reads.
A negative result describes what was examined.

acceptedIdeas: That no explanation turned up in the exons, and changes in the rest of the genome were not read
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That no explanation turned up in the exons, and changes in the rest of the genome were not read

choices.label: That the seizures have no genetic cause, since the exome holds every part of the genome that matters
That the sequencing failed, since a genetic cause would always be found within the exons
That no explanation turned up in the exons, and changes in the rest of the genome were not read

extracts.text: Because most known mutations that cause disease occur in exons, whole exome sequencing is thought to be an efficient method to identify possible disease-causing mutations. However, researchers have found that DNA variations outside the exons can affect gene activity and protein production and lead to genetic disorders--variations that whole exome sequencing would miss.
extracts.who: MedlinePlus Genetics, "What are whole exome sequencing and whole genome sequencing?" (US National Library of Medicine, public domain)
extracts.kind: A health information page from a US government library

questions.onCorrect: The exome covers the protein-coding parts of the genome. A negative result leaves open the changes outside them, which genome sequencing would read.

misconceptions.feedback: Exons are only about 1 percent of the genome, and changes outside them can alter gene activity and cause disorders that exome sequencing misses.
A negative exome can be a true finding about the exons. Most known disease-causing changes lie there, though not all of them do.

questions.prompt: Each description below is a weakness in a genetic test. Which of the three checks does each one fail?
hints: For each one, ask what is failing: reading the variant, the variant's link to disease, or what the result lets anyone do.
Analytical validity concerns the reading of the variant, clinical validity the link to disease, and clinical utility the use of the result.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The method that misses a variant fails analytical validity. The weakly studied variant and the variant common in healthy people fail clinical validity. The accurate, well-linked result that changes no decision fails clinical utility.

items.label: The laboratory's method sometimes reports a variant as absent when the sample carries it
items.explanation: The test is failing to show whether the variant is present.

items.label: The variant is read accurately, but few studies have linked it to the disease it is sold to predict
items.explanation: The weak link is between the variant and the disease.

items.label: The variant is read accurately and is found just as often in people without the disease
items.explanation: A variant that is as common in healthy people is poorly related to the disease.

items.label: The variant is read accurately and clearly linked to a disorder, but the result would change no decision about diagnosis, treatment, management or prevention
items.explanation: Detection and the link to disease are sound, and nothing follows from the result.

questions.onCorrect: Three questions can fail separately. Accurate reading, a real link to disease and a result that helps care are each needed for a test to be worth having.

questions.prompt: A scan compares one million SNPs between people with a disease and similar people without it. Suppose that none of the SNPs has any real link to the disease. Using the usual cut-off of $p < 0.05$, about how many SNPs would still look significant by chance?
hints: A result with p below 0.05 turns up in about 1 test in 20 when nothing real is going on.
Work out what 5 in 100 comes to for a million tests.

acceptedIdeas: About 50,000, since 5 in every 100 SNPs would pass by chance alone
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 50,000, since 5 in every 100 SNPs would pass by chance alone

choices.label: None, because none of the SNPs has any real link to the disease
About 50,000, since 5 in every 100 SNPs would pass by chance alone
About 500, since 0.05 percent of the SNPs would pass by chance alone

questions.onCorrect: Five percent of a million is 50,000, so a cut-off of 0.05 would flag tens of thousands of SNPs by chance alone.

misconceptions.feedback: A cut-off of 0.05 lets through about 1 result in 20 even when nothing real is there, and the scan makes a million tests.
A p-value of 0.05 is 5 chances in 100, which is 5 percent and not 0.05 percent.

questions.prompt: A second invented SNP has allele G in 450 cases and 300 controls, and allele A in 550 cases and 700 controls. What is the odds ratio for allele G, to one decimal place?
hints: Write A over B first, which is the cases' count of G over the controls' count of G.
Then write X over Y, the cases' count of A over the controls' count of A.
Divide the first ratio by the second.
questions.onCorrect: The ratio of the two ratios is 1.5 ÷ 0.786, which is about 1.9.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the first ratio, 450 over 300. The odds ratio divides it by the second ratio, 550 over 700.
That divides the second ratio into the first the wrong way round, or stops early. Put 450 over 300 on top and 550 over 700 underneath.

questions.prompt: An invented SNP has an odds ratio of about 1.9 for allele G. Which reading is right?
hints: Compare 1.9 with 1, the value that means no difference between cases and controls.
Recall the median odds ratio of the risk SNPs that scans have found.

acceptedIdeas: G is more common among the cases, with an effect larger than the typical one of 1.33
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: G is more common among the cases, with an effect larger than the typical one of 1.33

choices.label: G is more common among the cases, with an effect larger than the typical one of 1.33
G is less common among the cases, because an odds ratio above 1 points to protection
G causes the disease, because an odds ratio this far from 1 cannot arise through linkage

questions.onCorrect: A ratio above 1 means more of the cases carry the allele, and 1.9 is well above the median of about 1.33 for risk SNPs in scans.

misconceptions.feedback: An odds ratio above 1 means the allele is more frequent among the cases, which is the opposite of protection.
An odds ratio shows an association and does not show cause. A SNP can carry a high ratio because it travels with the variant that matters.

questions.prompt: A scan of one million SNPs reports a SNP with $p = 2 \times 10^{-6}$. What should a reader conclude?
hints: Multiply the p-value by the number of tests to see how many results this strong chance alone would give.
Compare that count with the 0.05 chance hits that the genome-wide threshold allows.

acceptedIdeas: That a scan this size would give about two results this strong by chance, so it falls short of the bar
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: That a scan this size would give about two results this strong by chance, so it falls short of the bar

choices.label: That it passes the usual cut-off of 0.05, so it is a confirmed association
That it is stronger evidence than a SNP at $5 \times 10^{-8}$, since its p-value is the larger of the two
That a scan this size would give about two results this strong by chance, so it falls short of the bar

questions.onCorrect: Two chance results are expected at that level in a million tests, so the SNP is the kind of result chance produces and does not clear the genome-wide bar.

misconceptions.feedback: A cut-off of 0.05 is the wrong bar for a scan of this size, because chance alone would pass about 50,000 SNPs at that level.
A smaller p-value is stronger evidence, and $5 \times 10^{-8}$ is far smaller than $2 \times 10^{-6}$.

questions.prompt: A different invented scan draws its threshold line at 7.3. Its three tallest stacks reach 12.6, 7.0 and 9.4. Which reading is the most careful?
hints: Compare the height of each stack with the line at 7.3.
Ask what a stack tells you about a region compared with what it tells you about one SNP.

acceptedIdeas: Two stacks clear the line, and each marks a region that may hold a causal variant
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Two stacks clear the line, and each marks a region that may hold a causal variant

choices.label: Two stacks clear the line, and each marks a region that may hold a causal variant
All three stacks are real, because each stands far above the scattered dots
Two stacks clear the line, and in each one the top SNP is the variant that causes the disease

questions.onCorrect: The stacks at 12.6 and 9.4 clear 7.3 and each points to a region. Fine-mapping is needed to find which variant in it has the effect.

misconceptions.feedback: The line is the bar and not the dots around a stack. A stack at 7.0 sits below 7.3, so it does not meet the genome-wide threshold.
A stack marks a region where nearby SNPs travel together, so its top SNP may only be tagging along with the variant that matters.

questions.prompt: A person's relative risk for condition P is 2, and the average lifetime risk is 10 in 100. About what is the person's lifetime risk?
hints: A relative risk of 2 means twice the average risk.
Multiply the average lifetime risk by 2.

acceptedIdeas: About 20 in 100 people
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 20 in 100 people

choices.label: About 20 in 100 people
About 12 in 100 people
About 5 in 100 people

questions.onCorrect: Twice 10 in 100 is 20 in 100.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 2 to the average. A relative risk of 2 multiplies the average by 2.
That halves the average. A relative risk above 1 raises the risk above the average.

questions.prompt: A person's relative risk for condition Q is 2, and the average lifetime risk is 0.5 in 100. About what is the person's lifetime risk?
hints: A relative risk of 2 means twice the average risk.
Multiply 0.5 in 100 by 2.

acceptedIdeas: About 1 in 100 people
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: About 1 in 100 people

choices.label: About 2.5 in 100 people
About 0.25 in 100 people
About 1 in 100 people

questions.onCorrect: Twice 0.5 in 100 is 1 in 100.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds 2 to the average. A relative risk of 2 multiplies the average by 2.
That halves the average. A relative risk above 1 raises the risk above the average.

questions.prompt: The same score doubles the relative risk of P, from 10 in 100 to 20 in 100, and of Q, from 0.5 in 100 to 1 in 100. How do the changes in absolute risk compare?
hints: Subtract the average from the doubled risk for each condition.
Compare the two differences as counts out of 100.

acceptedIdeas: The change is larger for P, about 10 more in 100 against half of one more for Q
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The change is larger for P, about 10 more in 100 against half of one more for Q

choices.label: They are the same for both, since the relative risk is 2 for each condition studied
The change is larger for P, about 10 more in 100 against half of one more for Q
The change is larger for Q, because doubling a rare risk is the bigger change

questions.onCorrect: The relative risk is the same for both, and the absolute change is about 10 in 100 for P and about 0.5 in 100 for Q.

misconceptions.feedback: The relative risk is the same, but a doubling applies to different baselines, so the absolute changes differ greatly.
Doubling a small risk changes it very little in absolute terms, and doubling a large one changes it a lot. Work out each change as a count out of 100 before comparing.

questions.prompt: Two people, aged 22 and 98, have the same high polygenic risk score for coronary heart disease. What is true of the two?
hints: The source says what a score does not provide.
Ask what extra information you would need to turn a rank into a chance over a stated period of life.

acceptedIdeas: They share the same standing among other people, yet their lifetime risks are different
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: They share the same standing among other people, yet their lifetime risks are different

choices.label: They share the same standing among other people, yet their lifetime risks are different
They have the same lifetime risk, because the score fixes a person's risk from birth
The older person certainly has the disease, because a high score means it has developed

extracts.text: A polygenic risk score tells you how a person’s risk compares to others with a different genetic constitution. However, polygenic scores do not provide a baseline or timeframe for the progression of a disease.
extracts.who: National Human Genome Research Institute, Polygenic Risk Scores (US government, public domain)
extracts.kind: A health information page from a US government research institute

questions.onCorrect: The score gives the same relative standing to both, and without a baseline and a timeframe it cannot give them the same lifetime risk.

misconceptions.feedback: The score ranks a person against others and has no baseline or timeframe, so it cannot fix the same lifetime risk for people at such different ages.
A score is a probability and not a diagnosis. It does not show that a disease has developed in anyone.

questions.prompt: A woman of non-European ancestry uploads her genotype data to a website that reports a high polygenic score for coronary artery disease. The score was built from a biobank whose participants were mostly of European ancestry. What is the fairest reading?
hints: The source gives a reason why scores perform better in one ancestry.
Ask whether the evidence supports full reliability, no value at all, or something between.

acceptedIdeas: The score may predict less well for her, because most of the data behind it came from European-ancestry people
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The score may predict less well for her, because most of the data behind it came from European-ancestry people

choices.label: The score is as reliable for her as for anyone, because the variants that matter are the same in every population
The score is worthless for her, because a variant studied in one ancestry can never apply to people of another
The score may predict less well for her, because most of the data behind it came from European-ancestry people

extracts.text: As of 2021, most available data have been primarily of populations with European ancestry, which is the reason why PGS generally perform better within this ancestry.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: The score reflects the data it was built from, so for someone from another ancestry it may be less accurate and should be read with that in mind.

misconceptions.feedback: Scores generally perform better in European ancestry because that is where most of the data came from, so equal reliability cannot be assumed.
Some causal variants are shared between ancestries, so the score may still carry some information, though it is likely to predict less well.

questions.prompt: In another invented scan, allele G appears 360 times among the cases and 240 times among the controls, and allele A appears 640 times among the cases and 760 times among the controls. What is the odds ratio for allele G, to one decimal place?
hints: Put the two G counts in the first ratio and the two A counts in the second.
The first ratio is 360 over 240, and the second is 640 over 760.
Divide the first ratio by the second.
questions.onCorrect: The ratios are 1.5 and 0.842, and 1.5 ÷ 0.842 is about 1.8.

misconceptions.feedback: That is only the cases to controls ratio for G. The odds ratio divides it by the same ratio for allele A.
That puts the ratios the wrong way round. The ratio for allele G goes on top.

questions.prompt: A critic says that a coronary disease score with an AUC of about 0.64 is useless, because it cannot diagnose most of the people who take it. Which reply fits the source?
hints: Separate predicting well for everyone from predicting well for a few people.
The source mentions people at the extremes of the score.

acceptedIdeas: A score that is weak across a whole population can still identify people at the extremes of risk
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A score that is weak across a whole population can still identify people at the extremes of risk

choices.label: An AUC of 0.64 is already strong prediction, so the critic has misread what the number means
A score that is weak across a whole population can still identify people at the extremes of risk
The critic is right, because a score that cannot diagnose has no value next to other information

extracts.text: However, even if a polygenic score might not make reliable diagnostic predictions across an entire population, it may still make very accurate predictions for outliers at extreme high or low risk.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: Average performance can be moderate while the extremes are informative. A score used alone still falls short of diagnosis.

misconceptions.feedback: A larger AUC means better prediction, and 0.64 from genetic information alone is well below the 0.80 reached once age and sex are added.
The source says a score can improve estimates when used with age, body mass index or smoking status, and can still be accurate for people at the extremes.

questions.prompt: A genome-wide scan has been published for a common disease. Which of these statements can the scan support on its own, and which can it not?
hints: Think about what a case-control comparison of allele frequencies can and cannot tell you.
Three of the statements go beyond association to cause, to a person's own chance, or to every population.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A scan can show a difference in allele frequency, a region worth searching and an odds ratio. It cannot show the causal variant in a region, one person's chance over a period, or that the result holds in every ancestry.

bins.label: A scan cannot show this by itself

items.label: An allele is more frequent among the cases than among similar controls in this study
items.explanation: Comparing allele frequencies in cases and controls is what a scan does.

items.label: A stretch of a chromosome is worth searching for variants that affect the disease
items.explanation: Associated SNPs mark regions of the genome that may influence risk.

items.label: An allele is linked to higher odds of being a case by a stated factor, as an odds ratio
items.explanation: The odds ratio is the effect size a scan reports for each SNP.

items.label: Which variant within an associated region is the one that causes the disease
items.explanation: The top SNP may only travel with the causal variant, so fine-mapping is needed.

items.label: How likely a particular person is to develop the disease in the next ten years
items.explanation: A scan gives associations. A risk over a period needs a baseline and a timeframe that it does not carry.

items.label: That the same association holds in people of every ancestry
items.explanation: Most data come from people of European ancestry, so a result may not carry over to other groups.

questions.onCorrect: A scan finds associations of a stated size in the people it studied. Cause, an individual's risk and other populations need further evidence.

questions.prompt: Cas9 cuts both strands inside the coding region of a gene, and the cell joins the ends back together. A few bases are lost or added at the join. What is the most likely effect on the protein?
hints: Recall what happens to the reading frame when bases are inserted or deleted in numbers that are not multiples of three.
Ask what the cell has available to repair the cut besides rejoining the ends.

acceptedIdeas: The reading frame is likely to shift, so the protein is often not functional
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The reading frame is likely to shift, so the protein is often not functional

choices.label: The cell restores the original sequence exactly, so the protein is unchanged
The missing bases are copied from the guide RNA, so the protein is repaired
The reading frame is likely to shift, so the protein is often not functional

questions.onCorrect: Random insertions or deletions at the join often shift the reading frame, and a frameshift usually leaves a protein that does not work.

misconceptions.feedback: Joining the ends does not copy the original sequence back. Bases that are lost or added at the join stay lost or added.
A guide RNA only finds the target. It is not a template for repair, and the cell does not read replacement bases from it.

questions.prompt: A researcher designs a guide whose 20 bases match her target gene exactly. The same sequence also matches a site on another chromosome at all but one base, and that site lies beside an NGG. What should she expect when cells are treated?
hints: Recall which part of the system picks out a site, and how common the PAM is.
Ask what a researcher should worry about when a second site closely resembles the target.

acceptedIdeas: Cas9 may cut the second site as well, which would be an off-target change in the cells
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Cas9 may cut the second site as well, which would be an off-target change in the cells

choices.label: Cas9 may cut the second site as well, which would be an off-target change in the cells
Cas9 cannot cut the second site, because a guide must match every base before it attaches
Cas9 cuts both sites equally, because the PAM is what chooses where the enzyme cuts

questions.onCorrect: A near match beside a PAM is a possible second cut site, and an unintended cut there is an off-target effect.

misconceptions.feedback: Off-target effects are changes at sites other than the intended one, and a site that nearly matches the guide is where they are a worry. A single mismatch cannot be assumed to prevent them.
The PAM is short and turns up every 8 to 12 base pairs, so it cannot choose between sites. The match with the guide does that.

questions.prompt: Six research goals are set. Which route would you choose for each one?
hints: Ask for each goal whether the exact result matters and whether a template is available.
A single-base change calls for the route that works on point mutations, and an exact chosen sequence calls for the route that needs a template.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Disabling a gene and stopping a gene from working go with end joining. Replacing a stretch of a gene and placing a new sequence at one site go with a repair template. The single A to G change and the C to T change with no template go with a base editor.

items.label: Disable a gene in a cell line, so that researchers can see what the cells do without it
items.explanation: Random insertions or deletions at the cut disrupt the gene, which is all a knockout needs.

items.label: Replace a stretch of a gene with a customised sequence
items.explanation: A template carrying the new sequence lets the cell copy it into the break.

items.label: Place a new sequence at one exact site in the genome
items.explanation: Only a supplied template places a chosen sequence at an exact site.

items.label: Change a single A to a G at one position in a coding sequence
items.explanation: An adenine base editor changes A to G directly, with no template.

items.label: Stop a gene working where the exact change at the cut does not matter
items.explanation: Any disruption will do, so the random outcomes of end joining are acceptable.

items.label: Change one C to a T when no repair template is available
items.explanation: A cytosine base editor changes C to T without a donor template.

questions.onCorrect: Random disruption is enough for a knockout, a chosen sequence needs a template, and a single-base change can be made directly by a base editor.

questions.prompt: A report on an edited embryo says that half of the cells sampled carry the intended change and half carry the original sequence. Which conclusion is justified?
hints: Ask whether every cell of the embryo has the same version of the gene.
Think about what a sample of a few cells can tell you about the rest.

acceptedIdeas: The cells of the embryo differ, so one sample cannot show how the whole embryo is edited
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The cells of the embryo differ, so one sample cannot show how the whole embryo is edited

choices.label: The embryo is fully edited, because the change is present in the cells that were checked
The cells of the embryo differ, so one sample cannot show how the whole embryo is edited
The edit failed, because a successful edit would be present in every cell of the embryo

questions.onCorrect: Cells of a mosaic carry different versions of the gene, so a sample describes only the cells in it.

misconceptions.feedback: Half the sampled cells still carry the original sequence, so the embryo is not uniformly edited.
The change is present in some cells, so the editing worked in part. The difficulty is that the individual is a mixture.

questions.prompt: Doctors edit a patient's blood stem cells to treat sickle-cell disease. Will her future children inherit the edit?
hints: Ask which cells have been edited and which cells a child's DNA comes from.
Blood stem cells are body cells, and a child develops from an egg and a sperm.

acceptedIdeas: No, because the cells that were edited are body cells and not eggs or sperm
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: No, because the cells that were edited are body cells and not eggs or sperm

choices.label: No, because the cells that were edited are body cells and not eggs or sperm
Yes, because every edit changes DNA, and children inherit their parents' DNA
Yes, because blood stem cells pass the edit to every new cell, including egg cells

questions.onCorrect: The edit is in body cells, so it stays in one person and is not passed on.

misconceptions.feedback: Only DNA in egg or sperm cells reaches a child. An edit in other cells stays in the tissues it was made in.
A change in body cells stays in those tissues and the cells descended from them. Only a change in egg or sperm cells, or in an embryo, could reach the next generation.

questions.prompt: A lab wants to restore a G at the one position where an invented patient's gene has an A, in cultured cells grown from her tissue, and has no repair template. Which route fits best?
hints: Ask whether the goal is to disrupt a gene or to make one chosen change.
Look for the route that works on a single base without a template.

acceptedIdeas: A base editor that changes the A to a G at that position directly, with no cut
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A base editor that changes the A to a G at that position directly, with no cut

choices.label: A cut followed by end joining, which leaves random insertions or deletions at the site
A base editor that changes the A to a G at that position directly, with no cut
A cut with a repair template that carries a whole new copy of the gene to put in place

questions.onCorrect: An adenine base editor changes A to G at one position and needs no donor template.

misconceptions.feedback: End joining disrupts a gene and gives no control over the result, so it cannot restore one chosen base.
A template can place a chosen sequence, but this lab has none, and the goal is a change to one base.

questions.prompt: After treating the cells, what should the lab check in the sequencing results?
hints: Recall what off-target effects are and where they are most likely to occur.
A successful edit at the target does not show that nothing else changed.

acceptedIdeas: The target position and also sites that resemble the guide, in case of off-target changes
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The target position and also sites that resemble the guide, in case of off-target changes

choices.label: The target position only, since a guide that matches it perfectly cannot act anywhere else
Only whether the cells survived, since survival shows that the genome is unchanged
The target position and also sites that resemble the guide, in case of off-target changes

questions.onCorrect: Changes at sites that resemble the guide are the off-target risk, so those sites are checked along with the target.

misconceptions.feedback: A guide can act at sites that resemble it, which is why off-target effects are a concern. A perfect match at the target does not rule them out.
Cells can survive with changes at other sites, so survival does not show that the genome is as intended.

questions.prompt: The lab later proposes making the same edit in a human embryo. What changes?
hints: Ask what happens to the edited cells as the embryo grows.
Recall why germline and embryo editing is treated as more controversial than editing body cells.

acceptedIdeas: The edit could be passed on, and that raises ethical concerns a body-cell edit does not
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The edit could be passed on, and that raises ethical concerns a body-cell edit does not

choices.label: The edit could be passed on, and that raises ethical concerns a body-cell edit does not
Nothing changes, because the edit is the same wherever it is made, whichever cells carry it
The edit could not be inherited, because only the cells that were treated would carry it

questions.onCorrect: An embryo edit could be inherited, and sources describe germline and embryo editing as raising ethical and safety concerns that editing body cells does not.

misconceptions.feedback: The cells that carry an edit decide whether it can be inherited, and an embryo edit raises concerns that editing body cells does not.
The cells that grow from an edited embryo carry the change, which is why an embryo edit could be passed on.

questions.prompt: A student reads Source A, a page with no date on it, and Source B, and decides that one of them must be wrong. What is the best way to handle the two?
hints: Look at what each source says about the present, and ask whether either gives a date.
Ask what could make two accurate sources disagree.

acceptedIdeas: Check when each was written, since 'currently' on an undated page may predate the approvals
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Check when each was written, since 'currently' on an undated page may predate the approvals

choices.label: Trust Source A, because a government health page outranks an encyclopedia article on the topic
Treat both as unreliable, because two sources that disagree cannot both be of any use
Check when each was written, since 'currently' on an undated page may predate the approvals

extracts.text: Currently, genome editing is used in cells and animal models in research labs to understand diseases. Scientists are still working to determine whether this approach is safe and effective for use in people.
extracts.who: MedlinePlus Genetics, "What are genome editing and CRISPR-Cas9?" (US National Library of Medicine, public domain)
extracts.kind: A health information page from a US government library

extracts.text: In November 2023, the United Kingdom's Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) became the first in the world to approve the use of the first drug based on CRISPR gene editing, Casgevy, to treat sickle-cell anemia and beta thalassemia.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: Both can be accurate for the time each was written. A sentence that begins 'Currently' is only as current as the page that carries it.

misconceptions.feedback: A page's authority does not make it current. A statement about the present can go out of date, and a later source may report events that an earlier page did not cover.
Two sources can both be right for the date on which each was written, so a disagreement is a reason to check dates before discarding either.

questions.prompt: A team cuts a gene with Cas9 to knock it out. Sequencing shows that different treated cells carry different small insertions and deletions at the cut. How should the team read this?
hints: Recall what the repair route that rejoins the ends leaves at the cut.
Ask whether the changes are at the intended site or at another one.

acceptedIdeas: As an expected result of end joining, which leaves random insertions or deletions
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: As an expected result of end joining, which leaves random insertions or deletions

choices.label: As an off-target effect, because the changes differ from one treated cell to another
As an expected result of end joining, which leaves random insertions or deletions
As mosaicism of an embryo, because the cells carry different versions of the gene

extracts.text: These end-joining pathways can often result in random deletions or insertions at the repair site, which may disrupt or alter gene functionality.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: End joining leaves varied insertions and deletions at the cut, which is the normal route to a knockout and not a fault in the edit.

misconceptions.feedback: Off-target effects are changes at other sites. These changes are at the intended cut, and their variety is how end joining behaves.
Mosaicism describes the cells of one individual carrying different versions of a gene. These are separate treated cells, repaired by a route that gives varied results.

questions.prompt: A team plans to carry the Cas9 gene into cells inside a small viral vector. Which pair of difficulties should it expect?
hints: Compare the size of the vector's capacity with the size of the Cas9 gene.
Cas9 comes from bacteria. Ask how cells may respond to a component of that kind.

acceptedIdeas: A small vector holds little and the Cas9 gene is large, and bacterial parts can provoke an immune response
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A small vector holds little and the Cas9 gene is large, and bacterial parts can provoke an immune response

choices.label: Viruses cannot enter human cells, so nothing can be delivered by them, and Cas9 is too small to matter
Cas9 cannot be made without a PAM site, and a guide RNA cannot be packaged together with the enzyme
A small vector holds little and the Cas9 gene is large, and bacterial parts can provoke an immune response

extracts.text: As the units of CRISPR system taken from bacteria, when they are transferred to host cells it produces an immune response against them. Physical, chemical, viral vectors are used as vehicles to deliver the complex into the host. Due to this many complications are arising such as cell damage that leads to cell death. In the case of viral vectors, the capacity of the virus is small and Cas9 protein is large.
extracts.kind: An encyclopedia article written by volunteer editors

questions.onCorrect: A small vector with a large gene is a capacity problem, and bacterial parts can set off an immune response.

misconceptions.feedback: Viral vectors are used to deliver editing components, and Cas9 is large, which is the opposite of small.
A PAM is a feature of the target DNA and not of how Cas9 is made, and a guide RNA can be delivered with Cas9.

questions.prompt: Six edits are described. For each one, can the change be passed on to the person's descendants?
hints: Ask for each edit whether the edited cells are egg or sperm cells, an embryo, or body cells.
Edits to body cells are limited to certain tissues.

acceptedIdeas: Every item in its group
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The dish cell line, the retina cells and the muscle cells stay in one person or are not part of a later generation. The egg cell, the sperm cell and the embryo could be passed on.

items.label: A cell line grown in a dish is edited to study one gene
items.explanation: The edited cells are not part of any future generation.

items.label: An egg cell is edited before it is fertilised
items.explanation: Changes to egg cells could be passed to future generations.

items.label: A sperm cell is edited before it fertilises an egg
items.explanation: Changes to sperm cells could be passed to future generations.

items.label: Cells in an adult's retina are edited to treat an eye disorder
items.explanation: Edits to body cells are limited to certain tissues and are not passed on.

items.label: A human embryo made by in vitro fertilisation is edited before it is implanted
items.explanation: Changes to an embryo's genes could be inherited.

items.label: Muscle cells of an adult are edited in a clinical trial
items.explanation: Muscle cells are body cells, so the edit stays in that person.

questions.onCorrect: Edits to egg or sperm cells and to embryos could be inherited, and edits to other cells stay in the person who received them.

questions.prompt: A bone-forming cell and a muscle cell of the same person have the same DNA sequence but make different proteins. What best explains the difference?
hints: Ask whether the two cells carry the same DNA sequence.
If the sequence is the same, ask what else could differ between the cells.

acceptedIdeas: Each cell turns on the genes it needs and leaves the remaining genes off
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Each cell turns on the genes it needs and leaves the remaining genes off

choices.label: Mutations in each cell type have removed the genes that it does not use
Each cell turns on the genes it needs and leaves the remaining genes off
Each cell type inherited a different set of genes from the fertilised egg

questions.onCorrect: The two cells share a DNA sequence and differ in which genes are active, and the marks described next are one way that difference is kept.

misconceptions.feedback: Nearly every cell has the same DNA, so the genes a cell does not use are still there. They are not switched on.
The fertilised egg passes the same DNA to every cell that grows from it. Cell types differ in which genes are active.

questions.prompt: For an invented imprinted gene, only the copy from the mother is active. A child inherits a harmful variant of this gene from her father and a normal copy from her mother. What do you expect?
hints: Ask which copy of an imprinted gene is switched on in the cell.
Then ask which parent supplied the harmful variant.

acceptedIdeas: She is unaffected by the variant, because her father's copy is not the active one
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: She is unaffected by the variant, because her father's copy is not the active one

choices.label: She is affected, because a harmful variant is present in every cell of her body
She is affected, because the father's copy overrides the mother's copy in every cell
She is unaffected by the variant, because her father's copy is not the active one

questions.onCorrect: Only the mother's copy is active, and that copy is normal, so the father's variant is not expressed.

misconceptions.feedback: Having a variant does not settle what a cell does with it. For an imprinted gene, which parent supplied the copy matters.
Imprinting concerns which parent's copy is active. It does not make one copy override the other.

questions.prompt: In the famine, the babies of the pregnant women carried germ cells that would later form the next generation. Who counts as directly exposed?
hints: Ask where a baby's germ cells are during the pregnancy.
A germ cell that is inside an exposed baby is in the same environment as the baby.

acceptedIdeas: The pregnant women, their babies and the germ cells inside those babies
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The pregnant women, their babies and the germ cells inside those babies

choices.label: Only the pregnant women, because they were the ones who went hungry
The pregnant women and their babies, but not the germ cells inside the babies
The pregnant women, their babies and the germ cells inside those babies

questions.onCorrect: A baby's germ cells are present before birth, so the exposure reaches the women, their babies and the babies' germ cells.

misconceptions.feedback: The babies were in the womb during the famine, so they were exposed as well.
Germ cells are present in a baby before birth, so they were in the womb during the famine too.

questions.prompt: The babies are F1 and their germ cells form F2. Which is the first generation with no direct exposure to the famine?
hints: Count from the women as F0.
Check whether the cells that formed each generation were in the womb during the famine.

acceptedIdeas: F3, the great-grandchildren of the women
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: F3, the great-grandchildren of the women

choices.label: F3, the great-grandchildren of the women
F2, the grandchildren of the pregnant women
F1, the children of the pregnant women

questions.onCorrect: F3 is formed from germ cells that were never in the womb during the famine, so it is the first generation free of direct exposure.

misconceptions.feedback: F2 grew from the germ cells that were exposed in the womb, so it is not free of exposure.
The babies were in the womb during the famine, so they were directly exposed.

questions.prompt: A raised risk of disease is reported in the grandchildren (F2) of women who were pregnant during the famine. What does that show?
hints: Recall which generations were directly exposed.

acceptedIdeas: It does not meet the criterion, because the grandchildren grew from germ cells exposed in the womb
